arxiv-2512-04279:
Simulators for self-driving cars know things the real world hides: lane geometry, infractions, time to collision. Turned into dense rewards, that privileged knowledge trains driving agents quickly, but the agents then chase the simulator's score instead of the objective. Feeza Khan Khanzada and Jaerock Kwon tackle that misalignment in a 2025 robotics preprint.

Their framework trains a DreamerV3-style teacher on the dense privileged reward. Then only the teacher's latent dynamics, not its actions or value estimates, are distilled into a student. The student learns its policy from scratch on sparse success-and-failure rewards, while its world model is regularised toward the teacher's. In CARLA lane-following and overtaking benchmarks, the students beat their dense-reward teachers and the sparse-from-scratch baselines. On unseen routes, success rose by about twenty-three percent over the teacher in lane following, and up to twenty-seven-fold in overtaking.
arxiv-2512-04479:
Arnav Gupta derives a rule that keeps crack positions honest in a fresh way of modeling how materials break. The inverse-deformation approach describes fracture by mapping the broken body back to its unbroken shape. Gupta studies the simplest case: a one-dimensional elastic bar pulled until it snaps, moving slowly throughout. His 2025 arXiv paper brings the second law of thermodynamics to bear on where cracks may sit.

Even with surface energy at the crack faces, a key derivative jumps at each face. The jump comes from a constraint that allows fracture while keeping matter's orientation intact. Gupta shows that shifting an open crack's reference spot would force entropy production below zero. The second law forbids that, so crack spots stay fixed in the reference body. Together with stability proofs for balanced states, the rule trims the space of allowed motions and tightens the theory.
arxiv-2512-04779:
Junjie Zheng, Chunbo Hao, Guobin Ma, and co-authors present a singing voice synthesizer that needs no hand-marked melody charts or phoneme timings. Singing synthesis usually demands exact alignment between lyrics and notes, drawn by hand at great cost. That burden blocks wider use. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a melody-driven framework on a Diffusion Transformer that can sing arbitrary lyrics along any reference melody it hears.

A dedicated module pulls the melody straight from reference audio. A teacher model guides that extractor during training, keeping its encoding robust. An implicit alignment mechanism steadies the match between words and tune without phoneme labels. The result is a system that learns from raw song pairs instead of costly annotation. Such freedom could let small studios and hobbyists turn lyrics into sung demos in voices and styles that annotation budgets once forbade.
arxiv-2512-05079:
Minghan Zhu, Zhiyi Wang, Qihang Sun, Maani Ghaffari, and Michael Posa work on a problem every robot hand faces: rebuilding the full shape of an object it can only partly see. Cameras miss whatever is hidden behind the object or other clutter, and a robot often cannot move for a better view. The authors combine two extra sources of information to fill in the unseen geometry.

First, generative models trained on common objects supply sensible guesses for the hidden parts. Second, contact — from video or from the robot's own touch — pins down sparse points on the true boundary. Their method steers the generation with those contact points, and short guidance paths turn out to matter. On synthetic and real data, the combined approach reconstructs occluded objects better than generation alone or contact-based fitting alone, a step toward robots that can grasp what they cannot fully see.
arxiv-2512-05279:
Eleonora Alei and nine co-authors plan how the Habitable Worlds Observatory should spend its first look at a new planet. The telescope will hunt Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars, and observing time is precious. A quick reconnaissance must say whether a faint dot is a promising Earth or a disappointing Neptune before deeper study begins. The coronagraph can image through colour bands at once; which combination extracts the most information on the first visit is the question.

The authors present an algorithm that picks band combinations by hunting degeneracies among orbit, brightness, and noise, then chooses bands to break them. Testing an Earth against cold and warm Neptunes of similar brightness, they find a basic two-band setup barely separates Earth from a cold Neptune. A three-band setup at higher signal quality cleanly tells Earth from either. The results feed into the mission's design requirements.
arxiv-2512-05379:
Taslim Mahbub and Shi Feng investigate a bias in language-model judges: they prefer their own answers. Model judges are now widely used to grade model outputs, and self-preference corrupts those grades. The bias is stubborn because strong judge models can recognize their own writing even when candidates carry no labels. The authors test whether disguising authorship — small black-box perturbations to the candidate answers — can break the recognition and the preference with it.

Perturbations as simple as swapping a few words for synonyms predictably reduce self-preference. But the deeper result is discouraging: when the perturbations are extrapolated toward fully neutralizing stylistic differences, the preference comes back. Self-recognition apparently operates at many semantic levels, not just surface style. The paper maps both the promise and the limit of obfuscation as a cure, warning evaluator designers that this bias has deeper roots than wording.
arxiv-2512-05779:
Kristóf Huszár and Clément Maria study how to represent three dimensional spaces sparsely, so that algorithms can work with them efficiently. Such spaces are usually given as triangulations: tetrahedra glued face to face. The key measure is treewidth of the dual graph, which says how tree-like the gluing pattern is. Their 2025 paper gives procedures that reshape a triangulation while keeping that sparsity under control.

First, they revisit a classic linear time conversion from a triangulation to a Heegaard diagram and prove it preserves treewidth. With that bridge, computing Kuperberg's quantum invariants of 3-manifolds becomes fixed parameter tractable. Second, a near linear time algorithm retriangulates so that no edge is shared by more than nine tetrahedra, while treewidth grows only moderately. Chained together, the two give Heegaard diagrams where each curve meets at most nine others. These guarantees turn invariants from theory into runnable code.
arxiv-2512-06179:
Shilin Hu and four co-authors split a problem vision systems have lumped together: shadows come in two kinds. Cast shadows fall on other surfaces; attached shadows are an object's own dark side. Most detectors output one mask or ignore attached shadows entirely. Physics grounds the joint detection.

The architecture is a feedback loop with two modules. Light and shadow modules refine each other in passes. A new dataset holds nearly fifteen hundred hand annotated images. Attached shadow error fell by a third. The reciprocity of light and shadow moves detectors toward physical inference.
arxiv-2512-07079:
Anton Morgunov and Victor S Batista argue that computer-aided synthesis planning cannot improve until its grading is fixed. Programs that propose routes to build molecules are judged by inconsistent setups, and by scores that reward finishing a route on paper over chemical soundness. Their framework, RetroCast, translates the varied outputs of rival systems into one shared schema, so comparisons become apples-to-apples, with stratified sampling and bootstrapped confidence intervals for rigor.

An interactive companion, SynthArena, lets chemists inspect proposed routes by eye. Running leading search-based and sequence-based planners through the new benchmarks exposes a split: high solvability. Meaning routes that end at stock chemicals, often hides invalid chemistry and matches laboratory ground truths poorly. Search-based methods also hit a complexity cliff, their performance decaying sharply on long-range plans where sequence-based methods hold up better.
arxiv-2512-07279:
Shreyas Jayant Grampurohit, Satish Mulleti, and Ajit Rajwade solve pooled testing with a neural network that can show its work. In quantitative group testing, many items are tested in a few pooled batches, each reporting how many defectives it contains, and the task is to name the defective few. Their multi-layer network reads the noisy counts and outputs which items are defective, recovering them accurately even when the measurements are perturbed within known bounds.

The deeper result concerns trust. The trained network turns out to have internalized the pooling design itself, the very table of which items went into which test. That structure can be read back out of the network's Jacobian, the matrix of its sensitivities. So the model is not reciting memorized patterns; it has learned the true combinatorial wiring of the problem.
arxiv-2512-07479:
Michael Heins wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a class of functions on Lie groups. A Lie group blends smooth geometry with group algebra, like rotations in space. Each such group carries a set of well-behaved analytic maps called entire functions.

Entire functions were first introduced to serve strict deformation quantization. Heins proves they match, one for one, with a second class of maps. Those maps are holomorphic functions on the group's universal complexification, its complex twin. The match respects the algebra structure on both sides, in the Fréchet sense. His method carries ideas from classical complex analysis into a left-invariant form. It also leans on the geometry of the complexified group itself. As a byproduct, he obtains a strict deformation quantization of a bundle. That bundle is the holomorphic cotangent bundle of any such complexification. The result ties function theory on groups to quantum deformation methods.
arxiv-2512-07779:
Matthew Sheinman and eleven co-authors wrote this 2025 optics paper on a delicate imaging method. Pump-probe microscopy reveals structure and chemistry in samples without labels. Its signals are tiny and usually swim in a large background glow.

 The authors enhance the signal while dodging saturation altogether. Their trick splits the light into reference and probe pulses, sheared in time. One pulse crosses the sample before the pump arrives, one after. The pair then recombine with opposing phases and nearly matched strengths. Background cancels in that interferometric subtraction, while the signal survives. A novel common-path interferometer performs the recombination step. Unlike earlier shearing designs, it adds almost no dispersion with viewing angle. That property is what makes convenient widefield imaging possible here. Tests on gold nanorod films show the payoff. Signal-to-background and signal-to-noise both improve by large margins.
arxiv-2512-08279:
Mingrui Jing, Mengbo Guo, Lin Zhu, Hongshun Yao, and Xin Wang, quantum information researchers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is programming open quantum systems, the noisy devices where quantum states leak into their surroundings. Programmability means running a whole family of transformations on one fixed processor, chosen by program states. That idea is well developed for closed systems, but not for open ones.

The team builds a framework that measures how programmable a Lindbladian evolution is. It combines retrieval maps a lab can implement with program states that vary in time. Symmetry and random structure create programmable classes, including covariant evolutions and some fully dissipative Pauli models. A necessary condition rules out many natural cases, such as amplitude damping, though explicit protocols still handle them with finite resources. They also define a programming cost, counted in samples, and prove its basic properties.
arxiv-2512-08379:
Kaiwei Liu, Yuting He, Bufang Yang, and colleagues, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their framework, DeepFeature, generates features from wearable biosignals for health applications. Machine learning on such signals leans on hand built features. Automatic methods miss task context, face a huge space of feature combinations, and often produce code that breaks.

DeepFeature uses a large language model guided by expert knowledge and by how features interact with each other. It refines features in rounds, scoring each set and reselecting based on feedback. A layered filter and verification chain turns feature descriptions into code that runs without crashing. Across eight tasks, it earned the best average detection scores under both testing styles, with the largest gains on blood pressure estimation from pulse signals.
arxiv-2512-08579:
Silvia Properzi and Yufei Qin study L algebras, an abstract algebraic system, with a focus on ideals and on the simplest cases. An ideal is a special subset that helps reveal the structure of the whole algebra. The authors look closely at ideals inside semidirect products, a standard way to build new algebras from old ones.

They give an exact description of those ideals and of the prime spectrum that goes with them. They also build a family of simple L algebras that are finite, and prove each simple linear one lies in that family. That family matches the simple cases in a known subclass of finite algebras. As a use, the results yield a clear picture of linear Hilbert algebras and their symmetric semidirect products.
arxiv-2512-08779:
Emre Havazli and coauthors study how well radar interferometry can measure ground movement when the signal is weak. The technique, called InSAR, tracks surface deformation with high precision. In places with low backscatter, low signal to noise can reduce coherence and hurt the accuracy of displacement estimates.

Using airborne radar data over the San Andreas Fault and the Greenland ice sheet, the team simulates weaker systems by raising the noise floor. They trace effects on coherence, phase unwrapping, and time series results. With enough averaging, millimeter level accuracy in a single image pair is still reachable. Yearly velocity precision also stays close to high signal systems, at the cost of spatial detail. An averaging window greatly improves coherence and removes bias. The findings guide design of cheaper future radar missions and processing in hard environments.
arxiv-2512-08979:
Daechul Ahn and coauthors study whether video multimodal models truly understand the temporal order of events. Such models score impressively on video tasks, yet the authors find a troubling pattern. Even when frames are scrambled, models still perform very well on existing benchmarks, suggesting they rely on prior knowledge of typical scenes rather than on the actual sequence.

To test temporal understanding directly, they propose a benchmark called VECTOR that asks models to identify the order of events. Leading models often fail on that test. Their remedy, MECOT, trains models on detailed event by event video descriptions and uses chain of thought prompts at inference to raise temporal awareness. The method beats prior work on the new benchmark and also improves scores on existing video benchmarks. Code, model, and data sets are released. The work shows that temporal skill can be taught, not just assumed from general video performance.
arxiv-2512-09379:
Lukas Kretschmann reports measurements from the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider on how single top quarks are produced. Top quarks are the heaviest known elementary particles, and one production route, the t-channel, creates a single top quark or antiquark in proton-proton collisions. Precise measurements of this process test the Standard Model of particle physics.

The analysis uses the full Run 2 ATLAS dataset from collisions at thirteen tera-electronvolts. It measures differential cross-sections, showing how production rates vary with the top quark's momentum and direction, separately for quarks and antiquarks. For the first time, it also presents the ratio of the two rates. Results are compared with fixed-order theory calculations, several event generators, and different models of the proton's internal structure. Finally, the data are interpreted within an effective field theory to limit the strength of a possible new four-fermion interaction.
arxiv-2512-09579:
Dimitrios N. Vlachogiannis and Dimitrios A. Koutsomitropoulos run a hands-on test of vision transformers against convolutional neural networks for spotting objects. Convolutional networks, the standard for computer vision, read images mainly through local patterns. Vision transformers, adapted from language models, use attention to relate every part of an image to every other, capturing global context that convolutions can miss.

They test pure, hierarchical, and hybrid transformer designs against convolutional models on image classification with ImageNet, object detection with COCO, and medical image classification with the ChestX-ray14 dataset. Hybrid and hierarchical transformers, most of all the Swin and CvT designs, offered the strongest balance of accuracy against computing cost. Experiments with data augmentation on the medical images brought gains, most for the Swin model. The authors find transformers competitive with, and often better than, convolutional networks, where global context matters most, as in medical imaging.
arxiv-2512-09679:
Naizhu Jin and colleagues conduct an empirical and information-theoretic study of chain-of-thought prompting in code generation. They ask not just whether making a language model reason step by step helps, but why. Models generate code well, yet why chain-of-thought helps was unclear, and practitioners had guidance on which style to use.

They compare five paradigms, from zero-shot and zero-shot chain-of-thought to self-planning, structured chain-of-thought, and reflective reasoning variants. The testbed spans six Python benchmarks, a benchmark across twelve programming languages, and six models ranging in size, using conditional mutual information as their lens. Externally guided reasoning beat generation, and structured methods raised pass rates while using fewer tokens than reflective reasoning. Benefits depended on the language's type system and the model's capacity, and reasoning quality mattered: structured reasoning helped, while naive zero-shot chain-of-thought could hurt.
arxiv-2512-10179:
A team led by Abolfazl Shahrooei tests whether a spiking neural network can decode fingertip force from muscle signals, as a brain style alternative to standard deep learning. High density surface electromyography reads the forearm's electrical activity through the skin, offering a noninvasive interface for assistive and rehab devices. The hard part is mapping that activity to what the user intends. The team split the signals into motor unit firing, the activity of single muscle fibers' control units, from recordings of a single participant wearing two forearm electrode arrays. Two decoders competed.

A temporal convolutional network was the more accurate decoder, tracking force with high correlation and low error. The spiking network trailed, with noticeably larger error, though its correlation with true force remained strong. The authors frame the spiking model as a realistic baseline, not a finished product: modest design and tuning improvements could close much of the gap.
arxiv-2512-10379:
Alberto Rota and Elena De Momi work on a hard vision problem inside the body: matching the same points across frames from an endoscope during surgery. Their 2025 paper explains why this matters, since surgeons rely on camera images alone. And matched points feed three-dimensional rebuilding, camera tracking, and scene awareness.

Their method trains itself without hand-labelled matches. A novel-view synthesis step creates trusted point pairs, which are then used to mine examples for contrastive learning. The team adds a transformer layer to the DINOv2 vision model so its features can be matched directly by similarity. On the SCARED surgical datasets, their pipeline matched points more precisely, with lower error, than leading earlier methods.
arxiv-2512-10579:
Manuele Maistrello, Romain Maccary, and Cristiano Guidorzi speed up MEPSA, an algorithm that hunts for peaks in evenly sampled time series buried in Gaussian noise. It was built for gamma-ray burst light curves, scans data with a fixed set of patterns at many timescales. And works well, but its cost balloons when data are rebinned at large factors.

FAST-MEPSA scans with a sparser offset strategy. It also adds one extra pattern, the fortieth. That pattern is shaped to catch faint peaks below threshold on the rising edge of broader structures. The original set often missed that class. On simulated burst light curves it ran hundreds of times faster at high rebinning, lost only a few percent of detections, and cut false alarms at low significance. Adding the new pattern recovered more of the faintest events, and the code is public.
arxiv-2512-10679:
Ambra Mariani and a large team built a cryogenic alarm that tags cosmic muons sneaking into superconducting quantum processors. Ionising radiation can burst quasiparticles through such a chip and cause correlated errors that threaten fault-tolerant computing. Muons are the worst offenders: energetic, deeply penetrating, and immune to ordinary shielding, so the practical defence is to notice them as they pass.

Their module stacks two kinetic inductance detectors and runs at about twenty millikelvin, cold enough to live beside a quantum chip. Geant4 simulations guided the design and set expectations for tagging efficiency and false coincidences from ambient gamma rays. In first operation, the measured muon coincidence rate between the two detectors matched the simulation closely. Tagging efficiency ran around ninety percent, with negligible dead time. This is a step toward veto systems built into multi-qubit machines.
arxiv-2512-10779:
Nachiappan Valliappan builds type theories for a neglected corner of modal logic. Intuitionistic modal logics add box and diamond operators to constructive logic, and their programming language counterparts, typed lambda calculi with modalities, support useful strong functors in functional programming. Diamonds, though, were long viewed as peculiar and unstable, so calculi with boxes raced ahead while diamond theories lagged.

Valliappan develops a family of typed lambda calculi matching sublogics of Lax logic, an intuitionistic modal logic with diamonds that earned the peculiar reputation. For each calculus he gives possible-world and categorical semantics, and constructively proves normalisation, equational completeness, and proof-theoretic inadmissibility results, the package that shows a logic and its programs behave. The main results are formalised in the Agda proof assistant, so the theorems are machine-checked. The article is set to appear at CSL 2026.
arxiv-2512-10979:
Sima Attar-Khorasani and co-authors review live migration, the technique that moves a running program or virtual machine to another host without stopping it. Users stay connected while the work shifts, which matters for cloud centres and busy services. Earlier reviews, the authors argue, missed key technical details and real world difficulties.

Their survey compares migration methods, what kinds of units can be moved, and the infrastructure each method needs. Container based and virtual machine based approaches receive the most attention, including why adoption differs between them. The review also weighs migration goals and operating limits, notes cases where costs outweigh benefits, and sets out guidelines for future research and practical deployment.
arxiv-2512-11179:
Wei Duan, Jie Lu, En Yu, and Junyu Xuan study how teams of learning agents can communicate when their message channels are severely limited. In graph based multi agent reinforcement learning, agents are nodes and links decide who talks to whom. Recent work optimises that wiring, but not what the messages themselves should contain when bandwidth is hard capped.

Simple shrinking of messages consistently hurt coordination in their tests. Their module, BVME, treats each message as a sample from a learned distribution and penalises how far that distribution strays from an uninformative one. That gives a principled dial for compression strength. Across three standard game benchmarks, the method matched or beat rivals while using far fewer message dimensions, with the biggest gains on sparse networks. Tests also showed performance dips at both extremes of the bandwidth dial.
arxiv-2512-11379:
Bettina Eick, Patali Komma, and Subhrajyoti Saha introduce a new tool for classifying a notoriously hard family of groups in algebra. The groups are p-groups of maximal class, finite groups built from a prime power with a particularly tight structure. A graph that links these groups together has long served as the main map for their classification, but it is vast.

The authors carve out a smaller subgraph, called the frame, using the Lazard correspondence that translates between groups and algebraic structures called Lie rings. They prove every maximal class p-group has a small normal subgroup, of order at most the prime itself, whose quotient lands inside the frame. Since the frame sits close to the full graph, little is lost by working there. Classification efforts can now focus on the frame and lift results back, a potentially major simplification.
arxiv-2512-12079:
Angiolo Huaman, Luis Enrique Rosas-Hernandez, and Salvador Barraza-Lopez compute the second order optical response of bulk materials with an old tool revived: atom centered orbitals. That response governs frequency doubling, where a material turns light into its double frequency twin, used in lasers, metrology, and quantum tech.

Early calculations used non orthogonal Gaussian orbitals; plane wave codes later took over, and Wannier based tools recently revived local bases. The new method uses numeric pseudoatomic orbitals with perturbation theory in the velocity gauge. Its edge is a symmetry guided way to get momentum integrals between orbital pairs. Tests on silicon carbide and gallium arsenide succeed, with linear responses reported alongside.
arxiv-2512-12579:
Malinda Iluppangama, Dilmi Abeywardana, and Chris Tsokos analyze survival outcomes after deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease in a 2025 paper. Parkinson's is a brain disorder that gets worse over time and harms movement and daily life. Deep brain stimulation, an implanted device that sends pulses to the brain, has improved motor symptoms and quality of life for many patients.

Using three families of survival methods on real data, they compare long term outcomes by sex. Female patients showed higher survival than male patients, with survival times following a lognormal distribution for women and a Weibull for men. A Cox model found side of first implant and a combined effect of revision count and implant size also mattered.
arxiv-2512-12879:
Romana Mikusincova and a large team report X-ray polarization measures of Cygnus X-3, a hidden system that shines very brightly in X-rays. They used data from the IXPE space telescope gathered in 2023, while the source was in its hard state. Polarization tells how X-ray waves line up.

They found a polarization degree of 21.2 percent, plus or minus 0.4 percent. The angle was 92.2 degrees, plus or minus 0.5 degrees. Both values match the first hard-state measure from 2022 well. That match suggests the shape of the inflow and the way the X-rays are made stayed very stable over about a year.
arxiv-2512-13079:
Daniel Rivas and co-authors use ultrafast X-ray spectroscopy to watch a molecule break apart in real time. The usual form of this method links electron binding energies to the local chemical setting, but only for systems at rest. Fast changes and crowded signals made the extension hard.

Working with fluoromethane, the team probed several atomic sites at once with a narrowband femtosecond X-ray pulse. They could follow the breaking of both carbon-fluorine and carbon-hydrogen bonds, even though the signals sit close in energy. A simple partial charges model described the motion well, backed by calculations and data.
arxiv-2512-13279:
Jinrui Liu and co-authors present AIR, a method for choosing post-training data that best teaches reasoning to language models. Distilling reasoning skill depends heavily on which examples are picked. Common pickers use length, entropy, or overall loss, none of which capture how much single reasoning steps matter.

AIR finds the attention heads most critical for reasoning, weakens them to build a reference model, and scores data by how much the loss rises. The score works at both step and sample level. Across several reasoning benchmarks, AIR improved accuracy over heuristic pickers, isolating the steps and samples that carry the most value.
arxiv-2512-13379:
Georgios Doultsinos, Antonis Delakouras, and David Petrosyan derive a fundamental error bound for creating entangled states of two Rydberg atoms. Entanglement generation is a building block for quantum computing with neutral atoms. Two error sources cannot be removed: the Rydberg states decay, and their interaction strength is finite.

Their bound states the minimum error as a simple formula set by the decay rate and interaction strength. No pulse shaping can beat it, assuming all technical errors vanish. Using quantum optimal control, they then design laser pulses whose error sits only 1 percent above that bound. The result gives experimenters a clear target for how good a Rydberg gate can get.
arxiv-2512-13479:
Kunal Pai and co-authors describe improvements to gem5, the open-source computer architecture simulator, and its Resources repository, aimed at reproducible research. Architecture studies need disk images, kernels, and benchmarks that line up exactly. In practice, custom images are slow to build, and running many workloads needs brittle external scripts.

Their updates standardize image creation across x86, ARM, and RISC-V with validated base images. They add 12 disk images, 6 kernels, and over 200 workloads across three instruction sets. A redesigned exit event system, hypercalls, remote monitoring, and built-in parallel suites replace ad hoc scripting, making full-system experiments easier to repeat.
arxiv-2512-13579:
Mathias Hilfiker and co-authors use machine learning to improve hydration free energy estimates in chemistry. Such estimates depend on partial charges set for each atom, and weak charges hurt accuracy. They link the poor results of AM1-BCC charges on polar species to errors in hydration energy.

Their XGBoost model predicts charges that match high-grade density functional theory, using atomic traits as inputs. They add a Boltzmann Percentile method, based on a 1 ns gas-phase run, to pick charges that fit a molecule's full shape range. On a FreeSolv subset, error fell to 1.69 kcal/mol, versus 3.05 kcal/mol with AM1-BCC charges. Ranking of compounds also improved a lot.
arxiv-2512-13879:
Ishan Banerjee and co-authors study the stable cohomology of universal character varieties. A character variety parametrizes local systems on a curve, and the universal version sits over the moduli space of curves. Their fiber over each curve is the space of PGL_n local systems on it.

Using nonabelian Hodge theory and Saito's mixed Hodge modules, they show the Leray-Serre spectral sequence for the projection degenerates at the E2 page. As a result, the rational cohomology stabilizes as the genus grows, and they compute the stable limit. Similar results hold for punctured curves with fixed monodromy, for GL_n and SL_n. An appendix by Anne Larsen and Mirko Mauri covers singular cases through intersection cohomology.
arxiv-2512-13979:
Ge Yan and co-authors study how self-reflection works inside large reasoning models, and how to control it. Long chains of thought give strong results, and reviewing earlier steps is seen as a key part of that success. Reflection also costs many tokens, and its inner mechanism was underexplored.

They find a reflection direction in the model's latent space that separates reflection steps from other steps. Activity along it strongly predicts answer correctness, suggesting reflection tracks the model's own uncertainty. Their ReflCtrl method steers only at the start of each reasoning step. It cut total reasoning tokens by up to 43.2% while keeping accuracy, beating steer-at-every-token methods at matched budgets.
arxiv-2512-14779:
Kornelius Raeth and Nicole Ludwig ask a plain question: does the weather forecast with the best usual scores also lead to the best choices? Standard tests grade forecasts by how close they land to what was later seen. Yet people use forecasts to decide, so the authors grade forecasts by how much they improve the choices made from them.

Their tool, called decision calibration, checks forecast quality at the level of the choice itself. They compare a machine learning model with a classic weather model across several tasks that depend on weather. Scores at the forecast level did not predict scores at the choice level, and rankings even flipped between similar tasks. The lesson is that picking a model for real use needs tests built around the choice at hand.
arxiv-2512-14879:
Jingwei Chen tackles a failure mode of AI systems that learn from their own output. Training a model on data it made itself can end in model collapse: text turns repetitive, image models drop whole modes, and game agents over exploit one trick. Fixes exist, but no single rule explained both the failure and why the fixes work.

Chen's framework, called Entropy Reservoir Bregman Projection, views the loop as repeated projections in the space of distributions. Without input from outside, noise shrinks the support step by step and entropy decays until collapse. Mixing in a reservoir of high entropy data adds a steady entropy flow that can hold the system stable. The theory gives conditions for collapse and for safety, plus rates that depend on sample size. Tests on language models, a control agent, and GANs match the predictions.
arxiv-2512-15179:
Xiaoqi Li and four coauthors hunt bad practices in Ethereum smart contracts, the flaws that are not quite security holes. Poorly written contracts may not break at once, but they raise the risk of trouble later. The team presents the first systematic study of these practices, covering more than 47 specific issues.

Their framework, SCALM, pairs code analysis with language model reasoning. A hybrid design slices functions with context in mind, then matches patterns semantically with help from an extensible knowledge base. A multi layer verification step ties low level code patterns to high level security principles across syntax, design, and architecture. In wide experiments with several language models and datasets, SCALM beat existing tools at spotting bad practices. The work aims to raise the standard of contract writing as Ethereum matures.
arxiv-2512-15279:
Le Hao and six coauthors teach a smart mirror for millimeter wave networks to keep up with a moving user. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces steer radio reflections to boost coverage and signal quality. Liquid crystal versions are cheap and frugal with power, even at large sizes, but they reconfigure slowly, taking tens of milliseconds.

That lag has confined most work to static scenes or hardware fixes. The authors fill the gap with a reinforcement learning controller based on the DDPG algorithm. It adapts the surface's phase shifts without perfect channel knowledge, balancing signal to noise gains against configuration time. High fidelity ray tracing simulations, fed by measurements from a real liquid crystal prototype, validate the design. The study shows adaptive control can bring such surfaces into dynamic millimeter wave networks.
arxiv-2512-15579:
Carlos Sanchez and co authors demonstrate stable three dimensional vortex bullets in a 2025 paper. A vortex bullet is a pulsed beam carrying orbital angular momentum that traps itself as it travels. Attractive self interaction, needed to form bright solitons, usually makes such 3D vortex modes collapse or split apart.

Using a variational method and numerical simulations, the team shows these bullets can self trap in a two dimensional waveguiding structure. A critical trapping depth secures their stability. Collisions between bullets moving along the free direction turn out to be elastic. The authors identify lab conditions for making these modes with coherent optical and matter waves, aiding control of 3D topological solitons.
arxiv-2512-15879:
Tomohiro Oishi and Masaaki Kimura show that two proton emission can source spin entangled proton pairs in a 2025 paper. Some unstable nuclei emit two protons at once. If the starting state holds a spin singlet diproton correlation, the emitted pair may keep a quantum link worth measuring.

Using a time dependent three body model of neon 16, viewed as oxygen 14 plus two protons, the authors analyze the spin correlation of the emitted protons. When emission proceeds as a democratic three body process from a diproton correlated state, the correlation exceeds the local hidden variable bound and resembles a pure spin singlet pair. Sequential emission, or no starting correlation, erases the pattern.
arxiv-2512-15979:
Mia Mohammad Imran and Tarannum Shaila Zaman present OLAF, a framework for language model based labeling in software studies, in a 2025 position paper. Researchers increasingly use language models to label commits, issues, and descriptive artifacts. The steadiness of those labels and whether they can be repeated, though, are rarely measured with standard tools.

The authors argue annotation with language models should be treated as a measuring process, not mere automation. OLAF organizes the key ideas: steadiness, calibration, drift, consensus, combining, and openness. Many studies omit setup details that decide if work can be repeated, the paper notes. It aims to spur methods debate and future hands on work toward open labeling practice.
arxiv-2512-16079:
Alice Devillers and four co-authors study two ways of picturing symmetry in a mathematics paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025. A group can act by shuffling objects, a permutation picture, or by matrices, a linear picture. The authors study linear representations that intertwine with a given permutation action, and ask how small the matrices can be.

That smallest size is the linear dimension of the action, a quantity with uses in cryptography. The team develops the theory using permutation modules and proves structural results about minimal representations. They work out how faithfulness, transitivity, and primitivity constrain the dimension. They compute the dimension for several families of primitive groups and for wreath products, and settle it for almost simple 2-transitive groups. The results open fresh questions for representation theory.
arxiv-2512-16279:
Yiliu Yang and seven co-authors build a guard system for AI agents in their arXiv preprint, posted in 2025. Agents that use tools and message each other can cause harm, yet safety policies written in plain language are too vague for software to enforce reliably. Rules need to be machine-checkable.

Their system, QuadSentinel, writes policies as logical sequents built from predicates over observable state. Four cooperating agents do the guarding: a state tracker, a policy verifier, a threat watcher, and a referee that settles conflicts. A top-k updater keeps costs low by checking the most relevant rules first. On two public benchmarks, QuadSentinel improved guardrail accuracy and rule recall while cutting false alarms, beating a leading single-agent guard. The pattern can wrap existing agents without changing their cores.
arxiv-2512-16579:
Gyeongjun Lee and five co-authors switch on quantum light sources in an arXiv paper published in 2025. Single-photon emitters, defects that release one photon at a time, are building blocks for quantum communication. In monolayer tungsten disulfide, a two-dimensional semiconductor, such emitters hide in defect-bound exciton states that are hard to activate on demand.

The team annealed samples, sealed in boron nitride on a suspended microheater, at about 1100 kelvin inside the measurement setup itself. A sharp emission line appeared, shifted about 80 milli-electron volts below the neutral exciton, with a width under 200 micro-electron volts at cryogenic temperatures. Photon correlation tests showed clear antibunching, with the key statistic below 0.5, the signature of a true single-photon source. In-place heating thus becomes a controlled switch for quantum emitters in van der Waals materials.
arxiv-2512-16879:
Arnab Adhikary and coauthors show that a smart starting state pays off when quantum computers simulate electron-phonon systems, where electrons drag lattice vibrations along. Most work targets the simulation circuits, not the start state for phase estimation.

For the single-electron Holstein model, they propose a starting ansatz with much higher overlap with the true ground state in the strong coupling regime. Better overlap means fewer phase estimation rounds to reach a set accuracy. The ansatz can be built efficiently on hardware. The payoff is an exponential cut in total circuit cost versus standard guesses, a case for baking physics insight into state preparation.
arxiv-2512-17079:
Saraswathy Amjith and coauthors ask whether training on flawed reasoning can make language models tougher at math. Chain-of-thought models are brittle: one early slip usually poisons the final answer.

The team made training prefixes with exactly one controlled error, either a calculation slip or a reasoning fault, and fine-tuned Qwen3-4B with GRPO on final-answer reward. Their Mixed-CoT-RL model matched standard training on clean problems, 41 percent each, and beat it on flawed-prefill problems, 24 percent to 19 percent. Clean-only training fell below the untuned baseline on flawed inputs. Training on reasoning errors helped most, and mixed training did best of all.
arxiv-2512-17179:
Xiaotang Du and coauthors improve long-document summarization with self-planning, where a model first picks highlight sentences as a content plan, then writes the summary guided by that plan. Long inputs strain faithfulness, and plans make the output easier to trace.

Both end-to-end and two-stage variants were tried, and the two-stage pipeline did better on long, dense documents. On long-form data sets the method lifted factual consistency while keeping relevance and quality. On GovReport, the best variant gained 4.1 ROUGE-L points and about 35 percent on SummaC scores. Case checks show highlight guidance keeps key details that plain summaries drop.
arxiv-2512-17379:
Hadrien Kurkjian solves, exactly, how a thin gas of fermions carries flow, heat, and spin as it slides between two regimes. Cold and dense, the gas acts like a quantum Fermi liquid. Hot and thin, it acts like a classical gas. Labs that trap ultracold atoms live right in the messy crossover between the two.

Kurkjian builds custom polynomial sets for each direction of motion, which lets the full quantum kinetic equation be solved without guessing a shape. The results give the gas's viscosity and its heat and spin diffusivities to leading accuracy. A popular shortcut, the relaxation-time approximation, misses the truth by up to 25 percent at low heat, the paper shows. The exact method now serves as a yardstick for messier simulations.
arxiv-2512-17579:
Marco Faroni and coauthors compare neural networks that learn how much a safety system slows a robot down when a person works beside it. Mechanisms such as speed and separation monitoring cut the robot's speed as a person draws near, and those cuts make cycle times hard to forecast.

Rather than assume a standard safety model, the team predicts the robot's safety scaling factor straight from records of the process running. Real installations often depart from standard models after their own risk assessments, so learning from data fits practice better. They test several network designs side by side and find that a simple feed forward network estimates the slowdown well. Better slowdown estimates feed directly into sharper cycle time forecasts and smarter schedules for shared workspaces.
arxiv-2512-17679:
Zhou Lu, Mohammed El-Hajjar, and Lie-liang Yang fix the biggest flaw in a rising radio waveform design. AFDM packs data onto chirp-like carriers that handle fast-moving receivers well, a need for future wireless. Like its older cousin OFDM, though, its signal spikes demand power-hungry amplifiers that waste energy and distort the wave.

Their redesign, A2FDM, swaps out a matrix the original scheme never needed for signalling. The replacement folds data mapping and a small Fourier step into one operation, offered in interleaved and localized flavors. Simulations show the peak-power problem disappears. Better still, the new scheme keeps the full diversity gain that plain AFDM loses under harsh settings. Phones and base stations could get the motion-proofing without the power penalty.
arxiv-2512-17979:
Matthieu Mastio, Paul Saves, Benoit Gaudou, and Nicolas Verstaevel model how factories might trade waste as a resource. One plant's leftover can be another's raw input, a pattern called industrial symbiosis. In practice, distance, hauling costs, and poor matches keep such trades rare.

Their market places learning firms in a shared space, where prices and amounts arise from local bids in a double auction. Firms adjust their bids to weigh hauling costs, dumping fines, and scarcity. Runs show when this bazaar settles into steady, waste cutting trades, and sellers' play lands near a Nash balance. The model gives policy makers a test bed for nudges toward circular trade.
arxiv-2512-18079:
Jorge Casalderrey-Solana, Lucía Castells-Tiestos, Jéssica Gonçalves, and David Mateos use holography to keep cosmic inflation going without balance. Inflation is the early burst that stretched space at a wild pace. In their setup, a strongly linked quantum field theory sits in curved de Sitter space, and its out of balance state feeds the stretch.

The model stays inside the range where gravity can be treated in the classic way. The tuning it needs grows only slowly as key scales part, a mild demand next to most models. Horizons in the setup grow in area, which tracks a steady rise in disorder. The team suggests a normal young universe could settle into this self fed state late in its growth.
arxiv-2512-18179:
Ben Bakary Junior Siriki and Adama Coulibaly study how to calm a bending beam whose stiffness fades at one end. The beam also feels a push along its length, and the calming control at its edge acts with a time delay, which can stir up the very shaking it should stop. Such delays make the math delicate.

The pair restate the system in a broad space that tracks both the beam and its recent past, then prove the setup is sound. A custom energy score, built with weighted parts, shows the shaking dies away at a steady exponential rate, and they give that rate in exact form. The frame covers wider control laws than past work.
arxiv-2512-18579:
Yifei Jia, Yi Du, and Lihui Guo study the Ekman layer, the thin sheet of fluid near a boundary whose flow is twisted by Earth's rotation. Nearly all theory treats the boundary as flat, yet real coastlines and seabeds curve. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, asks how boundary shape changes the layer, a question Lions first raised and Masmoudi studied for small wavy walls.

The authors build multi-scale approximations tailored to the boundary's geometry and prove they converge in the strongest, uniform sense. Their results need no small-amplitude assumption, only a bound on the boundary's Gaussian curvature. When the wall is flat, the theory reproduces the classical results. In the zero-viscosity limit they derive a limiting system that depends on the geometry directly. The work should sharpen models of ocean and atmosphere flows over real terrain.
arxiv-2512-18779:
Thorsten Hellert and seven co-authors tackle a mundane problem that slows down big science: finding the right control signal. Accelerators, fusion devices, and telescopes expose hundreds of thousands of channels, named inconsistently over decades. Operators hunt them through folklore and fragmented docs. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, formalizes semantic channel finding, mapping a plain-language request to the right signal.

They propose four design paradigms, from dictionary lookup and tree navigation to exploring agents and ontology-based search, and match them to facility data conditions. Proof-of-concept systems at four working facilities, from compact free-electron lasers to large synchrotrons, answer expert-checked operational queries with 90 to 97 percent accuracy. As language models move into control rooms, a principled way to find channels becomes essential infrastructure.
arxiv-2512-18879:
Leonardo Colombo designs control schemes for open quantum systems that respect the physics at every step. Steering a qubit that leaks energy is governed by Lindblad dynamics, and optimal control is framed by Pontryagin's Maximum Principle. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds a discrete version of that principle together with an integrator that preserves the flow's structure exactly.

The contact Lie-group variational integrator keeps the evolution completely positive and trace-preserving, and maintains the contact geometry tying state, costate, and cost together. A standard Runge-Kutta scheme of the same order slowly drifts: trace leaks, positivity breaks, and shooting iterations destabilize, especially over long horizons. On a dissipative qubit test, the geometric method stays stable and physically faithful. For quantum engineers, structure preservation is not elegance, it is reliability.
arxiv-2512-19079:
Yuming Qin and Hongli Wang analyze the long-time behavior of a vibrating plate with memory. The equation is a viscoelastic Kirchhoff plate model, where past bending still shapes the present motion. Outside forces change with time, so the system is non-autonomous and harder to pin down.

First they show weak solutions exist for all time and form a continuous process. Then they prove a uniform attractor exists, a set that draws all motions in, in both subcritical and critical growth cases. Last, they show the attractor family behaves in an upper semicontinuous way as the perturbation shrinks to zero, settling open questions for such systems.
arxiv-2512-19179:
Yitao Yuan, Chenqi Zhao, Bohan Zhao, and Zane Cao fix a scheduling blind spot in systems that serve large language models. Requests in one batch vary wildly in length, and the attention step hates that mix. With context windows now past one hundred thousand tokens, the waste has become a main bottleneck.

Their runtime, CascadeInfer, sorts live requests across several copies of the same model. Each copy takes one length band, and requests flow between bands like a pipeline. A dynamic programming step picks the band layout, and load is rebalanced within and across groups as traffic shifts. The aim is lower latency with fuller use of each graphics processor.
arxiv-2512-19479:
Guoli Jia, Junyao Hu, Xinwei Long, and Kai Tian teach image generators to aim at feelings, not just objects. Emotion-driven images matter in advertising, yet current systems take a shortcut: they treat emotion as if it were the same as semantic content. Two decades of emotion research say that shortcut is wrong.

Their Emotion-Director pairs two parts. A diffusion model guided by both visual and text prompts generates beyond plain semantics, tuned by an improved preference method with negative visual prompts. An agent system then rewrites text prompts to carry the intended emotion without falling into templates. Cross-modal teamwork is the theme throughout.
arxiv-2512-19779:
Thirteen members of the CTEQ-TEA collaboration report progress toward CT25, their next generation of parton distribution functions. These functions describe how a proton's momentum is shared among its quarks and gluons, and nearly every precision prediction at the Large Hadron Collider depends on them. The update rests on a global analysis at next-to-next-to-leading order, folding in substantial new collider data.

A baseline fit previewed here adds Drell-Yan, top-pair, and inclusive-jet measurements at eight and thirteen tera-electronvolts, and it pulls noticeably on the high-momentum gluon and the flavor makeup of the quark sea. Companion studies weigh lattice-QCD input, extract the strong coupling within the same framework, and treat parametrization choice as an explicit uncertainty. Partial higher-order corrections and their effects on Higgs and vector-boson benchmarks also feature.
arxiv-2512-19879:
Jorg Bornschein and six co-authors merge the two standard ways to adapt a language model. One way is prompting with worked examples in the prompt. It is cheap with data but plateaus as data grows. The other way is fine-tuning on task data. It scales with data but starves when examples are scarce. Their unified recipe fine-tunes on task data that itself holds in-context examples. The training mimics the shape of few-shot prompts.

Across a broad study, the hybrid matched both parent methods. It often beat them by a clear margin. Picking settings in the low-data regime uses prequential evaluation. That method trains and checks on the same stream, in order. It needs no costly cross-validation, and it uses each example. The study maps which method wins where. The unified one was the most steady of the three.
arxiv-2512-19979:
Yun-Mei Li, Yongwei Huang, and Kai Chang propose a new species of topological superconductor. They name it for a multipole moment. Quantized quadrupole superconductors host Majorana corner modes. The link runs through a bulk-corner correspondence. What sets them apart is the invariant. It is the superconductor's own quadrupole moment. Particle-hole symmetry pins it to a half-quantized value.

Two recipes realize the phase. Both mix d-wave pairings with opposed phase windings. The pairings are induced in bilayer electron gases with Rashba spin-orbit coupling. The phase survives wobbles in the relative pairing phase. It also survives disorder, per their checks. Majorana zero modes are candidate parts for fault-tolerant quantum computers. Platforms that host them at corners thus carry real weight.
arxiv-2512-20079:
Tarakanta Nayak and Pooja Phogat map the fractal geometry of an iterative root-finding method. Chebyshev's method, a higher-order cousin of Newton's iteration, is applied here to polynomials with exactly two distinct roots, turning the complex plane into competing basins of attraction. The question is the global structure: which points converge to which root, and what the boundary between the fates looks like.

They prove the Julia set, the boundary chaos where iteration is sensitive, is connected for this class. The Fatou set, where behavior is orderly, is exactly the union of the attracting basins of the two roots, with nothing left over. When both roots share the same multiplicity, the common boundary of their immediate basins is itself a connected subset of the Julia set.
arxiv-2512-20379:
Beatrice Nyiransengiyumva and co-authors ask a deceptively simple question: does it matter how the green valley is drawn? Galaxies fall into a blue cloud of star-formers and a red sequence of quiet systems. The valley between them should hold systems mid-change, so its definition shapes findings about how galaxies change.

Using Sloan survey optical data and GALEX ultraviolet data for nearby galaxies, the team applied the eight most common selection criteria. Different criteria picked genuinely different sets. UV-based cuts favoured more massive, less star-forming systems with more ellipticals and composites. Colour-based cuts were the most twitchy of all. The authors recommend avoiding pure colour picking in favour of star-formation-based cuts or combinations.
arxiv-2512-20479:
Yiming Zhao and co-authors built UTDesign, a approach for editing and generating styled text inside graphic design images. Posters and advertisements live or die by typography, yet diffusion image models garble small type and non-Latin scripts. UTDesign targets exactly that weakness, supporting English and Chinese text.

A style transfer model, trained from scratch on synthetic data, produces transparent text foregrounds that copy the look of reference glyphs. A conditional generation variant adds a multimodal encoder trained on annotated designs, so text can be synthesized to fit a background, prompt, and layout. An automated pipeline with a language-model layout planner completes the text-to-design flow. Experiments put UTDesign at the front of open-source methods for style consistency and text accuracy.
arxiv-2512-21079:
Mohsin Iqbal Khan, Matti Hamalainen, and three co-authors measure whether a private 5G network can run inside a working hospital without disturbing anything else. The test site is an operating room at the new Oulu University Hospital in Finland, where the network occupies the 3.9 to 4.1 gigahertz band alongside legacy LTE and Wi-Fi. High-resolution, long-duration spectrum scans look for interference in both directions, and radio-frequency exposure is checked against international safety limits.

No measurable interference appeared, in either direction, confirming the band's spectral isolation. Exposure levels sat well below the thresholds set by ICNIRP, the WHO, and the IEEE, so biological risk to patients and staff is negligible. The team adds spectrum-management proposals, adaptive sensing and guardband planning, giving other hospitals a template for going private-5G safely.
arxiv-2512-21179:
Jiaxin Pan and Longwen Zhou wire together a topological phase whose charges refuse to commute. Multigap materials can carry non-Abelian charges, quaternion-like quantities whose multiplication order matters, beyond the reach of the winding and Chern numbers used for ordinary phases. Higher-order phases, which park their protected states at corners rather than edges, had been catalogued almost entirely with the older invariants. The authors' coupled-wire construction assembles a second-order insulator whose corner modes are guarded by combined symmetries.

Its topology needs a two-part descriptor: a vector joining the non-Abelian quaternion charge to an Abelian winding number. Corner states appear only when both parts are nontrivial, while the quaternion charge alone produces weak edge states of non-Abelian origin, rewriting the bulk-edge-corner rulebook. Both kinds of phase transition coexist in one platform, and photonic or acoustic metamaterials could realize it in the laboratory.
arxiv-2512-21379:
Brian Knaeble, Qinyun Lin, Erich Kummerfeld, and Kenneth A. Frank write about a hidden assumption behind causal inference, the method used to claim one thing causes another. The consistency assumption says there are no hidden versions of a treatment, and that an outcome seen in nature matches the outcome the same treatment would produce under intervention.

Many sensitivity analyses ask how conclusions change if unmeasured traits of the subjects distort the results. Knaeble and his co-authors instead target hidden versions of the treatment itself. In surgery, for example, a patient's genes are background traits, while the skill of the individual surgeon is a version of the treatment that data rarely record. The authors introduce new mathematical notation for this distinction and build a sensitivity method around it, then describe example applications. The method shows how strong a hidden-version effect must be to overturn a conclusion.
arxiv-2512-21579:
K. De Commer, G. Schrader, A. Shapiro, and C. Voigt construct examples of locally compact quantum groups, the analytic objects generalizing groups in noncommutative geometry. Quantum groups deform classical symmetries; the locally compact ones are the analytically complete versions, described with operator algebras. Purely continuous, higher-rank examples from Lie theory had been missing.

The authors build quantum deformations of the positive part of higher-rank split Lie groups of type A, at a unimodular value of the deformation parameter. The construction starts from Drinfeld-Jimbo quantization, the algebraic deformation of Lie algebras. Their tool is quantum cluster theory, in the form developed by Fock and Goncharov, which coordinates the positive geometry of these groups. The result is the first family of purely continuous q-deformed quantum groups of Lie type in higher rank. The paper is a hundred-page contribution to operator algebra and quantum group theory.
arxiv-2512-21779:
Viet H. Do, Hoi H. Nguyen, Van H. Vu, and their co-authors begin a systematic study of anti-concentration for random permutations. Anti-concentration asks how unlikely a random quantity is to land in a tiny window. Most classical theory assumes the randomness comes from independent variables; a permutation, where every choice constrains the rest, is different.

Their variable is a sum where one fixed vector's entries are permuted against another fixed vector. On the discrete side, they characterize exactly which vector pairs allow the sum to hit a single value with large probability. On the continuous side, they bound the chance the sum falls in a short interval, with sub-gaussian decay. The inverse theorems strengthen earlier anti-concentration bounds. Applications follow: extremal points of random permutation polynomials are few, only logarithmically many in the degree. And permutation-row random matrices are nonsingular with high probability.
arxiv-2512-21979:
A third body near a merging binary black hole accelerates the binary's center of mass, imprinting a phase shift on its gravitational waves that current detectors largely miss. Suvikranth Gera and Poulami Dutta Roy ask what happens when that acceleration is present in the signal but ignored in the templates. Their testbed is the third-generation detectors Cosmic Explorer and Einstein Telescope.

For a low-mass binary, an unmodeled acceleration as small as about ten to the minus nine per second already biases chirp mass and mass ratio beyond statistical errors. Asymmetric binaries suffer most. Including the effect in the phase model turns the tables: accelerations around ten to the minus seven per second can be measured tightly, exposing the hidden companion.
arxiv-2512-22179:
Rajeeb Thapa Chhetri, Saurab Thapa, Avinash Kumar, and Zhixiong Chen build Latent Sculpting, a defense for networks facing attacks never seen in training. Intrusion detectors often ace known attacks yet collapse when traffic patterns shift, because their decision borders hug the training data too closely. Latent Sculpting instead reshapes the model's internal representation before judging how unusual traffic is.

First, a transformer encoder trained with a special loss pulls harmless traffic into one compact cluster and pushes odd patterns away. Then a masked autoregressive flow scores how probable each point is in that tidy space. Under a strict zero-shot protocol on the CIC-IDS-2017 benchmark, the system reached a zero-shot F1 score of 0.867 for unseen attacks. It caught most stealthy infiltration attempts and low-volume denial-of-service variants.
arxiv-2512-22379:
Tanayveer Singh Bhatia and six co-authors simulate how faculae, bright magnetic patches, change the surfaces of cool stars. Magnetic fields alter convection near a star's surface, and with it the light the star emits and its long-term evolution. Using 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations, the team modeled F, G, K, and M main-sequence stars at solar metallicity with faculae-like average field strengths.

Compared with small-scale dynamo simulations, the imposed fields lowered average density and gas pressure near the surfaces and dented the temperature profile just below them. Convective velocities dropped as well. Bolometric brightness changed by less than a percent, with trends that differed by stellar type. The size of every effect depended on both field strength and the star's effective temperature.
arxiv-2512-22479:
Hong-Bae Jeon proposes FARIS, a wireless surface that is both fluid and active, aimed at 6G networks. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces steer radio signals by reflecting them; FARIS adds two twists, antenna ports that can be repositioned fluidly, and per-element active amplification. To keep the design honest, Jeon first builds a circuit-level abstraction and a power model covering both port-switching control power and the direct-current bias the amplifiers need.

On that model, the paper formulates an ergodic-rate maximization that jointly tunes the amplification-reflection settings and the discrete choice of active elements under hardware constraints. An alternating optimization system improves the rate step by step, with complexity and convergence analyses alongside. Simulations show FARIS beating conventional baselines across environments, often with fewer active elements or a smaller surface.
arxiv-2512-22679:
José P. S. Lemos wrote this introduction to gravitational waves, walking from Einstein's theory to the detectors now listening to the cosmos. The article opens with general relativity and its major implications, then tells the history of gravitational waves from their prediction to their first detection a century later. It explains what the waves are and how they interact with suitable detectors.

Emission methods get detailed treatment, mainly compact binaries whose orbits evolve through inspiral, merger, and ringdown, each phase leaving a distinct signature. The giant interferometers LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA star in the detection story, anchored by GW150914, the Nobel-recognized first direct detection. Lemos also covers other observed events, possible cosmological waves from the Big Bang, and future observatories, closing by contrasting gravitational-wave astronomy with the electromagnetic view.
arxiv-2512-23279:
Hang Yang and Daiqin Su follow what happens to clouds of ultralight bosons orbiting inside binary black hole systems. Ultralight bosons are attractive dark matter candidates. A spinning black hole can grow a dense boson cloud through superradiance, extracting its rotational energy. In a binary, the companion interferes: self-interactions of the bosons and transition mixing between the two holes set up a dynamical contest over the cloud.

The authors focus on mass transfer between the holes in unequal-mass binaries, allowing the companion's spin to point in an arbitrary direction relative to the primary's. The mass ratio between companion and primary turns out to significantly control how much of the cloud the companion absorbs through this transfer. A misaligned companion spin further modifies how efficiently the cloud is depleted. Since boson clouds could imprint on gravitational wave signals, these transfer dynamics matter for what future observatories might actually see.
arxiv-2512-23579:
Alessandro Carotenuto, Antonio Del Donno, Réamonn Ó Buachalla, and Junaid Razzaq build new solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation, a relation that sits behind much of quantum group theory and integrable systems. Their solutions come from noncommutative geometry: starting from a quantum homogeneous space equipped with a covariant differential calculus and a special connection, they extract a flip map between tensor factors. The arXiv record's title and framing govern here.

When the connection is a bimodule connection, simple conditions guarantee the flip map solves the Yang-Baxter equation. Applied to cominuscule quantum flag manifolds, the solution splits into holomorphic, anti-holomorphic, and mixed parts. The familiar braidings appear in the first two, with a new involutive extension across the mixed terms. As a payoff, the degree-two relations of the Heckenberger-Kolb calculi get a uniform presentation. It is a work of pure math, built by proof, not by tests.
arxiv-2512-23679:
Gargi Mukherjee studies the overpartition function, which counts partitions of an integer where the first occurrence of each part size may be overlined. She applies a shifted difference operator, which compares values of the function a fixed step apart, and applies it repeatedly. The goal is an asymptotic expansion, a formula that captures the growth of those differences for large arguments, with a fully effective error bound.

To get there, she first derives an asymptotic expansion for the shifted overpartition function itself, for every nonzero integer shift. The main expansion for the iterated differences follows, and with it an answer to a problem posed by Wang, Xie, and Zhang about this sequence. Papers of this kind matter because differences of partition functions often carry congruence and monotonicity information that the raw counts hide.
arxiv-2512-23779:
Manu and seven co-authors benchmark a quiet way to attack language models: tricking them into never stopping. A model driven into over-generation emits thousands of tokens before its end-of-sequence signal, wrecking answer quality while inflating latency and cost; aimed deliberately, that is a denial-of-service attack. Earlier studies usually examined one attack method or assumed insider access to the model.

Their benchmark instead compares prompt-only attackers in a realistic black-box, query-only setting. One attacker evolves token prefixes that suppress the stop signal; the other trains a network to generate prefixes aimed at a target output length. A new metric, the over-generation factor, measures output against the context window. The learned attacker was far more severe, roughly doubling the evolutionary one's scores and driving nearly half its trials into budget-exhausting non-termination.
arxiv-2512-23879:
Andrew Zhu, Poramas Komonvasee, Arman Nejad, and David Tew compute how strongly carbon monoxide sticks to magnesium oxide, the textbook test case for surface sticking theory. For a single lonely CO molecule, accurate quantum methods now agree well with experiment. Denser layers are another matter: bigger cells cost much more to simulate, and the space of arrangements explodes, so coverage effects have rarely been probed at this accuracy.

Their method, periodic DLPNO-MP2, is a local-correlation version of second-order perturbation theory efficient enough for large supercells, which lets them approach the thermodynamic limit of an extended surface. In the dilute regime their sticking energies match existing benchmarks. As coverage rises toward a full monolayer, binding weakens, in agreement with experiment, and the authors blame the drop on growing sideways repulsion between neighboring CO molecules. The trend matches what labs actually see.
arxiv-2512-24179:
Joonhee Lee, Kichang Lee, and Jeonggil Ko design surveillance for wild places. Poaching patrols and forest fire detection need wide coverage. The regions are vast and hard to reach. Battery-free sensor nodes are attractive there. They harvest energy and need no maintenance. But standard designs make nodes sleep while recharging. A fire does not wait for that.

Their algorithm keeps sensing continuous instead. Computation shifts to neighbors holding more energy. Sensing itself never pauses for buffering. Early results show stable extra coverage. Thousands of additional square meters were monitored. Roughly a hundred more critical events were caught per day. The authors offer the scheme as a foundation. Resilient monitoring networks could be built from very limited devices.
arxiv-2512-24779:
Jan Lukas Igelbrink, Charline Smadi, and Anton Wakolbinger analyze Muller's ratchet under tournament selection, a model of how harmful mutations accumulate in asexual populations. Population size stays fixed, mutations arrive at a constant rate, and fitter individuals carry fewer mutations. In tournament selection only the sign of load differences matters, not their size, unlike the classical version.

In a slow-clicking regime, where the least-loaded class is lost rarely, they study the clicktime process and metastability in a Moran model. Probability readers get sharp tools for long quiet periods punctuated by sudden losses. The ratchet matters for understanding degeneration in small asexual populations.
arxiv-2512-24879:
Maria Lukacova-Medvidova and Simon Schneider propose a finite volume random collocation method for the Euler equations of gas dynamics with random inputs. Uncertainty in initial or boundary data makes the flow itself random, so numeric methods must track distributions, not single answers. They prove convergence of the random finite volume answers, assuming discrete differential quotients stay bounded in probability.

The proof joins deterministic finite volume convergence with random compactness arguments in the Skorokhod and Gyongy-Krylov tradition. Numerical analysis readers get rigorous backing for a useful scheme. Random compressible flow appears in aerospace and weather settings where data is never exact.
arxiv-2512-24979:
Adolfo Holguin returns to how to compute three-point functions of semiclassical probes with single-trace maps in holography, focusing on extremal and near-extremal cases. Earlier methods held conflicts, and the roles of wavefunctions and averaging over moduli needed clarification. Holographic computations, he finds, may be done with or without that averaging.

Careful use of the extrapolate dictionary explains an apparent mismatch between supergravity and field theory for extremal correlators using giant gravitons in type IIB supergravity. An ansatz for the other cases is offered. String theory readers get a cleaner recipe for a subtle class of correlators.
arxiv-2601-06679:
Matthew Gillespie and co-authors compare two notions of coaction invariance in 2026. A coaction of a locally compact group acts on a C-star algebra. Ideals of that algebra can be invariant in two different forms.

They study the relationship between those two forms of invariance. The ideals of the corresponding crossed product algebra enter the comparison. Crossed products encode the coaction in a larger algebra's structure. Knowing when the two invariance notions agree matters for classification work. Operator algebraists use such ideals to understand symmetry and duality. The paper clarifies a subtle point where definitions can diverge quietly. Readers get conditions linking invariance upstairs and downstairs in crossed products. It is a careful contribution to coaction theory's foundations.
arxiv-2601-06979:
Dongsuk Jang and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with MedTutor. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The learning process for medical residents presents significant challenges. Demanding both the ability to interpret complex case reports and the rapid acquisition of accurate medical knowledge from reliable sources.

Residents typically study case reports and engage in discussions with peers and mentors. But finding relevant educational materials and evidence to support their learning from these cases is often time-consuming and challenging. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07479:
Håkon Noren Myhr and Sølve Eidnes work on numerical methods that respect the physics they simulate. Their 2026 preprint concerns discrete gradient methods, integrators that preserve first integrals of ordinary differential equations exactly. Energy-like quantities then stay right even over long runs. The authors aim to build such a method without needing derivatives.

Their construction mixes order theory with the symmetrized Itoh-Abe discrete gradient and finite differences. The result is an integral-preserving method of fourth order that is derivative-free. Avoiding derivatives matters when derivatives are costly or unavailable in closed form. Readers in scientific computing get a careful example of structure-preserving design, where the method honors the equation's own conservation laws.
arxiv-2601-08279: I. V. Kolokolov and V. V. Lebedev build perturbation theory for phase correlations of light in turbulence. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies correlation functions of a light wave's phase after crossing a turbulent medium. The starting point is an equation for the logarithm of a wave packet envelope. That equation carries a second-order nonlinear term. The authors develop a diagrammatic technique to compute corrections beyond the linear approximation. Results aid optics work where turbulence blurs beams, from astronomy to free-space links.
arxiv-2601-08379:
Matina Mahdizadeh Sani and three co-authors adapt diffusion models to target data without retraining. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that pre-trained diffusion models act as strong generative priors. Their outputs often drift from the traits of a user's specific target data, though.

The mismatch bites hardest in domain adaptation, where only a few reference examples exist. Retraining the model there is usually infeasible. The authors guide generation with maximum mean discrepancy, a measure of distribution distance. Training-free guidance steers samples toward the target set at inference time. Medical and design users with small private datasets could benefit from adaptation that needs no new training run.
arxiv-2601-08779:
Shanshan Hua and Stuart White prove when two maps into a large algebra must be the same up to a twist. The algebras here are vast nets of operators, built as limits of plain matrix sets. The maps come from a well behaved source algebra. Each map is full and has a clean spread trait that such work needs.

They show that if two maps match on two counts, they must match in full. One count is a trace, a sort of mean value. The next is a deep shape count called K-theory. A twist by a unit in the target can turn one map into the next. A reader in operator work gets a firm sameness test. Two counts can pin down a whole map.
arxiv-2601-08879:
Nicolas Ruth and Manuel Burghardt study how sound in Nazi era films shaped the traits of roles on screen. Film study tends to lean on image and script. Sound holds clues too: tone of voice, pace, and word choice can mark a hero or a foe. The pair build a three step chain to pull those clues out by machine.

Step one splits who speaks when. Step two turns speech to text. Step three reads the text for mind and mood traits. The first step still errs at times, the pair note. Yet the chain shows clear role traits and tale lines. A reader in film or past study gets a sound first tool. It can scale to large film sets that no one staff could hear in full.
arxiv-2601-09579:
Fiona Murphy and Alessio Benavoli unify two ways of hunting cause and effect in time series. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns nonlinear Granger causality with kernels. Kernel methods let analysts spot causal links that bend and curve, not just straight-line effects.

The authors show that two leading kernel approaches both fit inside kernel principal component regression. Building on that shared frame, they add a method of their own.
