They report that the unified approach can improve causal identification. Cleaner causality tools matter wherever time series drive decisions, from climate to markets.
arxiv-2601-09679:
Adel Javanmard and David P. Woodruff advance a conjecture about noise and information on the Boolean cube. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns the Courtade-Kumar conjecture. It claims that dictatorship functions maximize the mutual information between a function's output and a noisy copy of its input.

The authors report two advances on the problem. One gives optimal entropy bounds in the high-noise regime. The other develops a generalized coordinate-wise mutual information. The conjecture sits where information theory meets analysis of Boolean functions. Progress on it sharpens tools used across learning theory and coding.
arxiv-2601-09779:
Jan Carlo Schumann, Igor Lesanovsky, and Parvinder Solanki stack two kinds of time crystals into one system. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies hierarchical time crystals. Time crystals are phases that break time-translation symmetry, ticking on their own like ordinary crystals repeat in space.

Discrete and continuous time crystals have mostly been studied on their own. The authors ask what happens when the two kinds interact. Coupled rhythms can lock, drift, or spawn new patterns. A hierarchy of time order would add a fresh entry to the catalog of exotic phases of matter.
arxiv-2601-09879:
Yang Xing and six co-authors unify three-dimensional medical imaging with language in one model. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents MedVL-SAM2, a 3D medical vision-language model. It handles multimodal reasoning and prompt-driven segmentation together.

Medical vision-language models already write reports and answer questions about scans at the image level. Fine-grained grounding and volumetric reasoning in 3D remain hard. Doing both inside one general framework is harder still. A single model that reasons about a scan and outlines anatomy from a text prompt could streamline radiology work in busy hospitals. It could also give smaller clinics tools that now sit only in large research centers with big teams.
arxiv-2601-10179:
Senning Wan, Bin Li, Hongbin Chen, and Lei Liu place drone base stations in three dims. Drones can act as cell towers in the sky. They serve ground users with wide data needs. But hills, towers, and blocks can block their paths.

The team plans where drones should sit and how users link to them. They build a score for how well each user is served. The plan must dodge blocks in the air space. It must also fit the varied needs of users. The aim is a sky net that serves each user well, not just the mean user.
arxiv-2601-10679:
Zirui Ren and Ziming Liu ask whether a new kind of reasoning model truly reasons. The hierarchical reasoning model, or HRM, scores far above large language model reasoners on many tasks. Such a gap calls for a close look inside. The authors run a mechanistic study of how HRM works through problems.

Their study turns up three surprising facts. One is that HRM can fail on extremely simple puzzles. That mix of high scores and basic lapses hints at shortcut behavior in places. The paper gives researchers a map of where HRM is strong and where it may only guess. It warns against trusting benchmark scores alone.
arxiv-2601-10779:
Qingyue Zhang and co-authors study multi-source transfer learning, where a model borrows from several source tasks at once. Transfer helps most when target data are scarce. But blending sources blindly can hurt: poor sources drag the model down, a flaw called negative transfer. Past methods tune either the source weights or the sample counts, rarely both.

The authors build an asymptotic framework that optimizes both together. Source weights say how much to trust each source. Transfer quantities say how much data to take from each. Tuning the pair jointly should dodge the worst blends. The work gives a firmer theory base for teams that pool models across tasks or sites.
arxiv-2601-11179:
Noor Ul Ain, Lorenzo Miretti, Renato Cavalcante, and Slawomir Stanczak study cell-free networks here. Their 2026 preprint looks at a vast MIMO setup with no cells. In such a setup, many access points serve users at once. The team asks what flaws in phase tracking do to speed and quality.

Most past work took one of two extreme views. Phases were seen as known in full, or not known at all. The team here picks a more true-to-life middle case. Phase estimates still hold some error from flawed parts, motion, and sync faults. That shift lets the study test how much such error costs the network.
arxiv-2601-11279:
Gaetano de Marino reports rare B decay searches for the Belle II group. The 2026 preprint covers work at Belle and at Belle II. Both are particle physics experiments built around B mesons. The team collected a large sample of collisions for the search.

The sample sits at the Upsilon 4S resonance energy. That choice gives clean events with few extra particles. Known starting states make the math of each event tight. The team hunts decays with missing energy in the end state. Neutrinos carry that energy off without a trace in the detector. Two rare classes are in scope: electroweak penguin decays. The second is decays that break lepton flavor rules.
arxiv-2601-11379:
Morgane Hoffmann and four coauthors probe how language models judge job seekers. Their 2026 preprint tests LLM behavior in hiring tasks. Models show real promise for screening in recruitment. Hiring needs thought over loose text and many mixed traits.

Fit and skill must be read from weak, indirect signals. It is not clear how models weigh each such signal. Their weights may clash with economics or with recruiter taste. They may also clash with broad norms of fairness. The team checks weights across groups of applicants. They also set model picks next to human picks. The goal is a fair read of a fast-spreading practice.
arxiv-2601-11479:
Yohai Trabelsi and four coauthors plan health facility upgrades in Ethiopia. Their 2026 preprint uses language models to aid the planning. Ethiopia's Ministry of Health is upgrading rural health posts. Better posts widen access to essential care in the country.

Funds are limited, so upgrades must be picked with care. The aim is to maximize population coverage per upgrade. Expert and stakeholder preferences add more goals to the mix. The team lets LLMs fold that expert knowledge into algorithms. Human judgment then enters the planning in structured form. The blend aims at plans that are both fair and feasible. Rural access gains the most from such careful picks.
arxiv-2601-11679:
Richard Hartley explains two linked notions in image geometry. The 2026 preprint covers the conformal point and the calibrating conic. Both notions help users visualize how images encode space. They lead to intuitive ways to compute geometry.

Angles and directions in an image are the payoff examples. A photo flattens the world, yet angles can be recovered. The conformal point and conic carry that recovery data. Hartley gives information on each notion in turn. He also sets out their relationship to one another. Such tools serve camera calibration and 3D vision work. A clear account helps students grasp projective geometry.
arxiv-2601-12079:
Jing Zhang, Bingjie Fan, Jixiang Zhu, and Zhe Wang move the mood of an image by text brief. Their tool, called EmoLat in the work, builds an emotion latent space. That space links text sense to visual mood traits in a fine way.

In that space, they build a graph of how emotions, objects, and visual traits relate. A user brief can then steer the transfer of mood. Fine mood control helps ads, art, and therapy images. The work tests text-led mood shifts that keep the scene intact.  The graph keeps mood shifts tied to the right objects.
arxiv-2601-12479:
Miquel Kegeleirs, Lorenzo Garattoni, Gianpiero Francesca, and Mauro Birattari bring language into robot swarms. Their task is person re identification: telling whether two sightings show the same person. In a swarm, no single robot holds all the data, so the task must be decentralized. Past methods lean on opaque visual embeddings, long number vectors pulled from images.

The team use natural language as the main way to store what a robot saw. A phrase like a short verbal sketch can be read by humans and shared with ease. That choice makes swarm perception open to inspection, not a black box. It also lets robots with distinct views compare notes in words. The work points to swarms that explain what they think they saw.
arxiv-2601-12979:
Qingyu Lu and four co authors run a reality check on diffusion language models for agent work. Real time agentic interaction drives interest in these models as alternatives to autoregressive backbones. Diffusion models promise to break the sequential latency bottleneck of token by token generation. The team ask whether such efficiency gains translate into effective agentic behavior.

Their title calls the expected answer a bitter lesson. They present a comprehensive evaluation of diffusion language models on agentic workflows. Speed alone may not yield agents that plan, act, and recover well. Honest evaluations of this kind steer the field away from hype. Labs choosing a backbone for agents need exactly this evidence.
arxiv-2601-13179:
A. Spatafora and co-authors, for the NUMEN team, test new large silicon carbide sensors. Such sensors will track charged bits in atom core tests. The team uses a beam led charge method with a fine proton beam to probe them.

Their mark is deplete depth, how deep the live zone of the sensor runs. The sensors are p-n junction types with a large face, a form that is new for this stuff. A right deplete depth is key for clean counts of charge. For the NUMEN plan, which hunts a rare core change, sound sensors are a must. The tests show if the new large forms are fit for the task.
arxiv-2601-13379:
Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, Chenhao Tan, and Alexander K. Zentefis watch how radiologists use AI on chest scans for lung clots. The team tracks more than one hundred thousand scans read by near four hundred doctors. The scans came in as an FDA cleared AI tool rolled out step by step in one hospital group.

When the AI flags a clot, doctors concur most of the time, in 84 per cent of cases. When the AI says no clot, they concur in 97 per cent of cases. The step wise roll out lets the team split tool effects from trends. For care teams, the split shows trust is high but not blind, a key fact for safe joint work.
arxiv-2601-13479:
Thitaree Tanprasert, Young-ho Kim, Sidney Fels, and Dongwook Yoon study peer agents that argue on aim in on line classes. A peer agent is an AI mate set to learn with a student. Off line courses lack live peers, so agents may fill that gap. A theory called constructive controversy says folks learn deep by clash and then by fix of views.

The team asks if that gain holds for AI peers. They vary how much an agent fights a point. They also vary if the agent's design is told to the student. Both picks may sway how much a student trusts and learns. For course teams, the finds guide how frank an AI peer should be.
arxiv-2601-13679:
Sangwon Park, Dongjun Kim, Sung-Hoon Byun, and Sangwook Park build a tiny sound classifier for ships in 2026. Ships give off sounds as they move, and those sounds can reveal the ship type. Small devices at sea must do this job with little power and weak chips. Heavy AI models do not fit that task well.

Their model, ShuffleFAC, uses frequency-aware convolution tuned for low cost. It splits work into light steps and shuffles channels to mix traits cheaply. Tests on the DeepShip dataset showed strong results with far less complexity. Light tools like this suit long, quiet watch at sea.
arxiv-2601-14079:
Paul Walker and co-authors model natural light so 3D scenes can be relit in a true way in 2026. Inverse rendering works backward from an image to the scene and light behind it. The problem is ill-posed, with many possible answers. Illumination priors simplify it by favoring plausible light.

Past work either ignores the spherical, rotation-equivariant nature of light environments, or lacks a well-behaved latent space. Their VENI is a rotation-equivariant variational autoencoder for natural illumination. It models light on the sphere without 2D projections. True light models aid film, design, and robot vision.
arxiv-2601-14279:
Brady Steele reports a negative result on speeding up language models in this 2026 paper. The target is KV cache compression, a way to shrink the memory a model keeps while it writes. His method is Speculative Importance Prediction, a scorer with 1.7 million parameters. It predicts how much each token will matter, from the cache alone.

The scorer does not look at the live query, by design. It has bold parts, such as multi-horizon lookahead and cross-attention. Still, it does not beat simple baselines, not even random selection. Steele ran five seeds, four retention levels, and three tasks. His study marks a clear limit for this kind of learned scoring.
arxiv-2601-14679:
Yiran Zhang, Xingpeng Sun, and Aniket Bera work on virtual reality walking in this 2026 paper. Natural walking enhances immersion in virtual environments. Physical space limitations and obstacles hinder exploration, though, especially in large virtual scenes. Redirected Walking techniques mitigate this problem. They subtly manipulate the virtual camera to guide users away from physical collisions within pre-defined virtual environments.

The team's system is HCVR Scene Generation. It generates virtual reality environments with high compatibility for extended redirected walking. In plain terms, the scenes are built so the redirection tricks work over longer walks. The gain is ease of use. A guest can walk a large fake world and still feel at home in a small room. Readers get scene generation designed around the limits of a real room.
arxiv-2601-15079:
Chenyu Liu, Haige Li, and Luca Rossi make graph neural networks cheaper to train. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with networks that learn from graph data, passing messages between nodes. Quantization shrinks such models and speeds them up for small devices.

For graphs, the features matter more than in language models. The authors present LoRAP, short for Low-Rank Aggregation Prompting. It is aimed at training quantized graph networks. The method guides the quantized model with low-rank prompts, so accuracy survives while the model stays small, lean, and quick to train and run.
arxiv-2601-15379:
Sebastian M. Banaszak, Caitlin A. Witt, and Adam A. Miller compare ways to hear the tick of two black holes in orbit. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with supermassive black hole binaries hidden in active galaxies. Simulations say such pairs should make the galaxy's brightness vary in a periodic way.

That signal must beat the galaxy's own random flicker. The authors simulate binaries with damped random walk noise plus an orbital sine wave. They test three detection methods against each other. The study asks which method recovers the true period best, to guide optical searches.
arxiv-2601-15479:
Sydney Anuyah and three co-authors test whether language models can reason about cause and effect in a 2026 arXiv paper. Safe use of these models in fields like biomedicine needs such skill. A model that confuses correlation with cause can mislead care. The team studies one basic task. It is pairwise causal discovery from text: given two things, judge which causes which, if either.

Thirteen open-source language models face the test. The setting spans biomedicine and other domains, per the title. Pairwise judgments are the atoms of larger causal maps. If models fail here, bigger causal claims rest on sand. The benchmark gives builders a clear check. It shows where current models stand on a skill that high-stakes use demands.
arxiv-2601-15579:
Philip Korman studies periodic solutions of first-order problems in a 2026 arXiv paper. He uses continuation methods and bifurcation theory. The goal is exact counts of periodic solutions, not just existence. He also maps the global structure of solution curves. Knowing how solutions appear, merge, and vanish gives a fuller picture. Two applications anchor the theory.

One is a population model with fishing. There, periodic solutions describe seasons of growth and harvest. The other concerns limit cycles, closed loops that systems settle into. Existence and stability of such cycles matter in many models of nature. Exact multiplicity results are rare and valuable. They tell modelers how many steady rhythms a system can truly support.
arxiv-2601-15779:
Liuyun Jiang and five co-authors grow training data for brain mapping in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neuron segmentation in electron microscopy aims to rebuild the full connectome. Deep learning methods lead the field. They depend on large training sets with costly manual annotations. Classic augmentation warps images geometrically or shifts brightness. The results stay highly correlated with the originals. They lack structural diversity, so models still starve for variety.

The team uses diffusion models for augmentation instead. Generative models can create fresh, varied examples. New structures in training data teach models to handle real variety. Connectome projects generate petabytes of imagery. Any gain in annotation efficiency compounds hugely at that scale. This paper adds a generative route to that efficiency.
arxiv-2601-15879:
Jiajun Zhang and a large team benchmark controllable code completion in a 2026 arXiv paper. Code completion is now a central task for language models. It powers the assistants many programmers use daily. Completion skill has improved fast. Evaluation methods have not kept equal pace, the authors note. Their benchmark is C3-Bench. It evaluates and aims to achieve controllable completion in code models.

Controllable means the model completes code as directed, not just plausibly. Length, style, and scope of a completion all matter in real editing. A benchmark that tests control exposes gaps that accuracy scores hide. Tool builders can then tune models for steerable help. For working programmers, a completer that follows instructions beats one that merely guesses well.
arxiv-2601-15979:
W. Kollatschny and a large team follow a restless galaxy over five years in a 2026 arXiv paper. The galaxy is IRAS 23226-3843. Optical spectra marked it as a highly variable Seyfert galaxy. It even qualifies as a changing-look active galactic nucleus. In such objects, the nucleus changes its spectral type over time. The title promises extreme line profile variations in this repeating case. Emission lines shift and reshape as the center brightens and fades.

The team presents follow-up observations from the past five years. They track ongoing photometric and spectral variations. Long baselines are rare and valuable for these objects. They reveal whether changes cycle or wander. Changing-look galaxies test models of how black holes feed. A well-documented case gives those models something firm to match.
arxiv-2601-16379:
Junjie Yang and coauthors speed quantum sums for crystals with a fit trick. Their 2026 preprint deals with sums that join embed steps and local links. Crystals need sums that use the repeat form of the build. The fit trick splits charge clouds in a way that keeps that form. It is built from points that span the cloud with few terms.

Few terms cut the sum cost to a straight growth in size. Straight growth lets teams treat big crystals with high care. High care sums test new stuff for chips and power gear. The work joins two sum paths in one fast frame. It aims at real stuff, not toy sets.
arxiv-2601-16779:
Luke Southall, Joshua Ammermann, Rinor Kelmendi, Domenik Eichhorn, and Ina Schaefer test claims made for quantum compilers. A compiler turns code for one chip to code for the next. Chip firms build their gear in vast, unlike ways. Sellers say their compilers retarget code with ease. Their 2026 preprint checks if those claims hold in real use.

The team runs code through such tools across chip types. They note where moves fail or lose skill. Clear grades help buyers pick tools with proof. They also push sellers to back claims with tests. Sound moves are key as quantum gear grows more mixed.
arxiv-2601-16979:
Dayal Singh Kalra and a team of six co-authors gauge the bend of a net's loss hills. Loss hills guide how a net learns from data. Their steep bends set how stable training is. The chief gauge is the top Hessian eigenvalue. That gauge shifts as the learning rate shifts. Their 2026 preprint builds a bend gauge that scales to vast nets.

Old bend gauges cost too much for big chatbots. Their gauge tracks bend through the full train run. It can flag when training nears a cliff. Such flags help labs tune big runs with less waste. They also deepen our grasp of why nets learn.
arxiv-2601-17279:
Sonu Kumar and four co-authors present SPADE, a compute engine for neural network work at the edge. Edge devices need math units that are exact, lean, and small. SPADE uses posit arithmetic. Posits taper their precision by value size. They span a wide range and resist some numeric flaws of older formats. The engine is built with SIMD lanes, so many values move at once.

The design targets deep network speed on tight power budgets. It must serve mixed numeric formats without waste. Such hardware could help phones, sensors, and small robots run AI on site. Local runs cut delay and keep data private. SPADE shows how new number formats can aid that goal.
arxiv-2601-17479:
Buddhadev Hajra studies how homotopy traits pass down maps between surfaces. He works with smooth complex affine surfaces. The maps are finite and surjective. A key trait is the Eilenberg-MacLane property. Hajra gives a clear counterexample. It shows that trait need not descend under proper maps in general. That negative result drives the rest of the work.

He then defines a weaker trait, finite homotopy rank-sum. The weaker trait may descend where the strong one fails. Knowing which traits survive maps guides algebraic geometry at large. Maps are how geometers link unlike shapes. A sound descent rule saves false proofs. Hajra's counterexample alone redraws the map.
arxiv-2601-17579:
Andreas Buchinger, Kresimir Burazin, Ivana Crnjac, and Marko Erceg study how rough media can be replaced by smooth rules. Their problems use a fractional form of diffusion. The local traits of the medium shift fast from place to place. The team asks which smooth rule the rough one acts like at large scale. Two kinds of convergence give the answer.

One kind covers the local part of the problem. The other covers the far-reaching part, which comes from the nonlocal form. A full answer tells users which end model they can trust. Such rules serve work on mixed materials and flow below ground. The study joins local and far effects in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17679:
Md Sazzadul Islam Ridoy and three co-authors present BanglaRobustNet for Bangla speech recognition. Bangla is one of the world's most spoken languages. It stays underrepresented in top speech research. Noise and speaker diversity make the gap worse. Their hybrid framework builds on Wav2Vec-BERT. It pairs denoising with attention in one design.

Robust recognition serves Bangla speakers in real settings. Streets, markets, and homes are noisy by nature. A model trained for quiet rooms fails there. Denoising up front gives the recognizer cleaner input. Attention then weighs the sounds that matter. The work pushes low-resource language tech forward. It shows gains need not wait for huge datasets.
arxiv-2601-17979:
Ahmad Abdelfattah and Massimiliano Fasi build a faster batch solver for a core matrix task on graphics chips. Their 2026 preprint deals with the singular value decomposition, or SVD. The SVD underpins tools like principal component analysis, low-rank fits, and randomized methods. Many jobs need not one SVD but thousands of small ones at once. That batch regime is where the authors aim.

Small problems behave unlike large ones on a GPU. Launch costs and memory moves can swamp the math. An efficient batch solver packs the work so the chip stays busy. Fast batch SVD speeds up data analysis, signal tools, and learning pipelines that call it again and again.
arxiv-2601-18079:
Edwin J. Son, Kyungmin Kim, and John J. Oh test whether a gap between star types survives a change in gravity theory. Their 2026 preprint works in Hořava-Lifshitz gravity. In general relativity, black holes and neutron stars differ in compactness, with a gap between them. Compactness says how much mass is packed into a given size. The authors show that this gap may vanish in the altered theory, where fermionic matter forms compact dark objects.

If the gap can close, some dark compact objects could be fermionic stars, not black holes. That possibility changes how odd objects in surveys get classified. The work gives observers a new hypothesis to test with mass and size data.
arxiv-2601-18179:
Yimeng Wang and co-authors explore tools that help therapists support clients between sessions. Their 2026 preprint deals with therapeutic homework, the tasks clients do on their own time. Such homework is essential to good therapy. Yet therapists face scattered client logs, assessments, and reflections, with very little prep time to sort them. The team ran a formative study with licensed therapists to learn what support they need. From that base, they explore customizable interactive tools for the task.

Tools that sort and surface the key parts of homework could save scarce minutes. They must still respect the privacy and nuance of care. The study grounds design in real clinic workflow, not in guesses.
arxiv-2601-18279:
Jiale Tang and Bin Zhu estimate the tones hidden in a noisy signal, using a filter bank with many outputs. Their 2026 preprint deals with line spectral estimation. The task is to find the frequencies of complex sinusoids buried in noise. Their estimator uses atomic norm minimization joined with Georgiou's filter bank, known as the G-filter, across multiple output vectors. A prior version of the method was limited to a single filtered output. The new one integrates several outputs at once.

More outputs can steady the estimate when noise is strong. Frequency estimates feed radar, sonar, and communications. A method that uses all filtered views should beat one that throws most away.
arxiv-2601-18379:
Joydeep Roy studies how dark matter may have formed in the young cosmos through a slow path called freeze-in. In that path, dark stuff speaks only in a faint way with the stuff we can see. It builds up bit by bit and never quite joins the hot mix around it. The path stands as a real choice next to the more known freeze-out path.

Roy adds a new part to the cast: a leptoquark, a thing that can link quarks with leptons. In his setup the leptoquark talks both to dark matter and to the known parts of the world. The math then traces how much dark matter such talks would leave behind. A match with the share seen in space would mark the setup as one worth a search at labs.
arxiv-2601-18779:
Yuxiao Qu and four colleagues give hard tasks a new way to train thought tools: let a guide show the path, but never hand it the goal. On hard tasks, a tool that learns from its own tries may make no good try at all. With no good try, there is no gain to learn from, and training stalls. Past fixes train the tool on pro-made solves. That can bend the tool to a style not its own.

Their plan, named POPE, uses pro solves just to steer where the tool looks. The tool still makes all tries in its own style and learns from its own wins. The guide's facts are used as a map, not as a text to copy. That split could free training on the hard-est tasks. It may also keep the tool's own voice whole as it grows.
arxiv-2601-18979:
Supriya Khadka and Sanchari Das set out design rules for extended reality tools for young children. Virtual and augmented reality can draw young learners in, but children change fast as they grow. Tools built without care can overload their minds or clash with their senses.

Their frame, called Augmented Human Development, models the child's mind, senses, setting, and growth stage together. It aims to keep the pull of immersive tech while cutting the risks for the youngest users. Teachers and builders get a way to check a design against how young children truly take in the world.
arxiv-2601-19179:
Qipeng Zhan and four co-authors order the inner codes of an autoencoder so they reveal a data set's true dimension. Autoencoders squeeze data into a small inner code and then rebuild it. In a plain linear case, the right tweaks make that code match the ordered axes of principal component analysis.

The team builds a principal component autoencoder that keeps that order in curved, nonlinear cases too. Ordered codes let them read off the intrinsic dimension, the number of true degrees of freedom in the data. Knowing that number guides how big a model needs to be for a given data set.
arxiv-2601-19379:
Yidong Wu and Luo Luo give an async optimizer that keeps its speed under heavy tailed noise. In distributed training, workers finish at wildly unlike times. Gradient noise can also be heavy tailed, with rare huge spikes that wreck plain methods.

Their method is an asynchronous normalized stochastic gradient descent with momentum. Workers update on their own clocks, and the normalization tames the spikes. The analysis shows the method hits the optimal time complexity under a mild moment assumption. Robust async training matters as models and clusters grow ever larger.
arxiv-2601-19479:
Victoria Catterall, Cise Midoglu, and Stephen Lynch forecast when elite women's footballers will get hurt. Injuries in football carry personal, competitive, and financial costs for players and teams. The team sets a time to injury task: not just whether a player gets hurt, but when.

Their method uses DeepHit, a survival model that handles competing risks over time. Athlete monitoring data and clear visual displays feed the work. A fair warning window lets medical staff ease loads and target prevention, though such forecasts must be handled with care around selection and privacy.
arxiv-2601-19679:
Pooja, Dana Avramescu, and Tuomas Lappi study the first instant of a heavy-ion collision. When two nuclei smash at near light speed, they briefly form the glasma, a state of intense colour fields. Tiny disturbances in those fields grow with time. How they grow controls how fast the chaos spreads and heat begins to form.

The authors show the growth is exponential in the square root of time. They read this rate as a Lyapunov exponent, the standard measure of chaos in a system. A Lyapunov exponent links microscopic chaos to entropy production, the creation of disorder. It also sets the thermalization timescale, when the system starts behaving like a hot fluid. The result sharpens theory of the universe's earliest microseconds, recreated in colliders.
arxiv-2601-19879:
Zach Hunter, Cosmin Pohoata, Jacques Verstraete, and Shengtong Zhang connect two problems in combinatorics. One concerns point-line incidences: points and lines in a finite geometry, and the graph recording which points lie on which lines. The other is the Furstenberg-Sárközy problem from arithmetic combinatorics, about patterns in dense sets of integers.

Using that connection, the authors construct unexpectedly large induced matchings in the incidence graph. A matching pairs points with lines exclusively; induced means no extra incidences sneak in. Large matchings in turn yield small Nikodym sets, sets that contain a full line in every direction. Such constructions test the limits of finite geometry. They often feed back into number theory and theoretical computer science.
arxiv-2601-19979:
Temple He, Jaeha Lee, and Hirosi Ooguri use reinforcement learning to explore a structure from quantum gravity. The holographic entropy cone collects all entropy patterns that holography allows for several regions. A vector inside the cone can be realised by a graph whose minimum cuts reproduce its entropies. Vectors outside admit no such graph.

Their algorithm searches for a graph realisation matching a target entropy vector. When none exists, it finds the graph whose entropies come closest. That near miss helps probe where the cone's boundary lies. Mapping this cone constrains how information can be organised in holographic theories. Machine search reaches cases that hand analysis cannot. The work blends learning algorithms with deep questions in theoretical physics.
arxiv-2601-20179:
Xuanyu Pan, Dingxin Zhang, and Xiping Zhang bound the topology of hypersurfaces inside a possibly singular projective variety. They look at the total Betti number, a count that summarizes the holes and cycles of a shape. For a hypersurface of a given degree inside the variety, they show this count grows in a controlled way with the degree.

Their bound depends on the degree of the ambient variety and an explicit constant that does not depend on the hypersurface. Such bounds matter in algebraic geometry, where they limit how complex a space cut out by equations can be. The result extends control to ambient spaces that are themselves singular.
arxiv-2601-20379:
Zhengbo Jiao and a large team present Policy of Thoughts, a way to scale the reasoning of large language models at test time. Models struggle with long, complex reasoning, and one cause is their frozen policy: their strategy cannot change mid-task. Current test-time methods use execution feedback only to filter or rewrite attempts.

Policy of Thoughts instead lets the model internalize that feedback and evolve its own policy while it works. The reasoning strategy itself improves during the task. If it works, models could handle longer problems without retraining, by learning from their own trial and error in the moment.
arxiv-2601-20579:
Hui-Chun Zhang and Xi-Ping Zhu study a heat flow for harmonic maps in this 2026 math paper. A harmonic map is a map between shapes that stretches them as little as possible. The flow slowly changes such a map over time, much like heat spreads out. Here the maps land in CAT(0) spaces, a broad class of spaces with no positive curve.

The authors trace the line of work behind their question. In 1964, Eells and Sampson proved long-time existence and convergence for flows into spaces that do not curve up. Hamilton later took up the same flow with boundary conditions added. In 1992, Gromov and Schoen built a theory of such maps into CAT(0) spaces. Zhang and Zhu ask how smooth, in the Lipschitz sense, these flows stay.
arxiv-2601-20779:
Théo Delemazure studies a fairness rule for elections in this 2026 paper. The rule is the independence of clones axiom. Two candidates count as perfect clones when every voter ranks them side by side. If they are true clones, removing one should not change who wins. Delemazure asks whether this still holds for approximate clones.

The paper works with ordinal elections, where voters rank candidates in order. Approximate clones are pairs that voters rank nearly, but not exactly, side by side. Real elections often have such near-duplicate candidates. The question is whether the clone rule survives small errors in the rankings. The answer matters for voting systems that want to resist spoiler effects from copycat candidates.
arxiv-2601-21079:
Maximillian Newman builds a new backward-in-time model of family lines in split populations. The 2026 paper concerns the structured coalescent for diploid populations. The model lives on finite graphs, where each node holds a subpopulation. It allows large migrations between nodes. It also allows uneven offspring distributions, where some parents contribute far more than others. Both features strain older models.

The new model is quenched, meaning the environment is fixed before averaging. It generalizes two earlier models. One is the mean-field model of Birkner and co-authors. The other is Möhle's haploid structured model. Diploid organisms carry two gene copies, which complicates ancestry. Newman's framework handles that case with big moves and skewed families allowed. It serves population geneticists who reconstruct history from present-day genes.
arxiv-2601-22279:
E. Lopez-Saavedra and a large team take a deep look at one reaction that fuels X-ray bursts on dead stars. Their 2026 preprint studies how a proton strikes copper and frees an alpha particle, leaving nickel behind. The reaction also runs in winds blown off a fresh neutron star after a collapse.

The team set tight bounds on how fast the reaction runs in real bursts. That rate helps fix the heat and light a burst gives off. It also shapes which new nuclei the burst can build. Better rates mean burst models rest on firmer ground. Observers can then read burst light with more trust.
arxiv-2601-22379:
Bailin Wang, Dan Friedman, Tao Lei, and Chong Wang fix a flaw in fast attention for long texts. Block-sparse attention reads only picked chunks, which saves huge cost. Their 2026 preprint notes that dropped chunks take their context with them, and picks can miss the mark.

Their method, SPLA, picks chunks with a sharper score, drawn from second-order cues. It then keeps a light linear path so dropped chunks still leave a trace. The goal is long memory at low cost. That goal matters for book-length and code-length tasks. The work refines a key speed trick.
arxiv-2601-22479:
Muzzamal Shaukat, Charles Wallace, Anatoly Svidzinsky, and Marlan Scully study paired atoms that fall through space at a steady push. Their 2026 preprint explores Dicke states, where two atoms act as one in how they glow. The pair sit in the right Rindler wedge, the zone of space an accelerated watcher can see.

The team find the terms under which the pair glow as one bright state, or hide in a dark one. Such work tests quantum effects tied to acceleration and horizons. It links lab atom physics to deep claims about space. The states may also serve future sensors.
arxiv-2601-23279:
N. Ahmadiniaz, F. Bastianelli, F. Karbstein, and C. Schubert continue a study of photon-graviton mixing in an electromagnetic field. Einstein-Maxwell theory predicts photons and gravitons can convert into each other inside such fields. At one-loop level, the effect produces magnetic dichroism, a difference in absorption by polarization.

Earlier work assumed only two diagrams contributed to the one-loop amplitude. The authors point out a third, involving a tadpole subdiagram. Complete amplitudes matter for proposals to detect gravitons through light. A constant electromagnetic field is the setting, where the newly noticed tadpole diagram completes the one-loop amplitude.
arxiv-2603-01879:
Chi-Ning Chou, Artem Kirsanov, Yao-Yuan Yang, and SueYeon Chung predict model failure from the shape of its internal representations. Their 2026 work borrows the biomarker idea from medicine: a system-level measure that flags future trouble. Reverse-engineering every circuit gives insight, but rarely a clear early warning for deployment.

The team designs network markers that probe how task-relevant object manifolds sit in representation space. Two geometric measures stand out: effective manifold dimensionality and a utility score for those manifolds. When both shrink on familiar data, performance on shifted data tends to fall soon after. The pattern holds across architectures, optimizers, and data sets in image classification. In transfer learning from a large pre-trained model, the same markers beat plain accuracy at forecasting shifted performance.
arxiv-2603-02179:
Jérémie Bettinelli and Dimitri Korkotashvili link two kinds of maps on surfaces in this 2026 mathematics paper. A map here is a graph drawn on a surface, split into faces. Some maps are bipartite, meaning their points split into two sets with links only across. The authors build a two-way match between general maps and bipartite ones.

Their method cuts along a chosen loop, slides one side by one notch, then sews it back. That small move flips the parity of loops that cross the cut. For doughnut-shaped maps with a single face, loops have a simple form. That makes the full link between the two map types clear. A paired swapping map on even-faced maps supports the argument.
arxiv-2603-02479:
Rituraj Sharma, Weiyuan Chen, and Noah Provenzano guide deep reasoning with step-level scores in this 2026 paper. DeepThink methods generate many candidate solutions, refine them, and merge the best. Without reliable correctness signals mid-search, deeper thought can amplify errors. Correct minority answers get drowned out, and extra compute yields little.

Their algorithm, PRISM, uses a process reward model that grades each reasoning step. Candidates act like particles in a landscape defined by those grades. Score-guided resampling and random refinement concentrate the population on strong reasoning while keeping diversity. On math and science benchmarks, PRISM matched or beat rival DeepThink methods. A mid-size model using it rivaled one six times larger. Analysis shows steady net correction during refinement, even from weak starting pools.
arxiv-2603-02879:
Fiona Spuler, Marlene Kretschmer, Magdalena Alonso Balmaseda, and colleagues separate the tangled influences of two oceans on East African rain. Their 2026 paper targets the short rains over the Greater Horn of Africa, which respond to both Pacific and Indian Ocean patterns. Untangling joint climate signals matters for seasonal forecasts, but model experiments carry model biases.

Their method, DAG-VAE, fuses deep learning with causal reasoning by planting a physics-based causal graph inside an autoencoder's hidden space. Trained on forecast archives, it recovered response patterns matching costly ocean-swap experiments. Trained on observations, it found a different Pacific influence, exposing possible model bias. It can also generate what-if versions of extreme rainy seasons for planning ahead.
arxiv-2603-03479:
Yacob Medhin, Tushar Sial, and Simone Servadio design a spacecraft and its flight path together instead of separately. Electric propulsion missions are usually planned with fixed thrust and efficiency, ignoring how power supply, propulsion, and trajectory pull on each other. Far from the Sun, where light is weak, those shortcuts can doom a design. Their 2026 framework optimizes all three at once as one coupled problem.

A detailed model of the SPT-140 Hall thruster ties thrust and efficiency to the moment-by-moment solar power available, including array degradation. The time-optimal trajectory problem runs on NASA's OpenMDAO and Dymos toolchains with efficient gradient methods. The demonstration case inserts a spacecraft into orbit around asteroid 16 Psyche, a regime where dim sunlight makes power-aware design critical. Results expose the key trade-offs realistic mission planning must respect.
arxiv-2603-03579:
Kunzhe Song, Maxime Zingraff, and Huacheng Zeng sense human movement with radio signals that already fill the air. Radio sensing sees through walls and darkness while preserving privacy, but the useful spectrum below ten gigahertz is scarce and contested. Their 2026 system, Ambient Radio Sensing, refuses to ask for new spectrum. It repurposes live 5G and Wi-Fi transmissions for sensing without disturbing their communication job.

A standalone device passively receives ambient signals, amplifies them to illuminate the surroundings, and captures reflections through a self-mixing radio design. That hardware extracts motion and angle features from ordinary communication waveforms. A cross-modal learning scheme lets a ready-made vision model supervise the radio model's training. The prototype, tested extensively on ambient 5G signals, estimates human skeletons accurately and segments body masks, proving the borrowed-spectrum approach.
arxiv-2603-03679:
Shunhao Ji and three colleagues report a burst of high-energy neutrinos from an exploding star, too powerful for the obvious explanation. The star, supernova 2017hcd, is a Type IIn, whose light comes from ejecta smashing into dense surrounding material. Analyzing public track-like data from the IceCube observatory, their 2026 paper finds a neutrino flare at nearly four-sigma significance. The flare lasted a month or two and was centered about two weeks before the supernova was even discovered optically.

The flare's total energy, spread evenly in all directions, comes out about a hundred times the energy of the explosion's ejecta. The ejecta-into-surroundings scenario cannot pay that bill. The authors instead point to a choked jet, a jet launched by the collapse but strangled inside the star's envelope, as the likely source of the flare.

The second volume of Twiss's Rolls Series edition of Bracton appeared in 1879. Bracton's thirteenth-century treatise set English law in order for the first time, and Twiss printed it with a facing English translation. Each volume of the edition carried the vast work one stage further.

Volume 2 treats the law of persons, property, and inheritance as Bracton's England knew it. It explains who could hold land, how estates passed at death, and what rights wives, heirs, and lords held. The rules are drawn from decided cases, so the reader sees the common law reasoning its way forward. For students of medieval society, the volume is also a record of how land and family bound people's lives together.
