Serial reports build a moving picture. Kirk could correct earlier views as events shifted. Readers watch an envoy adjusting his counsel in near-real time. The document also shows the burden on posts outside the room: Italy's fate was being weighed by men it could not address. Kirk's letters were its voice by proxy.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d879:
Britain's delegation circulated this memorandum on political principles for Germany at Babelsberg on July 24, 1945. It returns to two points the Economic Sub-Committee had raised but the foreign secretaries had not taken up. The Soviet side had argued both points were political, not economic.

The British ask that both points be written into the agreed text. One new clause would call for uniform treatment of the German population across all zones, so far as practical. A second clause would allow free travel by land and air for citizens of the four powers in every zone. The paper quotes the earlier sub-committee report to make its case.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d979:
William Clayton and Emilio Collado sent this secret telegram from London to Willard Thorp on August 16, 1945. Like its companion message, it explains the German economic decisions taken at Potsdam. The two men resist a reading they see growing in Washington: that the reparations operating deal means the end of four-power treatment of Germany.

The economic principles, they point out, still charge the Control Council with common policies. Those policies cover deindustrialization, reparation deliveries, import and export programs, living standards, and food distribution. Common rulings are still needed on external assets, restitution, Allied property, and gold. General Clay, they add, trusts he can win some shared policies, and that effort should not be dropped early.
frus-1958-60v19-d79: A 1958-1960 FRUS memorandum of conversation on China. The talks were recorded. This entry preserves that conversation. Coming generations can find it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
gao-gaoreports-b-295579: Systems, Studies, and Simulation ran its March 2005 challenge at GAO, and the ruling delivers the verdict. The simulator firm's protest was judged in full detail. The simulation ended at the gavel. The gavel had the last word. The verdict was delivered.
gao-gaoreports-b-295879: United Valve took its April 2005 contract fight to GAO, and the ruling lands the verdict. The valve maker said the award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Valve contracts get the same fair hearing. Valve contracts get the same fair hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297879: BAE Systems Norfolk Ship Repair took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Shipyards get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-400379: This 2008 GAO ruling is about designated Employee Agent at John Gage. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-179: DHS's buying shop got a GAO check in 2005, and the report covers the wins and the growing pains. The review grades the build-out. The homeland's shoppers deserved the competence. The competence was being built. The build continued. The shop was graded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-379: The national energy policy inventory got a GAO review in 2005, and the report catalogs major federal energy programs and recommendation status. The findings take the measure. The report shows the power plans were counted. The inventory had to be complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-479: Contractor suspension data needed better reporting in 2005, and GAO's report says additional data could improve the debarment process. The findings demand the information. The report warns that the banned vendors deserved tracking. The reporting had to be better. The banned vendors deserved tracking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-779: Drug price trends got a GAO tracking in 2005, and the report covers brand and generic prices from 2000 through 2004. The findings do the math. The report warns that the patients deserved honest prices. The trends had to be understood. The patients deserved honest prices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-879: Graduation rate definitions needed better Education help in 2005, and GAO's report says the department could do more to help states define rates. The findings demand the guidance. The report warns that the diplomas deserved honest counting. The help had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-979: The Byrd Amendment's dumping payouts got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines issues and effects of the offset act. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the tariff rebates deserved honest reckoning. The effects had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-379: Federal workplace safety needed strategy in 2006, and GAO's report says OSHA could improve agencies' safety programs with a more strategic approach. The findings demand the plan. The report warns that the government's own workers deserved safe jobs. The approach had to be strategic.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-479: America's far-flung outposts needed better math in 2006, and GAO's report says honest cost counts and yardsticks were due. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the global footprint's worth should be proven. The worth had to be shown.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-579: Clean water loan funds got a GAO review in 2006, and the report examines how states allocated the revolving funds and measured benefits. The findings do the accounting. The report shows the water dollars were being tracked. The benefits had to be measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-79: Fair housing intake needed more consistency in 2005, and GAO's report says HUD needed better assurance that investigations were thorough. The findings demand the rigor. The report warns that the discrimination claims deserved full probes. The processes had to be thorough.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-979: The Coast Guard's buoys and icebreakers were wearing out in 2006, and GAO's report says the condition of some vessels had declined, affecting the mission. The findings document the wear. The report warns that the guardians of the waterways needed sound ships. The fleet had to float.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-379: The Doha trade talks were at a crossroads in 2007, and GAO's report says Congress faced key decisions as the push intensified. The findings frame the choices. The report warns that the round the world was watching could collapse on America's watch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-679: Counting the true cost of government was a coin toss in 2007 — GAO's report finds cost-accounting habits varied wildly across ten agencies. The findings show a Tower of Babel in budget-speak. The report's plea: one honest math, so managers can actually manage.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-79: Hospital accreditation had a conflict problem in 2007, and GAO's report examines the Joint Commission's ties to its affiliated consulting business. The findings probe the relationship. The report warns that the hospital grader should not also be the hospital's paid coach. The grades had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-879: Mobile-home buyers deserved a fair shake in 2007 — GAO's report says the housing agency should study how proposed loan-rule changes would hit them. The findings put the spotlight on factory-built housing, the most affordable roof for millions. Policy tweaks, GAO warns, land hardest on those with the thinnest margins.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-379: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on defense Acquisitions: Termination Costs Are Generally Not a Compelling Reason to Continue Programs or Contracts That Otherwise Warrant Ending. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-79: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report warning that the Census Bureau needed to improve its risk management of the computer systems built for the decennial count. With 2010 approaching, the systems for collecting and processing census data faced schedule and performance risks. GAO's findings preview the IT troubles that would later force the bureau to scrap and rebuild parts of its 2010 technology.
george-progress-poverty-1879:
Henry George published Progress and Poverty in 1879 in San Francisco. George, a self-taught economist and journalist, asked why poverty deepens as wealth and progress grow. His answer made the book the best-selling economics work of the nineteenth century.

George blamed private ownership of land: rent rises with progress, so landlords gain what labor and capital earn. His remedy was a single tax on land value, replacing other taxes and leaving buildings untaxed. Millions read him, and land reform movements rose on several continents in his name. Critics disputed the remedy, but the question he posed, why progress and poverty travel together, still has force.
habeas-corpus-act-1679:
England's Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act in 1679 to stop prisoners from being held without answers. Under the old writ, a jailer had to bring a prisoner before a judge and explain the arrest. In practice, officials had found ways to delay, move, or hide prisoners.

The act sets firm deadlines for producing a prisoner and gives penalties for officials who dodge the writ. It also bars sending prisoners to distant places beyond the court's reach. These rules made unlawful detention much harder to sustain. The statute became a model for legal systems far beyond England.
haeckel-freedom-in-science-and-teaching-: Freedom in Science and Teaching, Haeckel's 1879 work. The academic freedom. This book preserves that book. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol1-1879:
Constantine Hering spent a lifetime gathering drug symptoms, and The Guiding Symptoms of Our Materia Medica began appearing in 1879. Volume I opens his great American materia medica, a work his students finished after his death. Hering tested remedies on healthy volunteers and recorded every change they felt.

The symptoms are sorted by part of the body, from mind and head down through the frame. Marks show which signs Hering trusted most, confirmed in practice again and again. Prescribers prized the set as a storehouse drawn from real provings, and the first volume sets the pattern the rest follow.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol2-1879:
Volume II of Hering's Guiding Symptoms, issued in 1879, carries the great symptom record forward. Constantine Hering had died with the work unfinished, so his students and family saw the volumes through the press. The plan stays the same: remedies in order, their signs grouped by region of the body.

What sets these pages apart is the grading worked into the text. Strong marks flag the symptoms seen most often and cured most surely, the true guiding signs. A prescriber could scan a remedy and find its heart at a glance. The volume keeps Hering's lifetime of proving work within easy reach.
hume-dialogues-natural-religion-1779:
David Hume wrote his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion in his last years, and they were published in 1779, after his death. Three speakers carry the debate: Cleanthes, who defends the argument from design; Demea, who speaks for orthodox faith; and Philo, the skeptic who asks the hard questions. Their topic is the being and nature of God.

Philo presses the design argument until its likeness between world and machine wears thin. Suffering, disorder, and rival causes all enter his case. Cleanthes answers with warmth, and the dialogue never quite declares a winner. The work became the classic demolition of natural theology in English, and the most readable of Hume's philosophical writings.
jevons-theory-political-economy-1879:
W Stanley Jevons published The Theory of Political Economy in 1879 in its second edition, first issued in 1871. Jevons, a Manchester economist and logician, helped start the marginalist revolution. That turn rebuilt economics on the value of one more unit, not on labor alone.

Jevons argued that utility, the satisfaction a good gives, rules value, and that each added unit gives less than the last. He cast exchange and labor in math, treating economics as a calculus of pleasure and pain. Ricardo and Mill had stressed cost; Jevons stressed the buyer. His theory, with Menger and Walras abroad, remade the science, and the second edition spread it in a fuller form.
jewett-old-friends-new-1879:
Early tales fill Old Friends and New, under copyright of 1879. Jewett was still in her twenties and finding her voice when she wrote them. A later list of her books shows how wide her output grew, from Deephaven to The Tory Lover.

Old neighbors, summer visitors, and village oddballs people these gentle New England stories. Readers can watch a fine writer take shape page by page. Her ear for local speech, her love of place, and her pity for plain folk are all here already. The book offers a warm window on the start of a classic American career that lasted three more decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ludassy-gans-mo:
Moriz Ludassy (1825–1885) was a Hungarian journalist born at Komorn, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer gives his career. As early as 1848 he edited two Budapest papers and argued the Conservative cause in both. He died at Reichenau, after decades spent between Budapest and Vienna.

About fifteen years after 1848, Ludassy helped found the Vienna paper “Debatte,” which backed dual government for Austria and Hungary and equal standing for both lands. Under Premier Andrassy he ran the Hungarian press bureau, and Minister Beust later set him to edit the court party’s paper during the war of 1870–71. He was made a Hungarian noble for his services. The entry also notes his son Julius, a Vienna editor and comedy writer. It records a press career spent close to power.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mantino-jacob-b:
Jacob ben Samuel Mantino, an Italian physician and translator, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His family left Tortosa, Spain, at the expulsion of 1492. He studied medicine and philosophy at Padua and Bologna. Settling at Bologna, he translated scientific works from Hebrew into Latin. He died at Damascus in 1549.

The article follows a career built on powerful patients. Pope Clement VII's courtiers befriended him, and war in 1527 drove him to Verona. At Venice the Council of Ten freed him from wearing the Jews' hat. A marshal of France he had treated made that privilege perpetual. Henry VIII's divorce case then put him in danger: consulted by the pope, he ruled against the king. Under Paul III he became the pope's own physician. He also crushed the messianic dreamer Solomon Molko at Rome. The entry shows a Jewish doctor at the summit of papal politics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-levi-1:
Meir ben Levi, an Austrian Talmudist and Bible commentator of the early eighteenth century, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn. A native of Zolkiev, he worked as an anthologist of the Geonim, the early medieval heads of the Babylonian academies. Under the title "Likkute Shoshannim," Gatherings of Lilies, printed at Jessnitz in 1722, he compiled their comments and fresh readings on the Pentateuch, arranged in the order of the weekly lessons.

The entry then follows the book through a second life. Meir revised the collection, added notes of his own, and published it under a new title, "Miksheh Zahab." From the preface of the second edition, printed at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1733, the editors infer that the first edition had actually been printed at Zolkiev without a date. Two bibliographies, Benjacob's and Steinschneider's, anchor the notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menelaus-known-:
Menelaus was the high priest who bought his office from Antiochus IV. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé judge him harshly in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article first settles his origin. Against Josephus, it follows Second Maccabees in making him a Benjaminite, brother of the Simeon who betrayed Onias III. He was no member of the priestly house. Sent to Antioch with the tribute, he outbid the sitting high priest Jason. Jason was his patron's candidate, and Menelaus took the office for a higher price.

His first act was to seize the Temple's sacred vessels to pay what he owed. When the deposed Onias III denounced the robbery publicly, Menelaus procured his murder through the king's lieutenant Andronicus, who had shared the plunder. The entry presents him as the extreme of the Hellenizing party. He professed contempt for his fathers' religion and was ready for any crime ambition required.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-10779:
Michael, whose name asks Who is like El, is the archangel presented in the book of Daniel as the chief prince and guardian of Israel. Joseph Jacobs, M. Seligsohn, and Mary W. Montgomery wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on him in 1906. It draws on Daniel, the Talmud, the Book of Enoch, and cabalistic writings.

In Daniel, Michael helps the prophet against the angel of Persia and stands by Israel in the time of trouble. Later writings make him Israel's advocate, the angel of mercy who taught Enoch the mysteries of justice. The article follows his feud with Samael, Israel's accuser, and his fights with the guardian angels of other nations on Israel's behalf.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mishnah-constru:
Mishnah is the oral law of Judaism. It gets a foundational Jewish Encyclopedia article published in 1906, by the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Solomon Schechter. The word comes from shanah, to repeat. It was taught and learned by recitation, handed down by mouth, not written. In its concrete sense it means the body of traditional doctrine formed by the early third century.

The article sets Mishnah against Miḳra, the written and read law. It counts the term's territory generously. The halakic midrashim belong inside it, as the sources use the term. So does the Tosefta, the explanatory additions. For a reader meeting the word across Jewish literature, the entry fixes both the etymology and the boundaries of the corpus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-evreux:
Moses of Evreux was a French tosafist of the first half of the thirteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was the older brother, and the teacher, of the tosafist Samuel of Evreux. He also wrote a siddur, a prayer book.

His lasting work is the Tosafot of Evreux, also called the Shittah of Evreux, which later tosafists used heavily. Moses wrote his glosses in the margin of a copy of Isaac Alfasi, whose authority he invoked. His name is quoted again and again in the printed tosafot. The entry shows how one school's marginal notes became a standard tool.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moszkowski-mori:
Moritz Moszkowski was a German pianist and composer born at Breslau on August 23, 1854. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Trained at Breslau, Dresden, and Berlin, he taught for some years in Berlin. In 1873 he toured Germany, Russia, and France with success.

An accident to his arm kept Moszkowski off the concert stage for years. In that quiet he wrote some of his best music. Chopin's influence runs through his works. His Spanish Dances and other piano pieces won great vogue, and his opera Bobadil pleased Berlin in 1892. In 1897 he removed to Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahman-bar-isaa:
Nahman bar Isaac was a Babylonian amora who died in 356, a pupil of Nahman bar Jacob. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His learning was honored early, and he was chosen resh kallah at Sura. When Raba died, Nahman succeeded him as head of the school at Pumbedita.

His great work was preservation: he collected, arranged, and transmitted the teachings of earlier masters. To fix them in memory he coined mnemonic sentences, an early step toward the Talmud's redaction. Of himself he said that he was neither sage nor seer, only a transmitter and codifier. His own maxims condemn pride, conceit, and anger, and his wit ran to puns and proverbs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-marcu:
Marcus Nathanson was a Russian scholar of old Hebrew books. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Wilna in 1793. He died at Telsh, in Kovno, on June 10, 1868. He married into the family of Joshua Zeitels.

Nathanson gave his life to ancient Hebrew literature. One work gives sharp notes on Midrash Tehillim chapters. Another treats Jewish proper names and their forms. A third study, printed in Debir in 1864, covers the Karaites. His writings appeared in Hebrew journals of his time. The entry is brief, but it marks a careful critic. His name rests on these three studies alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuss-11479:
Neuss is a city of Rhenish Prussia with a hard Jewish past. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish community reaches back to the eleventh century. Persecution and martyrdom mark its record throughout. Crusaders sheltered there briefly, then turned killer.

In June 1096 a mob massacred all two hundred Jews there. Samuel b. Asher and his sons died by torture. Jews returned and built a flourishing community within a century. In 1197 seven Jews were broken on the wheel. A mother was buried alive in that same fury. The town suffered again in the Black Death year, 1349. By 1903 only 240 Jews remained in Neuss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nola-elijah-ben:
Elijah ben Joseph di Nola served Rome as rabbi. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Isaac Broydé for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was an Italian physician of the 1500s. In 1563 he held the rabbinate at Rome. His name carried weight in Talmudic questions.

Rabbis consulted him on points of Jewish law. One ruling of his touched levirate marriages directly. He sent it to Eliakim of Macerata in writing. Lampronti later printed it in his Paḥad Yiẓḥaḳ. Nola was also a keen student of philosophy. He turned Robert of Lincoln's physics into Hebrew. Moses Alatino thanked him for help with Themistius. That help served a Latin rendering of Aristotle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oil-11679:
Oil, in the Bible, means olive oil for the most part. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Löw wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. With grain and wine, it was a chief good of Palestine. At an early date it was sent to Egypt. It was sent to Phoenicia, a land of trade, as well.

Oil stood in for fat and butter in the home. It served for food, for light, and for care of the skin. It served for drugs and cures as well. In old times it was kept in horns. Later it was kept in flasks and in jars. It came to stand for wealth and rich land. In the Mishnah age, oils came from more plants. Sesame, nuts, and the castor plant all gave oil then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orphan-11779:
An orphan is a child who has lost a parent or both. M. Seligsohn, the board, and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word is yatom, in the old texts. Most English texts render it as the word fatherless. One verse in Lamentations renders it as orphans in full.

The Bible shows orphans as weak folk with no shield. So its law bids men again and again to be just. No man was to press hard on such a child. God is called the father of the fatherless there. Job points to the wrong done to orphans as deep sin. In Talmud law the orphan holds a place of favor. No set age ends that place in the rules. It lasts while the boy can not run his own affairs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paltoi-b-abayi-:
Paltoi ben Abayi was Gaon of Pumbedita for years. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Gaon was the head of a great school in Babylon. Paltoi held that post from 842 to 858. He was the first of a line of great geonim.

Under Paltoi the school at Pumbedita grew strong in sway. The exilarch had to come there to call a great meet. Paltoi ruled with a strict and firm hand at all times. In one of his letters he pressed a point of law. He urged that the ban be brought back in full use. That ban cut a man off for breach of the Law. Many of his replies on points of law have been kept. They stand in a book called Sha'are Zedek.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-i-11979:
Pedro the First ruled Portugal from 1357 to 1367. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His motto held that justice is to the state what the soul is to the body. Jews found that motto real in his court.

Two young nobles robbed and killed a Jewish peddler. The king grieved for their long service to him. Nobles begged him to spare the killers. He still had both men beheaded for the crime. He also shielded the Jews of Coimbra from clergy raids. His own doctor was the chief rabbi, Moses Navarro.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peyrehorade-heb:
Peyrehorade is a small town in the Landes of France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews from Spain and Portugal settled nearby about 1500. They named their small community Beth-El, house of God. Their cemetery ranks among the first in the district.

The settlers first answered to the community of Bayonne. Later they refused its rule and faced a ban. In 1680 the Inquisition seized one of their men. He was condemned to burn at the stake. A royal decree of 1684 expelled ninety-three families. By 1904 only two or three families remained.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-piove-di-sacco-:
Piove di Sacco is a small town near Padua, in Italy. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was the first town there to admit Jews. A Jewish loan bank opened before 1373.

When Padua banned Jewish lending in 1455, business shifted here. Paduan Jews lent through their fellow bankers at Piove. The town never built a ghetto for Jews. Its fame rests on a Hebrew printing press. There the Arba Turim was printed in 1475. Whole copies of that fine edition are now very rare.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-wilma-12:
Wilma Popper was a Hungarian writer of tales, born at Raab in 1857. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was schooled in her home town. She began to write at an early age. German journals printed many essays from her pen.

Popper's books are volumes of stories and sketches. Her Fairy Tales and Stories came out at Leipsic in 1891. Old-Fashioned People followed in 1894. Miniatures came out in 1897. New tales followed a year later. She kept up a steady pace of new books. Later volumes include Eccentrics, Against the Stream, and Five from One Pod. Her last listed book came out at Vienna in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-professions-sta:
Professions held by Jews, counted in numbers, are the subject of an article by Joseph Jacobs. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. For long, Jews were shut out of most professions. Medicine was the one door left open to them. Few could enter the rest without a university place.

Once the universities opened, Jews poured into the professions. They came in shares far past their share of the people. Foes of the Jews cried out at this rush. They claimed the Jews were taking the professions over. Jacobs sets out the true counts trade by trade. He lets the numbers answer the loud charge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-hiyya-: Rabbah bar Hiyya of Ctesiphon was a Babylonian teacher of the second set. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is said to have done one rite in a rare way. The rite is halizah, the shoe rite of release. Most teachers held his way to be wrong. One tanna alone allowed the rite in that form. Samuel rebuked him for doing it so.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rappoltsweiler-:
Rappoltsweiler is a town in Upper Alsace, also called Ribeauvillé. Gotthard Deutsch and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its first known record of Jews dates from 1321. That year the emperor pledged its Jews for a loan.

The article tells a hard history of attack and return. In 1337 many Jews were killed or driven out. In 1349 the Black Death wiped out the community. Jews later settled again and stayed into the 1500s. Banishment followed, then return in the 1600s under a tax. By 1784 the town had 58 Jewish families. The entry shows a small town's Jewish life rebuilt many times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rivera-12779:
Rivera is a Spanish Jewish family found early in American history. Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The family seems to have come from Seville, Spain. Some members have been traced to Portugal instead.

The article says many Riveras settled in Mexico before 1650. Their names appear in an Inquisition trial there. Gabriel de Granada was tried from 1642 to 1645. Six Rivera women appear as accomplices in observing Moses' law. They were labeled Judaizing heretics in that record. The name is often written Ribera as well. The entry then profiles Abraham Rodrigues de Rivera. He was the first Rivera in North America, they say. He died at Newport, Rhode Island, in 1765.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-toby-:
Toby Edward Rosenthal was an American artist born at New Haven, Connecticut, on March 15, 1848. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His family moved to San Francisco in 1855, where he first studied art.

In 1865 Rosenthal went to Munich and trained under Piloty at the Royal Academy. He won medals at exhibitions in Munich and at Philadelphia in 1876. His Morning Prayers in Bach's Family, from 1870, hangs in the Leipzig museum. Other known canvases include Elaine, The Dancing Lesson, and A Mother's Prayer. Most of his pictures were also exhibited across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-senior-12:
Senior Sachs was a Russo-French Hebrew scholar born at Kaidany, near Kovno, on June 17, 1816. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His father, a rabbi, taught him Hebrew and Talmud as a boy.

Sachs early fell in love with Hebrew literature and the Haskalah movement. Books from a communal leader fed that hunger in his youth. After teaching at Dubno, he reached Brody about 1839 at last. There Erter helped him earn a living teaching Hebrew to others. He studied German and Syriac and read widely in science and philosophy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-13079:
Samuel was the son of Elkanah and Hannah, born in the hill country of Ephraim. Emil G. Hirsch, Wilhelm Bacher, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Childless Hannah vowed him to God before his birth.

Weaned, the boy was taken to Shiloh to serve God for life. While Eli's wicked sons disgraced the shrine, Samuel ministered in a linen ephod. By night God called him, three times, in the Temple at Shiloh. Eli at last understood, and taught him to answer, Speak, for Thy servant heareth. God then revealed the doom of Eli's house to the boy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanhedrin-court:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the treatise Sanhedrin. A treatise of that name appears in the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and both Talmuds. It stands fourth in the order Neziḳin in most editions. It has eleven chapters and seventy-one paragraphs. Its subject is courts, judges, legal process, and criminal law.

The first chapter sorts cases by court size. Money cases go before three judges. Capital cases need a small sanhedrin of twenty-three. The Great Sanhedrin at Jerusalem held seventy-one members. Later chapters cover the rights of the high priest and the king. They set rules for witnesses and for fair trials. The judges sat in a semicircle so all could see each other. Three rows of scholars sat before them, ready to fill any empty seat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seduction-13379:
Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It explains the law of seduction in Jewish sources. Seduction means inducing a chaste woman to unlawful intercourse. The Mosaic law speaks first. A man who entices an unbetrothed virgin must endow her as his wife. If her father refuses the match, the man pays silver instead.

The Mishnah drops the forced marriage and keeps only the money penalty. It never defines enticing itself. Consent is the line between this case and force. In a city, the girl's consent is presumed. In a field, where cries go unheard, force is presumed. The law guards girls still in their father's power. That means girls near the age of twelve. If the father dies first, the payment goes to the girl.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-b-so:
Shabbethai ben Solomon was a rabbi and scholar living at Rome in the late thirteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His age argued fiercely over studying philosophy in general. Maimonides' Guide for the Perplexed stood at the center of that fight.

Shabbethai sided with Zerahiah of Barcelona against Hillel of Verona. He censured Hillel sharply for his stance in the dispute. He wrote responsa and legal decisions of his own. He also gave time to philosophy itself, not just to the quarrel. The entry places one Roman scholar inside a debate that split learned Jews across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shiloh-or-origi:
Shiloh was a city of Ephraim that held the Ark and sanctuary of God. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Eli's family served as priests at its shrine. Samuel grew up there as a boy attendant.

When Philistines captured the Ark, it never returned to Shiloh. Eli's sons later served at Nob under King Saul. Scholars infer that Shiloh's sanctuary fell in that war. Under Joshua, though, the tabernacle had stood at Shiloh. All Israel gathered there to allot the land. Later the city was home to the prophet Ahijah. The entry traces a shrine town from national center to quiet memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-i-13679: Simeon I was the son of Hillel and the father of Gamaliel I. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this very brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He followed his father Hillel as president of the Sanhedrin. Almost nothing else about his life, teaching, or work has been kept in the sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-b-morde:
Solomon ben Mordecai was a Polish rabbi who died in 1609. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was a pupil of Solomon Luria, the Maharshal. He served as rabbi of Meseritz and of Ostrog. He also held a rabbinical post in Lemberg for a time.

He is called Rabbi Shelomtzi in a manuscript work of the time. His book Mizbah ha-Zahab explained a Talmudic passage on incense. That book was printed at Basel in 1602. Another work of his, Seder Gittin, is named in the same manuscript. Little else of his writing has survived to the present day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-simon-1:
Simon Spitzer was an Austrian mathematician born at Vienna in 1826. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on February 3 of that year. He studied mathematics at the University of Vienna. He graduated in 1850 and began teaching the next year.

In 1857 he became professor of algebra at the Handelsschule. He also lectured at the polytechnic institute in Vienna. By 1870 he was professor of analytic mechanics there. When the school became the Handelsakademie, he was its first rector. His many works dealt with equations and imaginary roots. Others gave tables for compound interest and annuity reckoning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szili-adolf-141:
Adolf Szili was a Hungarian eye doctor born at Budapest in 1848. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was educated at Vienna in medicine. He earned his medical degree there in 1872. In 1874 he returned to Budapest for hospital work.

Szili headed eye care at Budapest's Jewish hospital. He became a university lecturer in 1883. In 1895 he rose to assistant professor. King Francis Joseph raised him to the peerage in 1902. He then took the name Szilsárkány. His papers study the iris and the optic nerve entry. One Hungarian book explains spectacles to lay readers. Others test a drug for eye treatment. The entry traces a clinician honored by crown and classroom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tebul-yom-14279:
Tebul Yom is a Mishnah treatise on a bather's lingering impurity. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The name means one who has immersed that day. Leviticus says such a person stays unclean until sunset. The treatise ranks tenth in the order Tohorot.

The impurity here is slight in rabbinic law. Touching hallah or holy flesh only makes it unfit. It does not pass true uncleanness to them. Common things may be touched without any fear. Four chapters hold twenty-six paragraphs on the topic. Chapter one treats bread and foods of joined form. If part is touched, the whole may count as touched. Chapter two turns to liquids touched by the bather. The entry refines one day's wait into fine distinctions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wette-wilhelm-m:
Wilhelm Martin Leberecht de Wette was a Christian Bible critic. Joseph Jacobs and Crawford Howell Toy wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Ulla on January 12, 1780. He died in Basel on June 16, 1849. He taught theology at Heidelberg, then at Berlin. There he worked alongside Schleiermacher.

Sympathy for a political assassin cost De Wette his post in 1819. Basel called him as professor in 1822. He stayed there for the rest of his life. His 1805 study of Deuteronomy reshaped Bible criticism. His commentary questioned many psalm titles and claims. His German Old Testament translation spread widely. His textbooks summed up the critical method.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-ben-joseph:
Wolf ben Joseph of Dessau (1762-1826) was a German teacher, preacher, and author. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Orphaned young, he was raised by kin and schooled in Berlin. He taught in two small towns before he settled at Dessau.

At Dessau he taught at the Herzog Franz School. He also served as secretary to the Jewish town group there. He preached in the synagogue as well. His books join Hebrew text with German versions. One set gives the Minor Prophets in both tongues. A second set does the same for the Book of Daniel. He also printed books of sermons for synagogue use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarzal-moses-ib:
Moses ibn Zarzal was a Spanish doctor and poet at a royal court. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Abraham ibn Zarzal of Granada. He served as doctor to Henry the Third of Castile.

He worked in the late 1300s and the early 1400s. On March 6, 1405, he was at the town of Toro. There he sang the birth of John the Second in verse. That song stands in a famed song book of Spain. In three more years he lived on one street of Segovia. The year of his death can not be fixed with care. A tomb stone at Carmona gives the year 1432 for it. The entry says that stone and its date are both fake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zola-emile-1527:
Emile Zola was a French novelist who became the most famous defender of France's Jews. Isidore Singer and Ernest A. Vizetelly wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Zola was born in Paris on April 2, 1840, and died there on September 29, 1902. Jewish bankers, deputies, and speculators appear in several of his novels, often drawn from the world of finance.

Only late in life did Zola fight anti-Semitism openly. His 1896 article 'Pour les Juifs' called the campaign against the Jews monstrous and unjust. He then took up the cause of Captain Dreyfus, the Jewish officer falsely accused of treason. The entry quotes his Figaro pieces and stresses that anti-Jewish speeches in his fiction belong to his characters, not to him.
kelvin-tait-treatise-natural-philosophy-:
William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, joined Peter Guthrie Tait to write the Treatise on Natural Philosophy. Part one, in its 1879 form, was the complete work as published. Generations of physicists learned from Thomson and Tait, as the pair were known. The book carries Newtonian mechanics into the age of energy.

Kinematics, the pure study of motion, comes first and sets the terms. Dynamics follows, treating forces, work, and energy in depth. The authors insist on clear physical meaning behind every formula. Their approach shaped how Britain taught advanced mechanics. The treatise remains a monument of Victorian science. Its rigor set a lasting standard.
kumarasambhava-griffith-1879:
R. T. H. Griffith translated Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava in 1879 for Trubner's Oriental Series, under the title The Birth of the War-God. Kalidasa, India's most celebrated Sanskrit poet, tells how the gods scheme to wed Shiva to Parvati, daughter of the mountain. Only their son, the gods hope, can kill the demon Taraka, who torments heaven and earth alike.

Parvati wins the meditating god by matching his austerity with her own, in some of Sanskrit poetry's most loved and tender scenes. Spring, the high Himalaya, and the burning of the love god blaze along the way. Griffith's verse carried Kalidasa's epic of divine courtship to English readers in graceful, faithful form.
lessing-nathan-the-wise-1779:
Nathan the Wise, Lessing's verse play of 1779, reached English first in William Taylor's translation of 1791. In Jerusalem under Saladin, the Jewish merchant Nathan is asked which of three faiths is the true one. He answers with the parable of three rings, each claimed as the one true ring.

Around that parable Lessing weaves Templars, sultans, patriarchs, and hidden kinship. The plot slowly reveals a family divided by creed yet bound by blood. His plea is for tolerance among Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike. The play grew from Lessing's own quarrels with church authority in Hamburg. Its ring parable remains the Enlightenment's clearest statement against fanaticism.
lewis-short-latin-dictionary-1879:
Charlton Lewis and Charles Short published their Latin Dictionary in 1879, building on the work of the German scholar Freund. It became the scholar's standard Latin-English dictionary for a century and a half. Classicists still call it simply Lewis and Short.

Every classical word is given with its full range of senses, its grammar, and citations from the authors who used it. Entries trace a word from early Latin through the golden age and beyond. The detail lets readers weigh how Cicero, Virgil, or Tacitus used a term. For serious Latin reading, this remains the great one-volume authority in English.
mccrindle-commerce-navigation-erythraean:
McCrindle's 1879 volume presents the Commerce and Navigation of the Erythraean Sea. It holds the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and Arrian's Voyage of Nearchus. Both texts describe ancient sailing in the Indian Ocean world.

The Periplus, written around 50 CE, is a merchant's working handbook. Ports, monsoons, cargoes, and local rulers appear in practical order. Pepper, ivory, and silk moved along the routes it describes. Arrian's piece recounts Alexander's fleet sailing from India toward Persia. McCrindle's notes connect ancient ports to modern coastlines. Rome's trade with India speaks here in the words of men who sailed it.
mercurii-zweyfacher-schlangen-stab-1679: This German alchemical work of 1679 is credited to Paracelsus, the physician and pioneer of chemical medicine. Its title names Mercury's twofold serpent staff, and its parts treat a path to Paracelsus's chemical treasure and a universal solvent. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content beyond the title data and a library stamp. Readers therefore get the book's identity and subject only, not its arguments or procedures.
mesmer-memoire-decouverte-magnetisme-ani:
Franz Anton Mesmer, a German doctor working in Paris, published his Mémoire on animal magnetism in 1779. It is the founding text of mesmerism. Mesmer claimed to have found an unseen fluid that flows through all living things and governs health.

When the fluid blocked or ebbed, he argued, illness followed. His cures used magnets, touch, and a famous tub around which patients sat in Paris. Crowds thronged to him, and doctors argued fiercely over his claims. The memoir states his theory in his own words, before the storm broke. Few founding texts of a false science have had such real effects.
mesmer-memoire-magnetisme-animal-1779:
Franz Anton Mesmer published his Mémoire sur la Découverte du Magnétisme Animal in 1779 in Paris. Mesmer, a Viennese doctor, claimed he had found a subtle fluid, animal magnetism, that flowed through bodies and could heal disease. The memoir announced that claim to the learned world.

Mesmer set out twenty-seven short claims describing the fluid, its effects, and its use in cures. He described patients who trembled, swooned, or felt relief under his hands and magnetic rods. Royal commissions later tested his claims and blamed imagination, but his methods led toward hypnosis and talk cures. The memoir is the founding document of mesmerism.
my-first-years-as-a-frenchwoman-1876-187:
Mary King Waddington, an American bride, recalls her first years in France. Her book covers 1876 to 1879 and came out in 1914. Her husband rose to be a minister and then prime minister. Chapter one begins when MacMahon was president.

The contents move through the Assembly at Versailles and the Paris Exposition. A chapter weighs the social side of a minister's wife. The Berlin Congress and gay nights at the foreign office follow. Waddington writes as an insider with an outsider's eye. Her memoir shows French politics and high society in the young Third Republic, in clear and lively detail.
openalex-w2104154679:
Jose Luis Elechiguerra, Justin Burt, Jose Rubén Morones-Ramirez and colleagues showed that silver nanoparticles attach to the HIV virus. Their paper appeared in Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2005. Nanoparticle interactions with viruses were barely explored then. Silver was known to fight microbes in other settings. The team tested it against HIV-1 directly.

Only the tiniest particles attached to the virus. Particles in a narrow size range bound to its surface knobs. Their spacing matched the knobs' regular arrangement. Sulfur-bearing spots on the knobs likely drew them in. Bound particles blocked the virus from entering host cells. Cell tests confirmed that blocking effect. The work opened a route to nanoparticle antivirals.
openalex-w2126154479:
Nicholas Bates, Yrene Astor, Matthew Church, and colleagues published this review in Oceanography in 2014. They used long-running ocean observation sites to track how seawater chemistry is changing. The driver is human-made carbon dioxide, which the ocean absorbs from the air in huge amounts.

The authors pull together time-series records from stations around the world. They weigh how much extra carbon the ocean has taken up and what that does to its buffering power. Added carbon lowers seawater pH and changes the state of minerals that shell-building life needs. The records give a shared baseline for judging how fast ocean acidification is moving.
openalex-w2151624979:
David Cooke, Liliana Cano, Sylvain Raffaele, and colleagues published this genome study in PLoS Pathogens in 2012. They tracked a new lineage of Phytophthora infestans, the water mold behind the Irish potato famine. The lineage, called 13_A2, swept through Europe's potato fields with unusual speed.

Markers showed 13_A2 displacing rival lineages to pass three-quarters of the British pathogen population in under three years. Lab and field tests found its isolates among the most aggressive on farmed potatoes. They also outcompeted other aggressive lineages in the field. Genome analysis of the lineage helps explain these selective sweeps and warns breeders that management must adapt as populations shift.
openalex-w2901214479:
Rachel M. Sherman, Juliet Forman, and Valentin Antonescu lead a team that built an African-descent pan-genome, in Nature Genetics in January 2019. The standard human reference genome poorly represents African genetic diversity. Genomics in general has under-sampled people of African descent. A pan-genome, capturing sequences the reference lacks, was the remedy pursued here.

The team deeply sequenced nine hundred ten people of African descent. Assembling their genomes together surfaces DNA segments missing from the reference. Such segments can carry genes and regulatory elements invisible to reference-based studies. The pan-genome gives African-ancestry research a fuller coordinate system. It should improve variant discovery for health studies in these populations. The work also demonstrates assembly methods for population-scale sequencing. Its message: one standard genome cannot stand in for humanity.
openalex-w2958489179:
Paul Hessburg, Carol Miller, Sean Parks, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution. It asks what makes forests in western North America able to bounce back after fire and other disturbances. Their answer, in short, is climate, local environment, and past disturbance history.

Fire patterns have shifted in frequency, severity, season, and spread, and those shifts can remake whole ecosystems. Large, severe fires are risky for young trees that are still getting established. The review examines dry, moist, cold, and boreal forests across the western United States, Mexico, and British Columbia. It focuses on drier forests where fire and other stressors are most active, and what keeps them resilient.
openalex-w2960778279:
Jeetendra Aryal, Tek Sapkota, Ritika Khurana, and colleagues published this review in Environment, Development and Sustainability in 2019. It examines how climate change threatens farming in South Asia, where most farms are small family plots. The authors ask which adaptations can keep smallholder production going.

The paper is a systematic review of studies on climate impacts on crop production in the region. It gathers the main adaptation options that have been proposed and tested in farm production systems. The authors also weigh the social, economic, and political conditions that help or hinder adaptation. One key conclusion is that useful farming practices for adaptation already exist, so putting them into practice is the pressing task.
openalex-w3081939279:
R. Abbott, T. D. Abbott, S. Abraham, and colleagues of the LIGO and Virgo groups published this letter in Physical Review Letters in 2020. It reports GW190521, the merger of two black holes with a combined mass near one hundred fifty times the Sun's. The signal arrived on May 21, 2019.

Earlier mergers had joined far lighter pairs, with single black holes topping out near fifty solar masses. This pair weighed in at roughly eighty-five and sixty-six solar masses. Such heavyweights strain theories of how stars die, since ordinary stellar collapse is not expected to leave black holes that large. The short, clear signal makes GW190521 a landmark for testing how the biggest black holes form.
openalex-w3111092679:
Olivo Miotto, Makoto Sekihara, Shin-Ichiro Tachibana, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Pathogens in 2020. It reports the emergence of artemisinin-resistant malaria parasites on the island of New Guinea. The resistance marker, a mutation called C580Y in the kelch13 gene, had swept Southeast Asia but was not known elsewhere.

Surveys at two clinics in Wewak, Papua New Guinea, in 2016 and 2017 found three infections carrying the mutation among two hundred thirty-nine typed samples. Gene comparisons with parasites from nearby regions suggest the mutation arose there on its own, not by import. The local parasite line had slowly gathered a bundle of resistance-linked changes. The authors call the development worrying for malaria control in the region.
openalex-w3118018179:
Andrew Gloster, Demetris Lamnisos, Jeļena Ļubenko, and colleagues published this international study in PLoS ONE in 2020. It measures the mental health impact of the COVID-19 pandemic across countries. Governments had imposed vast lockdowns that upended daily life.

Whether those lockdowns harmed mental health was poorly understood when the team wrote. Broken routines could plainly hurt, yet shared hardship, borne by whole populations at once, might soften the blow. The authors surveyed people during lockdown to measure outcomes directly. Their data test both guesses against lived experience. The study helps separate the virus's own toll from the toll of the measures taken against it, a distinction policy needs.
openalex-w4221053979:
Carolina Rosai Mendes, Guilherme Dilarri, Carolina Froes Forsan, and colleagues studied how zinc oxide particles kill bacteria, in Scientific Reports in 2022. The particles are tiny grains of zinc oxide, widely used for their germ-killing power. Yet exactly how they work was not fully clear. The team measured the particles with X-ray tools and microscopes, then tested them on four bacteria.

The test species were Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, plus a common lab bacterium. Gram-negative bacteria proved sensitive at lower doses than Gram-positive ones. Images showed the particles damaging the cell membrane and disrupting cell division. Knowing the targets helps predict resistance and set the contact time needed to kill germs.
openalex-w4391848979:
Luca Longo, Mario Brčić, Federico Cabitza, and colleagues issue a manifesto for explainable artificial intelligence in Information Fusion in 2024. AI systems increasingly decide things in daily life while hiding how they work. Explainable AI, or XAI, tries to open those black boxes. The field has grown fast and shown practical and ethical value, yet deep problems remain unsolved.

Experts from many disciplines met to name the open problems honestly. They present twenty-eight of them, sorted into nine categories. The list spans technical methods, human factors, law, and ethics. Its purpose is to align research agendas across fields that rarely talk to each other. A shared map, the authors argue, will speed XAI's move into real use.
openalex-w7129018379:
Kenta Toyama and his co-authors at Juntendo University in Japan released a review in 2026 on physical literacy. The term means the motivation, confidence, skill, and knowledge that help a person stay active for life. Japan still has no settled national definition, even as research on the idea grows worldwide.

The review traces Japanese research and practical use up to the present and notes that the Japan Sports Agency first took up the topic in 2022. In talks on children's fitness and exercise habits. The authors say a Japanese assessment scale is still being finished. Once it is ready, they argue, intervention studies can spread across many fields and support the health of the whole population.
openalex-w7140293179:
Sudip Saha led a 2026 study, released in the Juntendo Medical Journal, of child leukemia survivors in low-resource settings. The team asked whether fear that the cancer will return changes how well survivors keep taking their drug. The cross-sectional study enrolled 444 children treated for acute lymphoblastic or acute myeloid leukemia at specialist pediatric cancer clinics.

Fear and adherence were measured with standard validated questionnaires. Stronger fear of recurrence went with weaker drug taking, a clear negative link. Girls found higher fear and lower adherence than boys. The authors argue that follow-up care in poor settings should treat fear as a practical risk to recovery, not a side issue, since missed drug can endanger a survivor's health.
openalex-w7148264079:
Toshiyuki Yanai and colleagues at Kurume University in Japan posted a 2026 preprint on a different approach to heart failure that keeps coming back. Instead of waiting for symptoms to worsen and rushing patients to hospital, their Kurume-HEARTS program plans hospital admission in advance, before clinical worsening. The study looks back at how that program worked in practice.

Heart failure is a leading cause of repeated emergency admissions, and each crisis worsens a patient's outlook. A planned admission lets doctors adjust treatment calmly rather than in an emergency. The retrospective design reviews the program's patients and outcomes to judge whether scheduled care can break the cycle of deterioration and readmission for people living with recurrent heart failure.
openalex-w7204643479:
Daiane de Lourdes Alves Velho led a Portuguese-language and documentary study, published in Brazil in 2026, on teacher training and inclusive education, between access and learning. Enrolling disabled students is only the first step. The study, built from a 2026 professional master's dissertation, draws on inclusion literature and Brazilian schooling law to ask what makes participation and learning real.

Inclusion does not happen through physical presence in the common classroom, the analysis shows. It depends on institutional culture, planning, mediation, assessment, and accessibility conditions. For deaf students, visuality and Brazilian Sign Language show that knowledge has different entry routes. Ongoing training rooted in daily school life and backed by institutional policy, the authors conclude, helps teachers revise conceptions, confront ableist practices, and build fairer plans together.
openalex-w7205014679:
Joseli Aurelio dos Santos Lima writes about play as a teaching tool for children learning to read and write, in a 2026 Brazilian education article. Her focus is the early years of elementary school, when literacy lays the ground for reading, writing, and taking part in social life. Drawing on published studies, academic work, and education documents, she asks what playful methods add to that first stage.

Lima finds that games, free play, songs, stories, and hands-on activities help young learners join in and build reading and writing skills, when teachers plan them with clear goals. Play used that way makes lessons livelier and better matched to how children actually learn. She closes by urging schools to treat playfulness as a serious part of literacy teaching, tied to learning aims and to each child's needs.
openalex-w7206151279:
Rosa Severina de Souza Oliveira and Everaldo da Silva Santana write about how the internet shapes who people become, and what that means for learning. Subjectivity, in their terms, covers ideas, feelings, behavior, and how a person reads reality, all formed through ties with other people, institutions, and culture. Their 2026 article argues that digital tools now sit inside that process every day.

Online life changes how students interact, find information, and build knowledge. The authors grant the gains: digital tools can aid learning, spark creativity, and widen access to knowledge. But the same tools can also spread habits of consumption, control, and sameness. Their answer is a critical use of technology in schools, one that supports thoughtful, self-aware human formation instead of passive scrolling.
openalex-w7213935679:
Thiago Valim Oliveira and co-authors survey auditory training for adults who use hearing amplification devices. Their 2026 integrative review searches Portuguese-language work across five sources, mainly 2005 to 2025. From hundreds of first hits, thirteen studies remained, nine clinical and four reviews.

Most studies agree that auditory training helps users adapt to and benefit from their devices, the authors find. Training builds and sharpens the brain's hearing skills. Comfort improves, above all in hard listening settings such as noise. Speech understanding also improves. The overview gives clinicians a compact picture of a rehabilitation step that device fitting alone does not complete.
openalex-w7215042979:
Vanessa Ramos Vieira Moura led a 2026 bibliographic study of teacher knowledge in the age of emerging technologies. Digital tools now fill school daily life, and teachers must constantly rebuild their practice around them. Grounded in Brazil's national curriculum and the specialized literature, the authors examine continuing teacher training, game-based learning resources, and the arrival of artificial intelligence in lesson planning.

Interactive formative assessment platforms, including quiz and response tools used in class, offer real potential, the review finds. Artificial intelligence brings both gaps and opportunities for planning. The authors argue against merely instrumental use of classroom media, pressing for technology that serves pedagogy. Effective innovation, they conclude, depends on joining institutional support, adequate infrastructure, and training programs that focus on the teacher's protagonism and autonomy rather than on the devices themselves.
openalex-w7220898379:
Amanda Santos Alves Freire led a 2026 review on grief and the brain, asking what brain science shows about bereavement in adults and its psychiatric effects. Grief is the natural response to losing a person who mattered, with emotional, cognitive, behavioral, and physiological changes. Usually adaptive, in some people the pain persists and impairs functioning, matching prolonged grief disorder. Searching five databases for studies from 2003 to 2025, the team cut hundreds of records to twelve eligible studies.

The findings point to changes in brain regions for emotion, memory, and reward, including the amygdala and the nucleus accumbens. They also point to changes in stress hormone systems, immune and inflammatory markers, and the oxytocin system. Persistent yearning, intrusive thoughts, trouble holding emotion steady, and changes in thinking and daily function come with these alterations. Grief engages complex brain mechanisms, the authors conclude, which helps explain why some losses become clinical disorders needing treatment.
openalex-w7220984579:
Cecilia Noemí Correa Martínez and two co-authors present a medical case report, published in Spanish in 2026. Their subject is a rare and aggressive cancer of the cervix. Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma grows fast, returns often, and carries a poor outlook, which makes each documented case useful for clinicians.

Their patient was thirty-seven years old, a mother and a smoker, who sought care after bleeding following intercourse. Examination found a large growth on the cervix, and special tissue tests settled a diagnosis that the first biopsy had left open. Staging showed advanced disease reaching nearby tissue and nodes, and she was referred for combined medical and radiation treatment.
pasteur-studies-on-fermentation-1879:
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist who proved that tiny living germs cause fermentation and many diseases. He studied why beer and wine often turned sour or spoiled. Faulkner and Robb translated his French work into English, and it was published in 1879.

Pasteur shows through careful experiments that each kind of fermentation comes from a specific microbe. He explains how brewers can protect beer by controlling those germs and by gentle heating. His results gave brewers a practical guide and gave medicine strong proof of the germ theory. The book changed both brewing and science.
petrarch-sonnets-triumphs-1879:
Francesco Petrarca, called Petrarch, shaped his sonnets to Laura across a lifetime in the 1300s. The 1879 English volume from Bell's library gives his Sonnets, Triumphs, and other poems in verse by several hands. It was the first complete English rendering of the whole body of his Italian poetry.

The sonnets trace love for Laura in life and grief for her after death. The Triumphs stage grand processions of Love, Death, Fame, and Time in vision form. Petrarch's careful music set the pattern for love poetry across Europe for centuries. Shakespeare and the Elizabethans drank deeply from this source. The Bell volume let Victorian readers meet the full Petrarch, not a selection.
phrenology-vindicated-being-a-reply-to-t:
A. L. Vago's Phrenology Vindicated is a one-shilling pamphlet of reply. Dr. Andrew Wilson had attacked the science in the Gentleman's Magazine for January 1879, in an article called The Old Phrenology and the New. Vago answers him for the London publishers Simpkin, Marshall and Company.

His opening admits the task may seem unnecessary: to those who know phrenology's history, Wilson's objections have often and long ago been raised, and answered. The pamphlet re-fights those old battles for a new magazine audience. It shows the science's defenders still organized, incorporated, and combative forty years after its heyday.
plos-pbio-0020079:
André P. Gerber, Daniel Herschlag, and Patrick O. Brown surveyed RNA-binding proteins in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. The Puf family of proteins grabs specific messenger RNAs and controls what happens to them. The team found which RNAs each Puf protein holds across the whole genome.

The bound RNAs grouped neatly by job and by where their proteins work in the cell. That means Puf proteins help coordinate whole teams of genes after their messages are made. This kind of control is a second layer of gene management, past the on-off switch of transcription. The study shows that layer is ordered, broad, and worth mapping in other species too.
plos-pbio-0020179:
Hiroshi Arakawa, Huseyin Saribasak, and Jean-Marie Buerstedde studied antibody gene editing in PLOS Biology in 2004. Birds and mammals improve their antibodies in two ways: gene conversion, which patches in stored variants, and hypermutation, which adds random point changes. An enzyme called AID starts both processes.

The team shows that one and the same first step, a cut-like change by AID, can lead to either outcome. The cell's later repair choices decide which path the gene takes. That shared start simplifies a once messy picture. It also helps explain how the immune system builds such a wide range of antibodies. The same enzyme can cause harm when it acts in the wrong place.
plos-pbio-0020379:
Ulrike S. Eggert, Amy A. Kiger, Constance Richter, and their team screened for cell division blockers in PLOS Biology in 2004. Cytokinesis is the final split of one cell into two. The team ran two screens side by side: one with chemical compounds, one by silencing genes across the genome.

Running both at once lets each check the other. Compounds that block division point to the genes they likely target, and gene hits predict new compounds. The screen found fresh inhibitors and fresh targets together. Such paired screening is now a standard drug hunt design. It is prized because it links a working compound to its mechanism from day one.
plos-pone-0000079:
Wataru Sonoyama, Yi Liu, Dianji Fang, and a large team regrew teeth in pigs in PLOS ONE in 2006. They used mesenchymal stem cells, the kind that can form bone, cartilage, and tooth support tissues. Placed in a pig's jaw, the cells helped build a working tooth root structure with its ligament.

A living root that anchors a crown like a natural tooth beats a metal post in key ways: it can sense pressure and heal. Pigs are a strong test since their jaws and teeth are close in size to ours. The study is a step toward bioengineered teeth for people who lose their own, though much work remains before clinical use.
plos-pone-0000179:
Chen Luxenburg, Dafna Geblinger, Eugenia Klein, and colleagues published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Osteoclasts are the cells that degrade bone, central to normal bone remodeling and to diseases like osteoporosis when their activity runs out of balance. The authors describe the architecture of the structures these cells build to grip bone, from podosomes to the sealing zone.

The sealing zone is the gasket that lets an osteoclast dissolve bone in a sealed pocket. Tracing how scattered podosomes organize into that ring shows how the cell assembles its demolition tool. The details matter for drugs that aim to calm osteoclasts in bone-loss disease.
plos-pone-0000279:
Sébastien Plumet, Florence Herschke, Jean-Marie Bourhis, and colleagues published this virology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. When measles virus copies itself, it makes a short leader transcript ending in a 5-prime triphosphate, a chemical flag. The authors show this viral RNA activates the RIG-I pathway, the cell's alarm that triggers an interferon response against viruses.

Interferon is the body's early warning signal that rallies antiviral defenses. Pinpointing which viral molecule trips the alarm shows how cells detect measles. The mechanism is a general one: RIG-I watches for exactly this kind of RNA in many virus infections.
plos-pone-0000379:
Patrick Pfister and colleagues traced the history of a family of smell receptor genes in fish, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The genes, called V1r receptors, detect chemical signals in the water. The team compared these genes across teleost fish, the large group that includes most modern bony fish.

The study finds that V1r genes have evolved in divergent ways across fish lineages, rather than following one shared path. Receptor families grow, shrink, and change as species adapt to different waters and ways of life. Tracing that patchwork helps explain how animals fine-tune their sense of smell over evolutionary time.
plos-pone-0000479:
Anan Yaghmur and colleagues tuned the properties of oily membranes with custom-made peptides, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Monoolein bilayers are fat films used to model cell membranes and to grow membrane protein crystals. The team added designer lipid-like peptide surfactants, small molecules built to sit in the film, and measured changes in curvature and stability.

Membrane curvature decides many cell events, from vesicle budding to fusion. A dial that adjusts curvature in a model film gives researchers new control. They can use it in basic studies. They can also use it when crystallizing proteins for structure work. The paper is a piece of soft-matter engineering with biological tools.
plos-pone-0000579:
Christian Iseli and colleagues tackled a string-search problem at genome scale, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Biologists constantly search genome sequences for short words: binding sites, primers, and short reads all require finding brief sequences fast. The team presented indexing strategies for rapid searches of short words in genome sequences.

Indexing pre-organizes the genome so searches that would take hours take seconds. Short words are the hardest case because they occur millions of times. Efficient strategies here underpin the alignment tools of the sequencing era, and the paper appeared just as short-read data began to flood in.
plos-pone-0000679:
André Catic, Edda Fiebiger, Gregory A. Korbel and colleagues screened for enzymes that react with a ubiquitin-like protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ubiquitin tags proteins for recycling and other fates, and a family of ubiquitin-like molecules resembles it in sequence, structure, or function. One member, ISG15, rises strongly after type I interferon, an immune alarm signal.

The enzymes sought are deubiquitinases, which remove such tags, but ones that cross-react with ISG15. Cross-reactivity matters because tag removal controls how long signals last. A screen that names the enzymes handling ISG15 gives immunologists new handles on the interferon response and its regulation.
plos-pone-0000779:
Onno J. de Boer, Jelger J. van der Meer, Peter Teeling and colleagues counted regulatory T cells inside human artery plaques, in PLOS ONE in 2007. T cell driven inflammation contributes to atherogenesis, the building of plaques, and to the onset of acute cardiovascular disease. Effector T cells are kept in check by regulatory T cells, a specialized subset. Nothing was known about their presence inside lesions themselves.

Staining for the marker FOXP3, the team found low numbers of regulatory T cells at all developmental stages of atherosclerotic lesions. Few peacekeepers amid many attackers fits a story of unchecked inflammation. Boosting those regulators is one idea this census supports.
plos-pone-0000879:
Stephane Aris-Brosou tackled the problem of dating family trees with molecular clocks, in a 2007 PLOS ONE methods article. DNA changes over time, so in theory it can date when species split. In practice, rates of change and split times cannot both be read straight from the data, so every method must assume something first.

Aris-Brosou proposes hybrid local clocks, which let rates vary across parts of a tree in a mixed way. The aim is more honest dates for when groups parted. Better dating underpins work on how species spread, how diseases emerge and how fast evolution runs in different lines.
plos-pone-0000979:
Mizuki Azuma, Lisa Embree, Hatem Sabaawy and colleagues studied a sarcoma gene's normal job in zebrafish embryos, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene, Ewsr1, is broken and fused to other genes in Ewing sarcoma and several other cancers. What the healthy gene does in a growing body was far less known.

Working in zebrafish, the team tie Ewsr1 to mitotic integrity, clean cell division, and to the survival of proneural cells, young cells bound to become neurons. A cancer gene with a day job in division and nerve development makes sense of its damage when fused. The fish work gives the gene a normal context.
plos-pone-0001079:
Natalia Norden, Jerome Chave, Pierre Belbenoit and colleagues found mast fruiting to be common in eastern South American trees, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mast seeding, many trees fruiting heavily in the same year, was thought rare in the tropics. Tropical climates vary less, and fruit eaters there tend to eat widely, both arguing against synchronized feasts.

Earlier tests rested on only a few tropical data sets. With wider data, the team report mast fruiting is a frequent strategy among woody species there. A frequent strategy needs a different explanation than a rare one. The result also matters for forests' animal communities, which ride those feast and famine cycles.
plos-pone-0001179:
Cloning a full gene is often blocked by introns, the non-coding stretches that split genes into pieces. Genes that exist in very few copies pose a second problem. Xiaoping An and colleagues present a shortcut in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Standard PCR, the workhorse copying method, usually cannot amplify a complete gene straight from genomic DNA in eukaryotes.

The authors describe rapid assembly of multi-exon cDNA directly from genomic DNA. Their method stitches the coding pieces together without the usual intermediate steps. A reliable shortcut like this saves time for any lab that needs the working copy of a gene rather than the raw genomic version.
plos-pone-0001279:
Ovarian cancer is the second most common gynecologic cancer and has its highest death rate, largely because it is found late. Anne Estep, Chana Palmer, and Frank McCormick analyzed mutations in three genes across 15 ovarian cancer cell lines, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The genes are BRAF, MEK1, and MEK2, links in one growth-signaling chain.

Cancer arises from accumulated mutations in critical genes, and the chain these genes form is a drug target in other cancers. The authors examine how often these mutations occur in ovarian lines and what that implies for therapy. Knowing which tumors carry them guides the use of pathway-blocking drugs.
plos-pone-0001379:
Philip Hill and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on tuberculosis, or TB, in The Gambia. People who live with a TB patient face a high risk of catching the disease. The team followed such close contacts over time. They wanted to know how often new cases arose and which tests best flag who is at risk.

Contacts were checked with a blood test and with the classic skin test. The authors then tracked who went on to develop TB. Their data weigh how well each test predicts real illness ahead of time. Such data can help clinics focus care and drugs on the contacts who need them most.
plos-pone-0001479:
Ashok Hegde and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on pancreas faults in zebrafish. A gene called mind bomb is needed to switch on the Notch path, a core growth signal. Fish with faults in this gene show pancreas flaws of unlike weight. The team read gene use across the genome in these fish.

By sorting fish by how grave the flaw was, they flagged genes that track with the flaw. Those genes are likely to answer to Notch in the pancreas. The list gives labs fresh leads on how the pancreas forms. It may also bear on human pancreas ills with Notch links.
plos-pone-0001579:
Aymé Spor and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two life plans in yeast. Some yeast strains eat fast and breed fast, like the grasshopper of fable. Others eat slow, store more, and live lean, like the ant. The team asked how much of that split is gene based and how much is set by the food at hand.

By growing many strains on set foods, they split the gene share from the food share. Both shares proved large. The yeast case gives a clean lab model for a deep life trade off. It may hint at why species split into fast and slow life plans.
plos-pone-0001679:
Charles J. Limb and Allen R. Braun scanned the brains of jazz pianists as they improvised, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The team wanted the neural basis of spontaneous musical performance, creativity as it happens. Professional jazz pianists played inside an MRI scanner under two setups that differed widely in how complex the music was.

By comparing improvisation with playing set pieces, the authors mapped which brain areas switch on or off when musicians create on the spot. The full text gives the scan design, the brain regions involved, and how the patterns changed with complexity. The work gives a rare look at the brain in a creative state. It also speaks to how training lets artists shut down self-monitoring while they play.
plos-pone-0001779:
Daniel G. Wootton, Hyginus Opara, Giancarlo A. Biagini, and their co-authors ran a malaria drug dosing trial in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The aim was to find the right dose of artesunate to pair with chlorproguanil-dapsone, sold as Lapdap, a fixed-dose drug for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Dosing matters: too little fails to cure and breeds resistance, too much adds side effects.

The open-label trial compared Lapdap alone against Lapdap with three different artesunate doses. The full text gives the cure rates and safety results for each arm. Combination therapy is the global standard for falciparum malaria, so dose-finding trials like this one write the recipe that clinics follow.
plos-pone-0001879:
