Nan Chiang and co-authors asked whether drugs that numb pain can also change how swelling heals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Local and inhaled numbing drugs are used in surgery each day around the world. Yet no one knew if they alter the calm, ordered steps by which acute swelling fades on its own.

The team tested lidocaine, a widely used local drug, along with a common inhaled one. They tracked how each drug changed the close of a swelling episode in their model. The question matters for care after surgery, since slow healing can mean more pain and more risk. Readers get an early look at a side effect few had thought to check.
plos-pone-0001979:
Anthony Wilson, Guy Teugels, and Axel Meyer traced the odd past of herring in an African lake, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Lake Tanganyika, the oldest of the African Great Lakes, holds a fauna so sea-like that early workers thought the lake once joined the ocean. Earth studies later showed no such link.

The team studied the lake's freshwater herring and their kin. As the title states, these fish are the product of a marine invasion into West Africa, followed by a move into fresh water. Their family tree solves a long puzzle about how sea fish came to live in a deep inland lake.
plos-pone-0002079:
Woonbok Chung and co-authors hunted new tumor markers by scanning DNA tags in three cancers, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In cancer, genes are often shut by hypermethylation, extra chemical tags on DNA. Those tags can serve as markers of disease and can point to genes that drive it. The team used a method that amplifies tagged CpG islands, the tag-rich stretches near genes.

They applied unbiased methylation profiling to prostate, colon, and breast cancers. New markers found this way could one day screen for these cancers or track them in blood. The prostate arm of the work anchors the method in a cancer with few early signs.
plos-pone-0002179:
Chrissa Kioussi and Michael Gross wrote a methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008 on building network models of how body patterns form. Networks of transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on and off, lie beneath pattern formation in animals with many cells. Drawing and reading these networks in mammals is a central problem for development, brain science, and regenerative medicine.

The authors lay out how to construct such models step by step. A good model turns long lists of genes into a map of who controls whom as tissues take shape. Their guide helps other labs turn raw gene data into testable pictures of how an embryo builds itself.
plos-pone-0002279:
Adam Schikora, Alessandro Carreri, Emmanuelle Charpentier, and co-authors showed that a food-poisoning bacterium can live inside plant tissues, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Salmonella typhimurium on raw vegetables and fruit is a major source of human infection, and salmonellosis is the most spread food poisoning worldwide. The bacterium was usually treated as mere surface dirt on plants.

The team found that Salmonella overcomes the plant Arabidopsis thaliana's innate immune defenses and takes up life inside the plant. A germ hiding inside produce cannot be washed off, which changes how food safety must think about fresh vegetables.
plos-pone-0002379:
Galli joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Soledad Galli, Valeria Gabriela Antico Arciuch, Cecilia Poderoso, among others. Its subject is tumor Cell Phenotype Is Sustained by Selective MAPK Oxidation in Mitochondria. Mitochondria are major cellular sources of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2).

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002479:
Riba led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Jordi Riba, Ulrike M. Krämer, Marcus Heldmann, among others. Its subject is dopamine Agonist Increases Risk Taking but Blunts Reward-Related Brain Activity. The use of D2/D3 dopaminergic agonists in Parkinson's disease (PD) may lead to pathological gambling.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002579:
Snaddon and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Jake L. Snaddon, Edgar C. Turner, William A. Foster, among others. Its subject is children's Perceptions of Rainforest Biodiversity: Which Animals Have the Lion's Share of Environmental Awareness?. Globally, natural ecosystems are being lost to agricultural land at an unprecedented rate.

This land-use often results in significant reductions in abundance and diversity of the flora and fauna as well as alterations in their composition. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002679:
Bertran Auvert and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was estimating the resources needed and savings anticipated from Roll-Out of adult male circumcision in Sub-Saharan africa. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Bertran Auvert, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Trials in Africa indicate that medical adult male circumcision (MAMC) reduces the risk of HIV by 60%. It goes on to note a further point. MAMC may avert 2 to 8 million HIV infections over 20 years in sub-Saharan Africa and cost less than treating those who would have. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002779:
Carmen Chak-Lui Wong and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was deleted in liver cancer 1 (DLC1) negatively regulates Rho/ROCK/MLC pathway in hepatocellular carcinoma. The catalog record names Carmen Chak-Lui Wong first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Deleted in liver cancer 1 (DLC1), a member of RhoGTPase activating protein (GAP) family. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002879:
Shehre-Banoo Malik, Arthur W. Pightling, Lauren M. Stefaniak and colleagues searched the genome of Trichomonas vaginalis in 2008 for genes tied to meiosis. Meiosis is the cell division that makes sex cells, and it marks true sexual reproduction. How widely it occurs among tiny single-celled eukaryotes was still unclear.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team first built a wider list of conserved meiosis genes from animals, fungi, and plants. They then looked for those genes in this parasite. Finding an expanded set present counts as evidence for sex in the organism, which changes how its spread and variation can be understood.
plos-pone-0002979:
Kristin Hartmann, Claus Bruehl, Tatyana Golovko and co-authors studied fast adjustment of inhibition in brain circuits in 2008. Activity in the central nervous system shifts rapidly, so the balance between excitation and inhibition must adapt constantly. The mechanisms behind fast adaptation were largely unclear.

Writing in PLOS ONE, they link homeostatic plasticity of inhibition to activity-dependent vesicular filling, how much transmitter is packed into release bubbles. Chronic changes in activity reshape that packing. The work offers a concrete mechanism for how inhibitory synapses keep pace with a changing network. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003079:
Matthias Dehmer, Stephan Borgert and Frank Emmert-Streib derived entropy bounds for hierarchical networks in 2008. Their paper starts from a recently introduced measure of topological entropy for non-hierarchical networks. Entropy here gauges a network's structural complexity in a single number.

The authors provide bounds for estimating the entropy of hierarchical graphs, networks built in layers. Bounds give a fast range without full computation. Published in PLOS ONE, molecular networks are often layered, so the result serves systems biology as well as pure graph theory. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003179:
Barry S. Taylor, Jordi Barretina, Nicholas D. Socci and colleagues work on finding functional copy-number changes in cancer in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Understanding cancer at the molecular level requires mapping its genetic defects. DNA microarray tools can give detailed raw data about chromosome aberrations in tumour samples. Computer analysis is then needed to deduce actual amplifications and losses from that raw signal.

The authors address that analysis step and which copy-number alterations are functional. Readers see the gap between raw array data and usable cancer genetics. Better deduction from arrays helps labs focus on changes that likely drive tumour growth.
plos-pone-0003279:
Frédéric J. J. Chain, Dora Ilieva and Ben J. Evans test cross-species microarray use in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Prefabricated expression microarrays are currently available for only a few species, but methods have been proposed to extend their application to comparisons between divergent genomes. The team demonstrate limits of using hybridization intensity of genomic DNA as a basis for such work.

Their subject is single-species microarrays and comparative transcriptomics. Readers learn caution about stretching a tool built for one genome across distant species. That matters for wildlife genetics, where custom arrays for each species are rarely affordable.
plos-pone-0003379:
Stella Quimbo and colleagues studied health insurance use in the Philippines for this 2008 paper. The country promotes social health insurance to help poor families get care. Yet many poor families were not using the cover they had. The team looked at use across thirty hospital districts to find out why.

Their data show that having a card does not ensure a person gets care. Costs, travel, and poor knowledge of benefits all kept people away. The paper argues that programs must fix those blocks, not just sign people up. The lesson applies to many poor countries building insurance schemes of their own.
plos-pone-0003479:
Murilo S. Baptista, Josué X. de Carvalho, and Mahir S. Hussein studied network wiring in this 2008 paper. Active networks, like neural circuits, pass information while their parts fire. The shape of the wiring shapes how much information moves. It also shapes how well the network falls into sync.

The team sought wiring layouts close to the best possible ones. Their method finds topologies that transmit large amounts of information. Such layouts link pure graph theory to working systems. Designers of real networks can borrow the same search logic. The tools apply to any network where parts pass signals to each other.
plos-pone-0003579:
Davide Lecca and co-authors studied a receptor tied to brain repair in this 2008 paper. Replacing damaged cells in the adult brain needs new neurons and oligodendrocytes. Oligodendrocytes make the myelin that insulates nerve fibers. A receptor named GPR17 had just been identified.

GPR17 resembles P2Y-like receptors that sense nucleotide signals. The team cast it as a sensor of brain damage. It also stands as a new target for brain repair strategies. A druggable sensor could help rebuild rather than just protect tissue. Brain repair has long been a goal that drugs could not reach.
plos-pone-0003679:
Lorenza S. Colzato, Wery P. M. van den Wildenberg, and Bernhard Hommel published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Beliefs and expectations are known to shape what people see. Yet no one had tested whether a religious upbringing changes basic visual attention. The authors compared Dutch Calvinists with atheists raised in the same culture.

The groups differed in how they spread attention between the whole scene and its details. The religious participants were more prone to miss the big picture in favor of local detail. The study shows a cultural force reaching down into the basic mechanics of seeing.
plos-pone-0003779:
Michaela Petter, Insa Bonow, and Mo-Quen Klinkert published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum spends several days maturing its sexual stages, called gametocytes, inside the human host. During that time it must evade the immune system and hide in body tissues.

The team tracked the rif multigene family, a set of variable surface genes, during gametocyte development. Different subgroups of the family switched on in diverse patterns as the stages matured. The shifting patterns show how the parasite varies its surface while preparing to infect mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0003879:
Ian P. Lewkowich, Stephane Lajoie, Jennifer R. Clark, and co-authors studied asthma in mice in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article focuses on dendritic cells in the lung. These cells take in allergens and switch on T cells, the immune cells behind allergic asthma. In asthma-prone mice, lung dendritic cells seem primed to drive that response.

The authors traced how allergen uptake by these cells leads to release of IL-23. That signal helps push airways toward overreaction, a core feature of asthma. The work names a step where treatment might calm the response. It also clarifies why some lungs react so strongly to common allergens.
plos-pone-0003979:
Dave J. Druce, Graeme Shannon, Bruce R. Page, and co-authors set out a savanna monitoring plan in 2008. Managers of protected areas need warning before vegetation shifts hard. Large trees, at least five meters tall, do key ecological work. Their loss can signal a regime shift in the landscape.

Their PLOS ONE article develops a protocol for tracking large trees. It covers both the mix of tree species and how animals use them. Repeated checks can catch change while response is still cheap. The plan supports adaptive management in African conservation areas. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004079:
Ruth Prassl, Magdalena Pregetter, Heinz Amenitsch, and co-authors measured fat particles in blood as heat sensors in 2008. Low density lipoproteins carry cholesterol through the bloodstream. Their fatty core changes state with temperature in a sharp transition. Whether that change is fast enough to matter was unknown.

Their PLOS ONE article used sub-second X-ray measures on LDL particles. The core responded quickly to small swings of about two degrees. A fast response could let LDL sense temperature in circulation. The result gives a physical side to a familiar risk factor. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004179:
Priyadharsini Nagarajan and colleagues published this skin cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ets1 is an oncogene, a gene that can drive cancer, acting as a transcription factor that controls many genes tied to tumour start and growth. It is over-produced in many human squamous cell cancers, and the amount tracks with how far the cancer has advanced.

The team switched Ets1 on in fully matured squamous skin cells, which normally no longer divide. They report that Ets1 alone drives abnormal, dysplastic changes in these cells. The result shows how one over-active gene can push settled skin cells back toward a cancer-like state.
plos-pone-0004279:
Lucas Joppa, Scott Loarie, and Stuart Pimm published this conservation study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protected areas are the first, and often only, line of defence for biodiversity. They might help or harm rural communities depending on how they change economic opportunities and access to natural resources.

Because of that, protected areas may attract or repel human settlement. The authors examine population growth near protected areas around the world. Whether people crowd toward park edges or drift away shapes both conservation planning and the lives of rural neighbours. The authors treat people as part of the landscape, not outside it.
plos-pone-0004379:
The tropics of the Americas hold more bird species than any other region on Earth. Yet how those birds split into separate species is still poorly mapped. Kevin Kerr, Darío Lijtmaer, Ana Barreira, and co-authors used DNA barcodes to probe the pattern. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper draws on short gene tags that can tell species apart.

Barcoding lets teams sort many birds fast, without full genome work. The authors compared tags across Neotropical birds to read regional divergence. Genetic data for the region had been thin before. Their survey adds a broad base for later studies. It also helps spot hidden diversity, where two look-alike populations differ in their DNA.
plos-pone-0004479:
Chemical marks on the packaging of one stretch of human DNA are mapped by Pelin Akan, Martin Sahlen, and Panagiotis Deloukas in PLOS ONE in 2009. The stretch lies on chromosome 20, in a region tied to conditions such as type 2 diabetes and obesity. The team searched it in a systematic way for regulatory elements, the switches that control genes.

They profiled six kinds of histone modification, marks on the proteins that spool DNA, across a region millions of letters long. They also tracked two key proteins that bind DNA. Marks like these show which parts of the region are open for business in a cell. The map gives diabetes and obesity research a detailed guide to one suspect neighborhood of the genome.
plos-pone-0004579:
The system that reads a cannabis-like signal made by the body is mapped in the human ovary by Mona El-Talatini, Anthony Taylor, Janine Elson, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal molecule is anandamide. It had been measured in the fluid around human eggs, and was suggested to play a role in follicle and egg maturity.

Its exact source and role in the ovary remained unclear. The team used staining methods on normal human ovaries to locate the endocannabinoid system's parts: the enzymes that make and break the signal, and its receptors. A map of where the system sits is the first step to learning what it does. The work may matter for fertility care, where egg quality decides success.
plos-pone-0004679:
Ivan Norscia, Daniela Antonacci, and Elisabetta Palagi watched mating trade in a wild prosimian for PLOS ONE in 2009. In nature, power can come from force or from trade with others. When males cannot use force, they must rely on females for chances to breed, and trade takes the lead.

The team asked how shifts in supply and need change what males offer and get. They tracked who groomed whom and how mating chances moved with those trades. The work treats mating as a market that rises and falls. It helps explain social bonds in early primate kin and how favors shape breeding.
plos-pone-0004779:
Laurent Roybon and colleagues showed that two factors split jobs in making new granule neurons in the hippocampus, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Building these neurons needs timed, placed action by inner and outer cues. Two related transcription factors, Neurogenin2 and NeuroD1, are key regulators of that building process in the dentate gyrus, a memory hub.

The team found one factor drives production and amplification of young neurons. The other specifies final neuronal fate. Split duties explain how numbers and identity are controlled separately. The work informs efforts to grow new neurons for repair. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004879:
Alexandra Aicher and colleagues showed cGMP dependent protein kinase I is crucial for angiogenesis and postnatal vasculogenesis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Endothelium derived nitric oxide plays important roles for the bone marrow microenvironment. Several effects of nitric oxide are mediated by cGMP pathways. Prompting investigation of the cGMP downstream effector kinase I in new vessel formation after birth and in adult ischemic tissues.

Without the kinase, vessel growth falters severely. Nitric oxide signaling requires this relay. Stimulating it could aid ischemic repair. Blocking it may starve tumors. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004979:
Mutations in myotubularin family genes cause human neuromuscular disorders. The pathways behind them were unclear. Jie Mei, Zhi Li and Jian-Fang Gui studied one family member in zebrafish. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The gene is Mtmr8. They examined its role in muscle development.

Mtmr8 cooperates with the PI3K signal in the fish. Together they regulate actin filament modeling. That modeling shapes growing muscle. The partnership reveals a new developmental role for the family. The fish model also lights a path toward the human diseases. Understanding development in zebrafish can show where the human process breaks.
plos-pone-0005079:
Flu vaccines change every year. Drifted viruses force constant updates. Heath Kelly and colleagues asked how well the vaccines actually work. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Australia had no regular review of vaccine effectiveness. The team built one from routine surveillance data.

Their method estimates effectiveness during or after each season. It turns data already collected into a yearly report card. Health officials can see whether the shot matched the season's viruses. Weak years can be spotted and studied. The work shows surveillance data can answer practical questions. It does so without expensive special studies. Other countries could adopt the same approach.
plos-pone-0005179:
Old retroviruses left copies of themselves scattered through the genomes of vertebrates. Their end sections, called long terminal repeats, can still switch nearby genes on or off. Benachenhou and colleagues traced how these repeats have been kept through evolution in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Single repeats left alone in the genome are hard to spot without a known match to search for. The team built a way to detect those lone repeats from sequence data alone. The method helps map viral fossils in DNA and shows where they may still shape gene activity today.
plos-pone-0005279:
MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that fine-tune how much protein genes make. They matter in growth and in many diseases, yet how their own production is controlled was less clear. Corcoran and colleagues mined binding data to find microRNA promoters in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Promoters are the start switches in front of genes. Using chromatin data for polymerase II, the enzyme that reads genes, the team identified features of mammalian microRNA promoters. Knowing the switches helps explain when microRNAs appear and how their tuning goes wrong in disease. These small RNAs can turn genes up or down in fine steps, so knowing where their start switches sit helps explain how cells fine-tune growth. Stress, and repair from day to day.
plos-pone-0005379:
An ethogram is a catalog of a species' behaviors, traditionally built by watching animals directly. For birds that range freely in remote places, direct watching is often impossible. Sakamoto and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether body acceleration loggers can build ethograms automatically.

Small loggers on free-ranging birds record how the body speeds and tilts through each action. If distinct behaviors leave distinct acceleration signatures, software can sort the record into an ethogram. That would let researchers catalog wild behavior without watching every minute. Birds that feed at sea or cross long land gaps at night leave no watcher a chance to log what they do. So a back-pack log is the one way to see a wild day in full.
plos-pone-0005479:
Melissa Da Silva and Chris Upton studied a virus protein with a familiar shape in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Copying DNA needs helper proteins that hold the copying machine on the strand. One helper, called PCNA, forms a ring that slides along DNA in cells like ours.

The authors showed that a vaccinia virus protein, G8R, is built like that ring protein. A virus carrying its own copy of such a helper may copy its DNA more freely inside host cells. The likeness also hints at how viruses borrow designs from the cells they infect.
plos-pone-0005579:
James Hughes and co-authors steered stem-like cells toward body layers in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In the early embryo, one group of cells must choose between forming gut and muscle layers or the skin and nerve layer. Growing those choices in a dish is a basic goal of stem cell work.

The team used cell-to-cell contact and a mesoderm-blocking signal to steer the choice. Adjusting those cues pushed cultured cells toward one lineage or the other. Reliable steering is what future cell therapies need to make the right tissue on demand.
plos-pone-0005679:
Yi Fu and colleagues lowered the level of a zinc carrier in rat pancreas cells in 2009 and watched what happened to insulin. The carrier, ZnT8, is made by the beta cells that release insulin. A gene variant near its code is linked to higher risk of type 2 diabetes.

When the team cut ZnT8 levels in the INS-1 cell line, the cells held less insulin. They also released less insulin when sugar rose, the normal trigger for release. The results tie the gene to the disease through a clear chain: less carrier, less stored insulin, weaker release. That chain is a useful target for future diabetes work.
plos-pone-0005779:
Jostein Gohli and Göran Högstedt modeled in 2009 how warning colors could evolve despite a basic snag. Bright prey warn predators they taste bad, but the first bright mutants should be eaten before predators learn. Kin selection and predator shyness were past attempts to solve that snag.

Their model adds a secreted chemical defense that predators can smell or taste before striking. Such a defense could shield the first conspicuous mutants long enough for learning to spread. The math shows the path can work. Warning coloration is a textbook puzzle, and this adds a credible first step.
plos-pone-0005879:
Rosângela Salerno-Goncalves and Marcelo Sztein explored in 2009 how human killer T cells learn to recognize the typhoid germ. Typhoid fever is worsening as Salmonella Typhi resists antibiotics, adding urgency to vaccine work. Dendritic cells normally teach T cells by presenting germ fragments.

The team used dendritic cells induced to die after loading, a suicide cross-presentation trick, to prime specific CD8 T cells in humans. That priming route may mimic how natural immunity forms. Better priming methods could yield stronger typhoid vaccines. The work addresses a step where many vaccine ideas quietly fail.
plos-pone-0005979:
The kidney's filter is lined with cells called podocytes, whose fine feet grip the filter wall. Nils Vogtländer, Henk Visch, Marinka Bakker and colleagues studied one protein that coats those cells in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper asks what happens when alpha-dystroglycan, a sugar-coated protein on the podocyte surface, is grabbed from outside.

Grabbing it fires signals inside the cell, the team reports. That firing may help explain podocyte effacement, the flattening of the feet that marks many kidney diseases. A new route to that flattening, if confirmed, gives kidney research a fresh place to look for causes and for drugs that keep the filter's shape intact.
plos-pone-0006079:
Standard HIV tests miss rare drug-resistant variants hiding below one fifth of the virus pool. Thuy Le, Jennifer Chiarella, Birgitte Simen and colleagues went hunting for those rare forms in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper samples treatment-experienced people whose therapy was failing, and asks how often low-abundance resistant variants occur and what they mean.

The hidden variants tracked the drugs each person had taken before, the title's link to historical use. A memory of past treatment thus lives inside the virus pool. Finding it could warn doctors away from drugs doomed to fail again, even when the standard test gives those drugs a clean pass.
plos-pone-0006179:
When a yeast cell divides, it must build a wall across its middle to split in two. Jae-Sook Park and colleagues studied the gene pik1 in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The gene makes an enzyme that adds a phosphate tag to fatty membrane building blocks, and it binds a partner protein called Cdc4.

Deleting the gene killed the yeast, proving it is essential for life. Cells forced to rely on a weakened copy showed faults in forming the dividing wall, called septation. The work pins down one required step in yeast division. Such basic maps later help explain division faults in larger organisms too.
plos-pone-0006279:
A worm's gut transporter, PEPT-1, pulls small protein pieces from food into the body. Britta Spanier and colleagues studied worms missing that transporter in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. The deficient animals grow slowly, develop late, and yet show an obesity-like pattern.

The study works out how the transporter contributes to that fat phenotype. Losing efficient protein uptake reshapes how the body stores energy. A tiny worm thus models the gut's role in body fat. The results may inform thinking about nutrient transport and obesity in larger animals.
plos-pone-0006379:
Friedreich ataxia is the most common recessive ataxia, caused by low levels of frataxin, a mitochondrial iron handler. Nadege Calmels and colleagues built the first cellular models based on frataxin missense mutations in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Most patients carry a repeated DNA expansion, but some carry single-letter changes instead.

The new models spontaneously reproduce the defects associated with the disease. Cells carrying patient-like changes mirror the iron-sulfur cluster faults of real disease. Good cell models let drugs be screened without animal trials first. They also let each mutation's severity be compared directly.
plos-pone-0006479:
David Courson and Ronald Rock shared a faster way to build microscopy chambers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fluid handling is gaining a bigger place in lab science. It ranges from simple buffer exchange systems to perfusion chambers and advanced microfluidic tools. Making laminar flow chambers at the bench is often slow and fussy.

The authors describe fast benchtop fabrication of chambers for advanced microscopy. A simpler build puts live-cell imaging within reach of more labs. It also speeds prototyping when a custom chamber is needed. Method papers like this one quietly raise what small labs can do.
plos-pone-0006579:
Phillip Pang, Paul Planet, and Jeffrey Glenn traced the family history of hepatitis C virus in PLOS ONE in 2009. People with long-term hepatitis C infection need very different lengths of drug care. They also respond to interferon therapy in quite different ways. Those gaps track with the major genotypes, the main virus families. The team asked how those families evolved.

Their title says the evolution of the major genotypes lines up with how patients respond to interferon. In other words, the virus family tree helps predict how well care will work. That link helps doctors set the length of care and what to expect. It also shows how virus evolution shapes daily clinic choices.
plos-pone-0006679:
Qingran Kong and colleagues studied why inserted genes behave unevenly in transgenic pigs for PLOS ONE in 2009. Transgenic animals help scientists study gene function and model human disease. They can also produce useful proteins. A major problem is that an inserted gene may be inherited or expressed unreliably. Its activity can fade or vary between animals.

The team linked expression levels to two features of the inserted gene. One was copy number, meaning how many copies landed in the genome. The other was methylation of the cytomegalovirus promoter driving the gene. Methylation can switch a promoter off without changing the DNA letters. Understanding both factors helps researchers design transgenic pigs with steadier expression.
plos-pone-0006779:
Markus Uhrig and co-authors searched for genes responding to Alzheimer's amyloid in human cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alzheimer's disease involves degeneration and loss of neurons. A protein fragment called Aβ42 is thought to trigger the disease cascade. Its shorter cousin, Aβ40, is considered less harmful. The team wanted the overall gene regulation picture.

They exposed human neuroblastoma cells to amyloid beta. Then they monitored transcriptome-wide responses, the full set of gene activity changes. Hierarchical clustering grouped the responsive genes. New responsive genes emerged from that grouping. The list gives fresh entry points for studying how amyloid harms neurons.
plos-pone-0006879:
Kati Räsänen and colleagues compared fibroblast behavior from healthy tissue and tumor surroundings in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tumors activate nearby fibroblasts, a reaction called the tumor-stroma response. One activation type is nemosis. Nemosis boosts growth factor and inflammatory protein production. At the same time, cytoskeletal proteins are degraded.

Samples came from patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma. Normal and cancer-associated fibroblasts answered nemosis differently. Different answers may help tumors recruit support. Comparing the two cell types isolates what cancer changes in its neighbors. That knowledge could lead to treatments targeting the tumor's support system.
plos-pone-0006979:
Zhenshan Wang, Vicky Li, Guy Chan, and colleagues weighed in on an obesity gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. A study of Swedish men had linked variants in the type 3 adenylyl cyclase gene with obesity. That hint suggested the gene helps control body weight. The team tested the idea in mice lacking the gene.

They followed the weight of these AC3-deficient mice over a long period. The adult mice became obese, as the title reports. A mouse result cannot settle the human question alone. Still, it strengthens the case that this signaling enzyme helps regulate energy balance.
plos-pone-0007079:
Charlotte Andreasen, Daniel Powell, and Nicholas Carbonetti studied whooping cough infection in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bordetella pertussis multiplies in the airways during the first week. The host immune response then clears it over the next few weeks. Pertussis toxin is a weapon secreted only by this bacterium.

The team measured the toxin's effect on one immune signal, IL-17. The toxin stimulated IL-17 production during infection. IL-17 helps rally defenses at mucosal surfaces. Knowing how the toxin bends that response may improve vaccines, since the toxin is both a weapon and a vaccine ingredient.
plos-pone-0007179:
Xiaoyan Yang, Sagar V. Kathuria, Ramakrishna Vadrevu, and colleagues published a 2009 PLOS ONE study on how proteins hold their shape. They examine small structural units in TIM barrel proteins, a common protein fold. Their focus is a set of hairpin clamps that brace neighboring parts of the protein.

Earlier work on one bacterial TIM barrel protein showed these clamps add clear stability. The authors test how general that effect is across similar modules. Protein scientists can use their results when they design stable enzymes or predict how a fold will hold together.
plos-pone-0007279:
Johan Waldemarsson, Margaretha Stålhammar-Carlemalm, Charlotta Sandin, and colleagues dissected a strep protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The M protein sits on the surface of Streptococcus pyogenes, the bacterium behind strep throat and invasive disease. M protein is a major virulence factor that blocks phagocytosis, the eating of bacteria by immune cells.

Little was known about M protein's role inside a living host. The authors test different regions of the M5 protein. They report that its hypervariable region is essential for virulence. That region may be a useful vaccine target.
plos-pone-0007379:
Raphael Roduit, Pascal Escher, and Daniel F. Schorderet studied mutations in an eye development gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. NR2E3 is a nuclear receptor essential for proper photoreceptor determination and differentiation. Photoreceptors are the light-sensing cells of the retina, divided into rods and cones with different jobs.

Human NR2E3 mutations cause an inherited cone syndrome and related retinal diseases. The authors examine mutations in its DNA-binding domain. They test effects on dimerization, where two protein copies pair up, and on interaction with the CRX protein. Their work explains how single mutations disturb retina development.
plos-pone-0007479:
Jesse Salisbury and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how a mouse egg prepares for fertilization. As an oocyte matures, it clears out stored genetic messages it no longer needs. Standard microarray analysis measures a gene's total message level. That hides a finer detail: many genes produce several message variants, called isoforms. The team re-read the data probe by probe to see them separately.

The finer view showed that specific isoforms degrade at different rates during maturation. The egg is not clearing its shelves evenly. It trims some variants while sparing others. That selectivity likely shapes which proteins the early embryo can make. The method also warns other researchers that gene-level averages can mislead. Reading at probe level reveals decisions the cell makes variant by variant.
plos-pone-0007579:
Sébastien Doucet and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how newborns find their bearings through smell. Around the nipple sit small glands, the areolar or Montgomery glands, which secrete a scented fluid in nursing women. The team exposed three-day-old infants to secretions donated by unrelated, unfamiliar lactating women. They then measured how the babies responded to that stimulus.

The newborns responded selectively and unconditionally to the areolar scent. The reaction did not depend on knowing the woman. That suggests the glands send a built-in chemical signal for newborns. Such a signal could guide a baby toward the breast before vision is useful. Human infants, like other young mammals, may be led by smell from their first days. The study gives that idea controlled experimental support.
plos-pone-0007679:
Hiroshi Tomita and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns a light-sensing protein from green algae. The protein, called channelrhodopsin-2, can make cells respond to light. The team put the gene for it into rats, under the control of a switch called Thy-1.2.

They then measured what the rats could see and how their eyes and brains reacted to light. Work like this tests an idea for restoring sight. If surviving cells in a damaged eye can be made light-sensitive, some vision might return. That hope drives work for people who have lost their sight cells.
plos-pone-0007779:
Antoine Disset and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It offers a way to find disease markers in mixed tissue samples. Gene profiling machines are reliable, but tissue samples mix many cell types. Differences in cell mix scatter the data. Real markers can drown in that noise.

Their approach analyzes tissue compartments separately instead of as one blend. Sorting signals by compartment sharpens the search for molecular markers. Cleaner markers mean better diagnostic tests for patients. The method is a general fix for a common problem in gene expression studies, not just one disease.
plos-pone-0007879:
Ainhoa Mielgo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It finds a second job for a protein best known in cell death. Caspase-8 is a lead enzyme of apoptosis, the program that kills unneeded cells. Development and aging programs guard against runaway growth, as in cancer.

Those growth-control programs are closely tied to cell death pathways. The authors show that one part of caspase-8, its death effector domains, can push cells to finish differentiating. Differentiation is the step where young cells take on their final role. A death protein steering maturity is a neat twist in cell biology.
plos-pone-0007979:
Konstantinos Mavromatis and colleagues described a gene-guessing aid inside a big microbe database in PLOS ONE in 2009. New genomes pour in with thousands of genes whose jobs are unknown. The classic guess rests on how alike two gene sequences look.

Their aid adds context: a gene's neighbors often share its line of work. Tools in the Integrated Microbial Genomes system let users read a gene's place and partners at a glance. Guesses built on both looks and context should miss less often, speeding the slow work of naming what each new gene does.
plos-pone-0008079:
Ping Liu and colleagues found a switch that routes the alarm during RNA virus infection in PLOS ONE in 2009. When such a virus enters, sensors wake two defense paths: one led by NF-kB and one by IRF3. A kinase complex at the crossing needs a part called IKK gamma.

A shortened splice form of that part tips which path the cell leans on. Change the form, and the balance of the response changes with it. The switch helps explain why the same virus can stir unlike responses in different cells, a point for antiviral design.
plos-pone-0008179:
Adam T. Szafran and co-authors studied androgen insensitivity syndrome in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The rare condition stems from faults in the androgen receptor gene. Those faults disrupt male sexual development before birth. Effects range widely, but loss of fertility is shared across cases. No firm treatment existed when the paper appeared.

The team used a high content analysis method, screening many receptor mutants in cells at once. Sorting mutants by how they behave could point care toward each patient's own fault. That is the heart of personalized medicine. The work links a rare hormone disorder to a practical screening plan.
plos-pone-0008279:
Robert B. Annan and colleagues screened for kinase targets in yeast in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Ste20p belongs to a kinase family involved in many cell processes. These enzymes help control the cell skeleton and activate MAPK signaling pathways. Despite many roles, few of their substrates had been identified. Substrates are the proteins a kinase acts on directly.

The team ran a biochemical genomics screen to find Ste20p substrates. Their results also enabled computer prediction of further novel substrates. A fuller substrate list clarifies what this kinase family controls. That aids basic research on cell signaling.
plos-pone-0008379:
Amanda Kwant-Mitchell and colleagues grew human NK cells in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Natural killer cells help suppress tumors. Studies of human NK cells were largely restricted to dishes in the lab. Those in vitro experiments lack the complexity of whole organisms. Mouse models, in turn, differ significantly from humans.

Using an immunodeficient mouse model, the team developed functional human NK cells. The cells were able to protect against a tumor challenge. A living system for human NK cells enables better therapy testing. It bridges lab findings and clinical hopes.
plos-pone-0008479:
Ellen Brooks-Pollock and co-authors model tuberculosis spread in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Math models help describe how TB spreads in a population. They also test what public health steps might do. Past models often treated all ages in a simple, uniform way. Real populations have a clear age structure, with mixing that varies by age. The team ask if that detail changes the results.

They build simple TB models with realistic age structure. They compare outcomes with the simpler uniform models. Age detail shifts forecasts for cases and for control effects. Modelers should thus take age mixing seriously when they advise TB policy.
plos-pone-0008579:
Siwang Yu and co-authors study a protective gene in prostate cancer in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The gene factor is called Nrf2. It switches on many genes that protect cells from damage. In TRAMP mice, a model of prostate cancer, Nrf2 expression was suppressed in tumors. The team ask if epigenetic mechanisms cause that suppression. Epigenetic marks silence genes without changing DNA code.

They find such mechanisms regulate Nrf2 in these mouse tumors. Silencing a protective factor may let cancer grow unchecked. Restoring Nrf2 could restore cell defenses against cancer. The study links epigenetic silencing to loss of a key guardian in prostate tumors.
plos-pone-0008679:
Alan Wilson, RajReni Kaul, and Orlando Sarnelle asked a simple growth question in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a harmful kind of phytoplankter, a tiny drifting plant-like organism. Such organisms sometimes live alone and sometimes join into colonies. Larger bodies usually grow more slowly per unit of size. Nobody had tested that rule inside one species.

The authors measured growth for single cells and for colonies of different sizes. Comparing the rates shows what colonial life costs or gains. Blooms of harmful plankton can poison water and kill fish. Knowing whether colonies grow faster or slower helps predict when a bloom will spread.
plos-pone-0008779:
Roland Stimson, Gerald Lobley, Ioanna Maraki, and colleagues fed rats different diets and tracked stress-hormone handling. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glucocorticoids are hormones that shape fat and sugar use. Tissues renew active hormone from inactive forms using an enzyme called 11beta-HSD1. Other enzymes break the active form down. Diet mix was already known to shift liver enzyme levels.

Obese rats ate diets with varied protein, fat, and carbohydrate shares. The team measured hormone renewal and breakdown in liver and fat. Results show diet composition reaches deep into hormone control. That reach matters for obesity and diabetes advice.
plos-pone-0008879:
Hassan Ashktorab, Alejandro Schäffer, Mohammad Daremipouran, and colleagues compared gene damage patterns in colorectal tumors from different groups. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Colon tumors often grow through chromosomal instability, gaining and losing big DNA chunks. Clinical and genetic hints suggested tumors differ between African American and other patients. Such differences could hide distinct drivers of the disease.

Their analysis catalogued which amplifications and deletions each group's tumors carried. Patterns indeed differed in notable ways. Distinct alterations point to group-specific paths into the same cancer. Fair cancer care needs research that maps all groups' tumors, not just one.
plos-pone-0008979:
So Young Kim and co-authors hunted for a weak point in certain breast cancers. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2010. Those cancers lean on one growth signal running through beta-catenin. The signal is also overactive in colon and liver cancers. Drugs that block beta-catenin directly have been hard to build, so the team looked elsewhere.

Their search singled out CK1 epsilon, an enzyme in the same signalling web. Breast cancer cells driven by beta-catenin needed CK1 epsilon to keep growing. Cells not driven by that signal cared less about it. A dependency like this gives drug makers a side door into a stubborn cancer type.
plos-pone-0009079:
Nouara Yahi, Anaïs Aulas, and Jacques Fantini examined how cholesterol steers amyloid's handshake with cell membranes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer's disease involves the beta-amyloid peptide changing shape and clumping. Membrane fats play a key part in that process. Reports disagreed on whether cholesterol helps or hinders it.

The team focused on glycolipids, fatty sugar-bearing molecules in membranes. Cholesterol constrains how those glycolipids fold and present themselves. That folded shape decides how well amyloid recognises and binds them. Membrane composition, not just the peptide, may set Alzheimer's in motion.
plos-pone-0009179:
Ulf Hensen, Oliver Lange, and Helmut Grubmüller published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. It tackles a hard measurement problem in molecular physics. Scientists who simulate proteins on computers need to know each molecule's entropy, a measure of how many shapes it can take. Older shortcuts for that number were known to be unreliable.

The authors built a new method they call the minimally coupled subspace approach. It works from computer-generated sets of molecular snapshots and splits the motion into parts that barely affect each other. That split lets the method produce absolute entropy values where earlier estimates, such as the quasi-harmonic approximation, break down. The result is a general tool for studying proteins and other large molecules.
plos-pone-0009279:
Justin Spinner and co-authors published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The body's first defense against bacteria pairs macrophages with neutrophils, fast-acting white blood cells. Yersinia bacteria, which include the plague germ, slip past that defense. They inject proteins into immune cells to disable them.

One injected protein, YopJ/P, can push cells into programmed death. The team found that neutrophils resist that death signal. The bacteria's own injection system also shields neutrophils from death by reactive oxygen. Knowing which immune cells refuse to die helps explain how the body keeps fighting Yersinia.
plos-pone-0009379:
Arne Gjuvsland, Erik Plahte, Tormod Ådnøy, and co-authors published this genetics theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Since Mendel, geneticists have described gene action by comparing mixed and pure gene copies. A trait can be additive, or one copy can dominate the other. Those labels, though, say little about how the two copies actually interact inside the cell.

The authors connect single-locus genetics with regulatory biology. They model how two alleles of one gene depend on each other's function. That deeper view can explain why dominance differs between traits and settings. It offers breeders and geneticists a mechanism behind numbers they already measure.
plos-pone-0009479:
Andre Brunoni, Laura Tadini, and Felipe Fregni reviewed sixty years of drug trials in mental health in PLOS ONE in 2010. Modern treatment with psychiatric drugs began around 1949, when lithium came into use. Since then, the design of clinical trials has changed many times. Faults in design can hide a drug's true effect or invent one.

The review traces how methods grew across six decades of work in this field. It notes where trials got stronger and where weak points remain. The result is a record of how the evidence behind mental health drugs was built. It can help planners design cleaner trials in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0009579:
Daniel Appledorn and co-authors improved a virus based vaccine platform in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adenoviruses can be rebuilt to carry genes from other germs, such as HIV. Past trials raised strong immune responses, yet they did not protect people. The team added a booster piece taken from a chicken parasite, Eimeria tenella. That piece switches on TLR sensors, which sound the immune alarm.

The boosted vaccine raised stronger cell based immune responses to its target. Stronger cellular defense is what such vaccines most need. The study tests whether a louder alarm at the start makes protection more likely. It offers a design tweak for a platform aimed at hard targets like HIV.
plos-pone-0009679:
Proteins are built from shorter pieces, and some pieces recur in many species. Ashish Tendulkar and colleagues described a new online resource called FragKB in PLOS ONE in 2010. The database gathers conserved peptide fragments, meaning pieces kept nearly unchanged across species, and adds notes on their shape and past research.

Each entry links a fragment to what is known about its structure and to papers that mention it. That lets scientists spot shared building blocks when they compare proteins from different organisms. Reusing proven fragments could also guide the design of new proteins for medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0009779:
Echinococcus multilocularis is a small tapeworm whose larvae can damage the liver. Bruno Gottstein and colleagues studied mice infected by mouth with the parasite's eggs. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The infection can be serious in people as well as animals.

The team read the liver's gene expression profile during infection. That profile lists which genes the liver switches on or off as the parasite takes hold. Peroral infection means the eggs entered by mouth, the natural route. The profile helps explain how the liver responds to this invader.
plos-pone-0009879:
Sudden cardiac arrest kills when the heart abruptly stops beating effectively. Dan Arking and colleagues scanned genomes to find gene variants that protect against it. Their genome-wide association study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most victims have little warning before the event.

The scan identified GPC5 as a novel genetic locus linked with protection. A locus is a specific address in the genome. Finding a protective variant differs from finding a risk one; it points to defenses worth copying. Such clues may one day guide prevention for people at risk.
plos-pone-0009979:
A drug used to stop organ rejection also quiets a master growth switch in the brain. Patricia Spilman and colleagues tested that drug in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The drug is rapamycin, and the switch it blocks is mTOR. Inhibiting mTOR abolished cognitive deficits in the mice. Cognitive deficits mean losses in learning and memory. It also reduced amyloid-beta levels, the protein that clumps in Alzheimer's brains. One drug easing both symptoms and buildup drew wide attention. The mice were bred to develop Alzheimer's-like disease.
plos-pone-0010079:
The authors were Sarah Jesse, Petra Steinacker, Stefan Lehnert, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sought a better test for meningitis. Telling bacterial meningitis from the viral kind can be hard. Standard lab results are sometimes unclear, especially when the usual stain finds no bacteria, yet treatment choices differ sharply.

The team used proteomics, a scan of many proteins at once, on spinal fluid samples. Their aim was a reliable marker that separates the two forms. A clear marker could speed the right treatment and spare some patients needless antibiotics.
plos-pone-0010179:
Francesco Gregoretti and two co-workers, Vincenzo Belcastro and Diego di Bernardo, led this team. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper sped up a tool for mapping gene networks. New lab tools were making huge sets of gene data. Old tools to infer gene networks from that data ran too slowly.

The team ran their method in parallel, split across many machines at once. That cut the time needed to build a network from a large data set. Such networks show which genes switch other genes on or off. A fast tool helps labs turn raw gene data into clear maps.
plos-pone-0010279:
The authors were Yuichiro Ohshima, Ichiro Yajima, Kozue Takeda, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study chased a cancer molecule called c-RET in melanoma. Melanoma is among the most aggressive cancers, and its rate is rising faster than any other cancer's. The team had earlier made mice carrying an always-on RET gene, and those mice developed melanoma on their own.

They examined c-RET in tumors from those mice and in human melanoma cell lines. A shared molecule in mouse tumors and human cells strengthens RET's case as a drug target. Melanoma badly needs targets that work after spread.
plos-pone-0010379:
Helena Safavi-Hemami and co-workers described a key enzyme in sea anemone partnerships for PLOS ONE in 2010. Many anemones host algae inside their cells, a partnership called symbiosis. The enzyme studied, nitric oxide synthase, makes nitric oxide, a messenger gas used in many body processes. Its role in sea animals like these was poorly known. The team characterized it across three such partnerships.

Finding how the enzyme is built and where it acts is a first step. Nitric oxide may help partners talk to each other chemically. It could also respond when the partnership is stressed, as in coral bleaching. Reef partnerships are vital and fragile. Basic enzyme work like this underpins later efforts to protect them.
plos-pone-0010479:
Anne Shemon and colleagues mapped the pocket where a cancer-related protein grips small molecules in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, RKIP, brakes a major growth signaling route in cells. It also helps suppress the spread of tumors. Finding small molecules that fit RKIP could restore its braking power. The team used NMR screening, a magnetic method, to fish for such molecules and locate the binding pocket.

Knowing the pocket's shape is the first step in drug design. Even weak initial binders can be improved once the site is known. RKIP loss is seen in several aggressive cancers. A drug that boosts its action would be a new kind of therapy. This study provides the structural foothold for that search.
plos-pone-0010579:
Jie Ma, Robert Naumann, and Jagmeet Kanwal studied hearing in mustached bats for PLOS ONE in 2010. Bat calls contain rising and falling sweeps of pitch. The team asked how finely bats can tell one sweep pattern from another.

The researchers linked certain sweeps to a mild shock, then watched heart rate for signs of fear. Bats learned to react to the paired sweep and not to similar ones. Their choices showed very sharp hearing for small changes in pitch movement. Sharp hearing of this kind likely helps bats sort social calls from echoes in the dark.
plos-pone-0010679:
Erumbi Rangarajan and colleagues studied a muscle protein that grips cell contacts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells hold onto neighbors and their matrix through complexes tied to internal cables. Metavinculin, a form of the linker vinculin found in muscle, has an extra piece that other forms lack.

The team solved how that extra piece changes the protein's tail. One helix in the tail swaps out for another when the protein binds its partners. That swap sets how strongly and in what way the protein can grip. Small shape tricks like this tune how heart and muscle cells hold together under constant strain.
plos-pone-0010779:
Christopher Brown and Kevin Brown stress-tested methods that detect co-evolving protein positions, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When two spots in a protein change together over evolution, they often touch or work together. Algorithms hunt those linked spots to infer protein shape. Several rival algorithms existed, and users had little guidance on which to trust.

The team ran three named methods through a full pipeline and varied each setting. Small setting choices changed results more than the choice of method did. That finding redirects attention from brand names to careful setup. Protein folders and evolution researchers both depend on these signals, so honest benchmarks matter.
plos-pone-0010879:
Wei Wang, Ruihuan Xu and Jinming Li published this antibody study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A bispecific antibody can grab two different targets at once. Such antibodies occur naturally in some allergy patients, when two antibody halves swap arms, but no one had shown the process in animals or built a model to study it.

The authors immunized New Zealand white rabbits with paired synthetic compounds and recovered antibodies that recognized both partners at once. Female rabbits tended to respond more strongly than males. The bispecific antibodies were single molecules of one main antibody class. Wang and colleagues establish the first animal model for this natural swapping. A working model lets researchers probe how these dual-grip antibodies form, which could inform both allergy treatment and drug design.
plos-pone-0010979:
Sohyun McElroy, James Byrne, Shawn Chavez and co-authors published this fertility study in PLOS ONE in 2010. About a fifth of eggs collected for fertility treatment are immature and thrown away. They have been stripped of the cumulus cells that normally mature them, so they could become a valuable resource for research and therapy if they could be matured in the dish.

The authors read single-cell data to find signals that cumulus cells send and eggs receive, then added those ovarian factors to the culture. Matured eggs were activated without sperm to form parthenogenetic blastocysts, early embryos that cannot develop into a baby but can yield research material. McElroy and colleagues work toward turning discarded eggs into a resource, which could supply stem cell research without using fertilized embryos.
plos-pone-0011079:
Casado, Colombo, Rauch and colleagues wrote a 2010 PLOS ONE study on HIV. They asked why the illness moves fast in some people and slowly in others. To answer, they looked for gene traits in both the virus and the person that track with how doctors define disease progress.

The team compared genetic patterns with clinical stages of infection. Any strong links could help explain why outcomes differ so much between patients. Such links might one day help doctors judge a person's likely course early on. The study adds to efforts to make HIV care fit the individual patient.
plos-pone-0011179:
Gesprasert, Wichukchinda, Mori and colleagues studied HIV in Thailand for PLOS ONE in 2010. A person's immune gene set pushes HIV to change a key viral protein to escape attack. In people infected with a regional virus type, the team linked that pressure to the amount of virus in blood.

As immune pressure reshapes the protein, viral load shifts along with the changes. That shows the contest between host genes and virus plays out in real patients. Vaccines must cope with a target that keeps moving under this pressure. The study helps designers pick parts of the virus that change least.
plos-pone-0011279:
Xu, Wagner, Bekerman and colleagues grew bone from fat stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stem cells from fat can turn into bone when the right cues arrive, including physical tension inside the cell. The team studied a growth factor that regulates that tension through a protein controlling the cell skeleton.

Their results show the factor helps steer fat stem cells toward bone formation. Mechanical cues matter as much as chemical ones in that choice. Such knowledge informs bone repair, where a patient's own fat could supply starting cells. A reliable tension cue could help fractures and bone defects heal faster.
plos-pone-0011379:
Irene Guendel and co-authors studied in 2010 how a chemical tag changes the helper work of BRCA1. The BRCA1 protein is best known for guarding against breast and ovarian cancer, but it also helps switch other genes on and off as a partner to the gene-reading machinery. Cells can attach small methyl tags to the protein itself.

The team mapped where those tags land on BRCA1 and tested how tagging alters its gene-switching help. Tagging changed which partners BRCA1 worked with and how strongly it supported gene activity. That finding adds a control layer to a famous cancer protein. It suggests cancer can arise not only when BRCA1 is mutated, but also when its tagging pattern goes wrong, a distinction that may matter for future tests and treatments.
plos-pone-0011479:
Eric Bernard and co-authors traced in 2010 how chikungunya virus enters mammalian cells. The virus, spread by mosquitoes, causes fever and joint pain that can linger for months. Blocking a virus at the door is the cleanest way to stop it, so the team mapped which door this virus uses and where it goes just after entering.

They showed the virus is taken in through clathrin-coated pits, the cell's standard cargo intake, and then sits in early endosomal compartments, the sorting stations just inside. Each mapped step is a place a drug might jam the process. The work also helps explain which cells the virus can infect, since a cell must offer the right door. For a virus with no specific treatment, an entry map is a practical start.
plos-pone-0011579:
Ignacio Marín published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It looks at RBR ubiquitin ligases, a family of enzymes found in all eukaryotes. These enzymes help cells tag worn-out proteins so they can be broken down and recycled.

Marín traces how RBR genes first appeared in plants and how the family later split into distinct groups. By comparing gene structures and family trees across plant species, the study shows members taking on narrower, more specialised jobs over time. Readers gain a clear map of how plants expanded a basic protein-recycling tool into a set of tailored parts.
plos-pone-0011679:
Gizelle Anzures and colleagues tested how culture shapes judging age from faces, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Judging a stranger's age feels like a basic skill, yet growing up in different cultures gives people very different experience with faces. Such experience is already known to shape face preferences and recognition.

The team found that people's backgrounds affect how efficiently they estimate age from a face. Observers did best with the kinds of faces their own culture had trained them on. The result shows that even an apparently obvious skill is partly learned, a point that matters for cross-cultural research and design.
plos-pone-0011779:
John Castle and co-authors counted non-coding RNAs across the human body, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Non-coding RNAs are key cell molecules, but they were hard to track on fast platforms because they often lack the tail that standard methods grab. The team used a method neutral to that tail, plus deep sequencing.

Their digital survey measured levels of these RNAs, snoRNAs included, across eleven human tissues. The result is an atlas of the genome's quiet bulk, tissue by tissue. That map is a resource for finding tissue-specific jobs of RNAs that long sat overlooked.
plos-pone-0011879:
Aurelie Hanin and colleagues screened in 2010 for genes that the bacterium Enterococcus faecalis turns on only inside a host. This germ normally lives harmlessly in the human gut, yet it has become a leading cause of hospital-acquired infection. Understanding that switch from resident to invader is the study's aim.

The screen covered insect and mouse infections as well as growth in urine, a common site of its hospital infections. Genes switched on in these real settings, but quiet in lab culture, form the bacterium's working toolkit for infection. That list gives researchers targets that matter during actual illness, not just in a flask.
plos-pone-0011979:
Oliver Jung and co-workers found in 2010 that blocking an enzyme in the kidney made a sign of kidney harm worse, not better. The enzyme breaks down a set of fatty signals called EETs, which are rich in the kidney and help keep blood pressure low and swelling down. The hope was that blocking the enzyme would guard the kidney by keeping those good signals high.

In mice with kidney disease that grows worse with time, the block led instead to more protein leaking into the urine, a core sign that the kidney's filter is failing. A hope that flips in a real disease test is a stern warning for drug work on this path. It shows why fine test-tube results still need proof in living disease before they reach patients.
plos-pone-0012079:
Cielo Pasay and co-workers tested in 2010 plant-based drugs against the mite behind scabies, the itch that burrows into skin and spreads in crowded homes. Care today rests on a cream called permethrin, with a pill added for the worst, crust-covered cases. Word had come that the mites were starting to shrug off the standard drugs.

The drugs tested rest on eugenol, the sharp oil that gives cloves their bite. In the lab they killed the mites outright. A fresh line of mite killers is not a small thing. The shelf for scabies is short. Each drug lost to resistance leaves sick people, most of them poor, with few ways out. A drug kin drawn from a spice plant also starts with a head start, since its safety in people is partly known.
plos-pone-0012179:
Jörg Fellenberg, Pierre Kunz, Heiner Sähr, and co-authors studied drug resistance in bone cancer cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Osteosarcoma, the most common bone cancer of the young, often returns because its cells learn to resist chemotherapy. An enzyme that builds one of DNA's letter chemicals had been tied to fast cell growth and division, making it a suspect in that resistance.

Cells making extra amounts of this enzyme withstood chemotherapy better, the team found. That makes the enzyme both a warning marker and a possible drug target: block it, and resistant cells might fall back under treatment's reach. For a cancer whose survival rates have stalled for decades, any new lever is worth attention.
plos-pone-0012279:
Ming-Hsi Huang, Su-Chen Lin, Chia-Hsin Hsiao, and co-authors tested a boosted bird flu vaccine recipe in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pandemic vaccine planning prizes two things: stretching each dose further, and protecting against drifted strains. Both can be gained by adding an adjuvant, an ingredient that provokes a stronger immune answer, to an inactivated virus vaccine packed into tiny emulsion droplets.

Their mixture included short DNA pieces known to alarm the immune system. The formulation shaped the mice's immune responses strongly, in ways the team measured in detail. Recipes proven in animals queue up for the human safety testing that a real pandemic would not leave time for.
plos-pone-0012379:
Niruparani Charles, Beena Thomas, Basilea Watson and colleagues surveyed people with chest symptoms in South India for a 2010 PLOS ONE study. India's revised TB program had moved services closer to villages, hoping patients would seek care sooner. Earlier work, before the program, showed most people first went to private clinics and reached free TB care late.

The team asked where symptomatic people went first, how long they waited, and what care they got. Many still started with private providers and faced delays. The results show that placing services nearby is not enough on its own. Programs also need to link private clinics into TB referral, so coughs get tested early and treatment starts fast.
plos-pone-0012479:
Swarnali Acharyya, Sudarshana Sharma, Alfred Cheng and colleagues traced how an inflammation signal shuts down muscle building, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The signal TNF blocks skeletal muscle formation, and NF-kappaB pathways carry much of that block. One target is Notch-1, a receptor needed for young muscle cells to develop properly.

The team showed TNF represses Notch-1 through the silencer Ezh2 and DNA methylation, locks placed on the gene. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, chronic inflammation may thus keep repair switched off. Releasing that lock is a candidate strategy for helping dystrophic muscle rebuild itself.
plos-pone-0012579:
Jim White and Reinhard Grisshammer tested the stability of a brain receptor used in drug research, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The neurotensin receptor NTS1 responds to a peptide involved in pain, temperature, and brain signaling, making it a drug target. Membrane receptors are fragile once removed from the cell, and purification usually needs detergent solution or attachment to a resin.

The team compared the receptor free in detergent with the receptor immobilized on affinity resin, checking which state keeps it intact and functional. Stability data decide whether structure studies and drug screens are even feasible. Their results guide labs working on this receptor and similar stubborn membrane proteins.
plos-pone-0012679:
Dozot, Poncet, Nicolas and co-authors described the sugar-handling system of Brucella melitensis, a bacterium that lives inside host cells. In many bacteria the phosphotransferase system, or PTS, controls how backup sugars are used. Their 2010 study found this bacterium's version is incomplete compared with free-living relatives.

They mapped which parts remain and what jobs those parts still do. A trimmed system fits a life spent inside cells, where food arrives in set forms. Knowing how this pathogen feeds itself may expose weak points for drugs. The paper catalogues the surviving parts gene by gene in detail.
plos-pone-0012879:
Mahdy, Al-Mekhlafi, Al-Mekhlafi and co-authors named the Leishmania species behind skin disease cases in Yemen. Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease with about one and a half million new cases each year worldwide. It is the most common form of leishmaniasis, spread by sandfly bites.

Their 2010 study used molecular methods to identify the exact species in Yemeni patients. Different species respond differently to drugs and carry different risks of worse disease. A national species map gives Yemen's clinics a firmer basis for treatment.  Samples were taken from patients across several regions.
plos-pone-0335879:
Essi Edjodjinam Kpegba-Fiaboe surveyed students at high schools in Togo's capital, Lomé, about risky sexual behaviour. Little local evidence existed for students still in school, a group health programmes often miss. The 2026 study questioned several hundred students aged from mid-teens to early twenties using a structured form.

Nearly half reported sex in the past year. Among them, many reported starting before eighteen, uneven condom use, and overlapping partners. More than a quarter of sexually active students said their first sex was coerced, with girls affected most. Owning a personal mobile phone and coerced first sex came with much higher odds of risky behaviour. The author argues school-based programmes must address coercion and digital life directly.
plos-pone-0336679:
Darren A. Brown and his team checked a form that gauges fits of ill health in women in Britain who have HIV. As drugs let these women age, bouts of poor function come and go. The form asks how harsh each bout is, and in which part of life it bites. Near one hundred women filled it in twice, a week apart.

The form held firm from week to week. Its scores fit most of the team's checks next to known forms. Care in read was best for day tasks and least sharp for mood parts. Four in five women met a mid mark for poor function. The team backs the form for wards, labs, and state plans.
plos-pone-0337679:
Sonya Gordon and colleagues validated an artificial intelligence tool that measures dog heart size on chest X-rays, a routine check whose hand measurements vary between observers. The tool, RadAnalyzer, runs on the web and on phones and reports two standard scores comparing heart dimensions against backbone length. Its readings on more than a thousand dogs of eighty breeds were set against a trained human observer's.

Agreement was strong for both scores, with average differences amounting to almost nothing and scatter well inside what clinicians tolerate. The authors say the tool can safely assist veterinarians measuring good-quality side-view films in dogs of any size. They note the next test is against ultrasound heart measurement, the deeper standard, before the scores can stand in for fuller cardiac workups.
plos-pone-0340179:
Ana Buadze and colleagues examined the attention disorder ADHD in women, a group long under-studied for a condition usually framed around boys. Using a Swiss population study of more than twenty-seven hundred adults. In it they compared women with full, partial, and lasting forms of the disorder. The comparison covered family history, childhood experiences, body markers, and early onset.

Partial and full forms shared heavier childhood adversity and weaker parental bonding. A family pattern and early onset marked the full form, while lasting symptoms leaned instead on immune and metabolic signals such as inflammation markers and insulin. Grouping women by profile revealed a burdened group, shaped by hard childhoods, whose symptoms persisted more than an idiopathic group. The authors stress that women's ADHD is several different stories, not one disorder at different volumes.
plos-pone-0342279:
Dylan Keegan, Linda O'Neill, and Peter Doran set out a plan to build a public survey about greener clinical research, together with patients and the public. Medical research saves lives but also burns carbon through travel, labs, and data handling. Their 2026 protocol describes two workshops where lay partners help shape the survey's topics, wording, and format.

The finished survey will then circulate through research and patient networks online. Answers will show what the public knows and thinks about research's climate footprint. The team will also report how the joint building process itself went. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; its aim is a survey the public helped design.
plos-pone-0344179:
Eshaghi and colleagues surveyed new medical students in Tehran on lifestyle and life satisfaction in a 2026 study. Starting university reshapes eating, movement, sleep, and stress handling all at once. Students completed checked questionnaires covering those habits plus smoking and drinking, alongside a life satisfaction scale.

Scores grouped students into healthy or unhealthy lifestyles and good or poor satisfaction. Testing the link between the two shows whether habits already track well-being in the first university year. Early patterns matter because medical students later counsel patients on the same habits. Universities could use such data to target sleep, food, and activity support during orientation.
plos-pone-0345579:
Yuta Okada and Hiroshi Nishiura chart how COVID-19 changed Japanese lifespans. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. They split shifts in life expectancy from 2020 to 2022 by age and cause of death. They worked at both national and prefecture level. They also tracked how evenly ages at death were spread.

Deaths past age thirty-five did most of the shortening. Heart and lung diseases added large losses beside COVID-19 itself. One pattern puzzled the team. The link between local case counts and lost years, clear earlier, vanished in 2022. Weak case counting may explain the gap. The rise in heart deaths warns of trouble ahead.
plos-pone-0345779:
Yumin Yan built two deep learning models for sorting Chinese news headlines into categories, a harder job than it sounds because headlines are short, sparse, and ambiguous. One model targets big datasets and the other small ones. Both start from a Chinese language model, then fuse features from several of its layers so word meaning and local phrasing reinforce each other.

On two standard headline collections, the large-data model edged past a leading lightweight rival by about a point of accuracy. The small-data model, hardened with multi-scale attention and adversarial training, gained roughly three points when trained on only a tenth of the data. The author concludes that matching the architecture to the data volume, especially adaptive feature fusion, pays off in real news applications.
plos-pone-0346479:
Sumit Das and Md Khorshed Alom propose a smarter way to organize wireless sensor networks, the scattered battery-powered devices used to monitor fields, forests, and infrastructure. Their 2026 paper presents a routing scheme that sorts nodes into zones by energy level, places stronger nodes farther from the base station, and uses a self-organizing map to position them well.

Cluster leaders are chosen by weighing leftover energy, distance, and the network's average energy, so no single node burns out early from relay duty.
