In simulations the scheme kept the network stable and alive far longer than four established rivals and moved more data. Longer-lived networks mean fewer battery swaps in places that are hard to reach.
plos-pone-0346979:
Daphna Oyserman, Yahan Huang, and Amabel Y. Jeon explored a subtle social instinct: people who prize group belonging work harder to find meaning in ambiguous statements from others, a habit that may prevent group friction. Across three experiments with nearly twelve hundred participants, plus pooled analyses, their 2026 paper tested when this meaning-making strengthens or fades.

Collectivist values reliably predicted reading more sense into vague claims, especially when the speaker belonged to the listener's own group. Remembering who spoke also mattered. Election-season data added twists by party. The authors conclude the effect is real but context-dependent, shaped by which group boundary is salient at the moment.
plos-pone-0347479:
Eva Purkey and a mixed team of academics and community researchers describe how they turned research about families facing hardship into a concrete community action plan. Standard studies often end in journals that change nothing locally. Working in Canada, the team first studied families' experiences of adversity and resilience, then consulted more than two hundred fifty residents across eleven community meetings.

Residents generated over two hundred action ideas, which the team organised into twenty themes and shared back through graphics, websites, and policy briefs. Funders and officials picked the results up in later applications and documents. The authors present the process as a working model for research that ends in action.
plos-pone-0348079:
Sara Vilar-Lluch and Dawn Knight analysed five years of British news coverage of diabetes, tracking how journalists write about its two main types. Using corpus linguistics on mainstream reporting from 2020 to 2024, they checked whether stories promote stigma, blur the two diseases, or follow official language guidelines meant to protect patients.

Coverage leaned on medical framing and personal free will while almost never mentioning the social conditions, poverty, environment, unequal access, that shape diabetes. Recommended respectful language is spreading, but dispreferred wording is fading more slowly. Reports often say diabetes without specifying the type and mention it beside unrelated conditions, inviting false inferences. The authors suggest practical fixes for newsrooms.
plos-pone-0348279:
Ali Shirzad and his team set three cures for a tired mind head to head. Each of the twenty-six grown-ups in the trial tried all three in turn. One cure was twenty minutes of mid-pace bike work. One was a dose of caffeine by body weight. One was a sham pill of corn starch. Then all did a half-hour task built to tire the mind.

The task did tire them, by word and by score. But no cure beat the sham pill. Caffeine did not help in a way the team could trust. Bike work did not help either, at this dose. The team asks for fresh trials with new dose and pace.
plos-pone-0348579:
Kyra F Mendes de Leon and colleagues tested whether people living with HIV can check their virus levels with a blood sample taken at home, sparing clinic trips. Sixty-two patients used a small arm device to collect blood themselves and post it in, and the team compared those readings with standard clinic tests, alongside stored samples with low virus levels.

About three in five participants returned a sample, and many returns held too little blood to analyse, a practical snag the authors flag clearly. Where samples worked, home readings matched clinic results well overall. Still, a few low samples read as near zero while clinic tests found measurable virus, a gap that matters for care decisions. The team calls the approach promising but not yet reliable enough to replace clinic testing.
plos-pone-0348679:
Kindu Yinges Wondie and a large team asked whether pregnancy care in Lesotho delivers real substance, not just visits. Many women there attend antenatal clinics, yet what happens inside those visits varies. Using a national survey from twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four covering more than eleven hundred recent mothers. From it they built a quality score using visit timing, visit count, skilled attendance, and ten specific services a mother should receive.

Only about two in five women reached the highest quality band, while more than a quarter landed in the lowest. Married women, better educated women, women who wanted the pregnancy, and those using the internet weekly all received fuller care, as did women in smaller households and better educated communities. The authors urge Lesotho to close the gap between showing up and being properly served.
plos-pone-0348779:
Ahmet Tugay Kuzu and Nuri Celik address a statistical puzzle: when many individuals' measurements wander over time, how do you recover the moving boundary they cross at moments that matter? Think of patients crossing a risk level or countries crossing a cancer rate. Their method treats each crossing as a first passage, pairs it with the level reached, and smooths those pairs into a boundary curve shaped by flexible segments.

Simulations showed the estimator rebuilt a variety of smooth boundary shapes accurately, improving as more crossings were observed. As a demonstration, the team applied it to colon cancer rates by country, drawing stable boundary curves for men and women while handling the blind spot at the start of observation. The framework suits any field where the first crossing, not the average, triggers action.
plos-pone-0348879:
Alexander Blagojevic and co-authors tested a laser surface treatment for nerve stimulation electrode arrays in 2026. Smaller, more efficient electrodes would let implants stimulate precisely while using less power, but adding new steps to device making is costly.

The treatment textures the metal surface at many scales, greatly expanding its active area. Applied to ready made commercial paddle arrays as a stand alone step after manufacture, it kept the arrays compatible with existing production. Performance gains reported for the treated contacts support the approach. A bolt-on upgrade path matters: factories resist processes that force full redesigns.
plos-pone-0348979:
Qian He and Xu Huang study a blood enzyme that drops sharply in sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection. Sepsis often ends with the immune system shutting down, and doctors lack a simple daily gauge of that slide. Their 2026 study joins patient records, public gene data, and a mouse sepsis model to test the enzyme as a marker.

Patients with lower enzyme levels carried worse severity scores and fewer key defender cells. Gene analysis singled out one hub gene whose levels fell across many sepsis datasets and tracked immune cell counts. Mouse spleens confirmed the gene's drop alongside the enzyme's. The pair could give intensive care teams a cheaper window on immune collapse.
plos-pone-0349379:
Shufeng Chen and colleagues isolated a bacterium from mud in an estuary and found it unusually good at stripping nitrogen from water. Too much nitrogen, washed from farms and cities, chokes lakes and coasts. The strain, a member of Enterobacter cloacae, feeds on all three common nitrogen forms and can carry out two cleanup steps at once that usually need separate conditions.

In lab tests the strain removed nearly all of each nitrogen form offered, and its top cleanup rate beat many comparable bacteria reported before. Genes for each step of the process were found in its DNA, confirming the ability is built in. It also kept working across a wide range of conditions. The authors nominate it for treating polluted water where nitrogen runs high.
plos-pone-0349579:
Michael Lebenstein-Gumovski and colleagues report an animal test of a glue like gel meant to help a fully cut spinal cord heal. No proven care restores function after a complete cut. Five pigs had the chest level cord cut through, with spine fixation and sixty days of rehab. Three pigs got the gel in the gap, while two did not.

Control pigs stayed with loss of movement, feeling, and bladder control below the cut. Gel treated pigs showed returning feeling and better scores on standard scales, plus tracer and tissue signs of regrowth across the gap. Numbers are tiny and pigs are not people, so claims must stay cautious, yet any recovery after a full cut draws close attention.
plos-pone-0349679:
Francesco Pichi and colleagues used eye scans to look for signs of multiple sclerosis activity in the retina, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. The retina is part of the central nervous system and can be imaged without touching the brain. They counted immune-like cells at the retina's front surface and measured the thickness of the nerve cell layer.

Patients with multiple sclerosis and healthy controls were compared on these eye measures, standard disability scores, hand tests, walking tests, and brain scan lesion counts. If retinal cell activity and thinning track disability and lesion burden, eye scans could become a quick, painless way to follow the disease between brain scans. The study tests that link directly.
plos-pone-0349879:
Jialong Tian and colleagues designed a control method for groups of machines, such as robots or drones. The groups must split into two camps, aligned with or against a leader's motion, with a set time delay. Groups like these cannot measure everything directly, and constant communication wastes energy, so their scheme pairs a fast observer with a trigger that only sends updates when needed.

The observer reconstructs the leader's state within a time the designer chooses in advance, not just eventually. Mathematical analysis shows the whole group reaches the split agreement within that set time, and that the trigger never fires endlessly in a Zeno loop. A simulation example backs the theory. Guaranteed timing matters for swarms that must coordinate on a deadline.
plos-pone-0350279:
Olaposi Joseph Olatoregun, Catherine Orrell, and co-authors adapted an HIV medication reminder app for young people in Benue State, Nigeria, working with the users themselves. Teenagers and young adults on HIV treatment often struggle to take doses on time, and the original app was built for South Africa. Their 2026 project let twenty-two young people in Makurdi test the app for a month, then gathered their views in discussion groups.

Testers loved the games, quizzes, and badges, which kept them opening the app and supported dose-taking. Needing mobile data was a real obstacle for some. Their top demands were offline access to key features, simpler navigation, and personal medication reminders. The team ranked wishes with a must-have to won't-have method, and they present the process as a model for fitting health apps to local realities.
plos-pone-0351079:
A fast-growing tumor of the brainstem is the deadliest brain cancer of childhood, and it cannot be removed by surgery. Madisen S Mason and colleagues describe a better way to grow this tumor in mouse embryos, in a 2026 PLOS One methods paper, so that new treatments can be tested.

Genes known to drive the human disease are delivered into the developing mouse brainstem with short electric pulses through three electrodes. One combined gene package replaces several separate ones, and the aim is sharpened on the cells that line a fluid space and later form the pons. The mice grow large, spreading tumors that resemble the childhood disease closely.
plos-pone-0351679:
Burn wounds grow stubborn bacterial films, and the drug-resistant staph germ MRSA is a frequent culprit. Wen Lin and colleagues packaged an antimicrobial peptide into tiny fat bubbles that also carry a light-sensitive dye, in this 2026 PLOS One lab study aimed at infected burns.

Shining red light on the bubbles released the peptide in a controlled way and boosted killing power. The amount needed to stop MRSA fell fourfold compared with the free peptide, and bacteria died faster. The bubbles also blocked new films from forming. Tests were done in dishes, not patients, so the team frames the system as a promising step toward light-activated wound dressings.
plos-pone-0351879:
Mariano Marques and colleagues investigated a worrying cluster of injection-site abscesses in Timorese infants after the hepatitis B birth dose in twenty twenty-four. Twelve affected infants were matched with twelve controls by clinic, date, age, and sex, and investigators interviewed caregivers and inspected facilities, records, vaccine handling, and the cold chain for differences.

No examined factor differed significantly between the groups, and with so few cases the estimates swung wildly, as the authors state plainly. They frame the work as descriptive and hypothesis-generating, not a verdict on any clinic or vaccine batch. Their recommendations are the safe ground: keep strengthening injection technique, multi-dose vial handling, and cold chain discipline, and keep watching. The study is a model of reporting an alarming signal without inventing a culprit the data cannot support.
plos-pone-0352179:
Hinselmann and colleagues studied mothers' waist size just before birth in old Swiss hospital records in a 2026 paper. The records cover more than four thousand single births in Lausanne from the final years of the First World War into the early twenties. Birth weight, length, and early survival were recorded alongside the mother's measurements.

Mothers were grouped by waist size, from slim to very large, and outcomes compared across groups. The team adjusted for the mother's age, past births, and home circumstances. Historical records like these show how body shape and newborn health linked before modern nutrition and medicine changed both. They also remind readers that some questions can only be answered with century-old data.
plos-pone-0352279:
Letsoalo and colleagues surveyed rabies knowledge in parts of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, in a 2026 study. More than seven hundred adults answered a checked questionnaire on causes, attitudes, and what they would do after a bite. Only about one in four could name what causes rabies.

Just over half said they would follow the full course of post-bite care, which starts with wound washing and vaccine doses. Most respondents still showed gaps that could delay life-saving care, since rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start. A baseline like this lets health campaigns target the exact misunderstandings that cost lives.
plos-pone-0352579:
Buttler-Stöbich and colleagues set out a long-term study plan in 2026 on children living in state residential care within Lower Austria. Little Austrian research asks how state care shapes children's growth and well-being. The plan follows children, parents, and care staff over time with several methods.

Five questions guide the work, from why placements happen to how daily life in homes actually runs. Findings will feed practice and policy for a deeply intrusive state intervention. Multi-sided evidence, hearing children as well as professionals, is the design's strength. The study could show which features of residential care help children thrive and which quietly harm them.
plos-pone-0352679:
Sirisak Sathorn, Garnpimol Ritthidej, and Wanatchaporn Arunmanee revisit, in 2026, a cheap method for purifying antibodies from blood plasma using fatty acids. Polyclonal antibodies are still needed to neutralise toxins and viruses, yet removing contaminating proteins without expensive equipment remains a challenge for producers.

The team compared fatty acids of different chain lengths and their salt forms. Plain acids separated proteins more selectively than salts. Shorter chains worked better than longer ones. One mid-length acid removed albumin well. It kept more of the desired antibody than the standard treatment. The purified antibody also kept its shape and binding strength. Tests on horse plasma confirmed the approach works on real production material.
plos-pone-0352779:
Pía Rojas-Cárdenas, Gabriela Nazar, and Juan Luis Castillo-Navarrete set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol. It plans a term-long study of study stress in Chilean university students. Students in one medical faculty will be measured three times across a term. The study mixes surveys, diet records, and saliva tests. Wearable devices will track sleep and heart rate.

As a protocol, the paper presents aims and methods, not results. The team expects heavier study stress to track with worse eating habits. They also expect poorer diet quality and more low mood as the term unfolds. Stress hormones measured after waking are expected to shift too. The authors aim to give campus health services proof for early support. That support would be timed to the school calendar.
plos-pone-0352879:
Vamsi Parimi and three colleagues refine how sharpness of vision is measured in this 2026 study. Standard eye charts suffer from glare, crowding, and optical distortions in the eye itself. The team instead used a Maxwellian view system with a tiny three-millimetre pupil. It projects a single letter E into a small field. The setup cancels most wavefront distortions and holds brightness steady. Thirty healthy controls and seventeen patients with eye disease were tested.

Even under cleaned-up optics, eyesight in controls tracked with their natural astigmatism. Higher-order distortions also grew with age among controls. Patients showed different patterns, reflecting their retinal and surface problems. Macular thickness from scans was compared against the optical measures. The message is methodological humility. Some influences on measured acuity survive even the best instrument design, and they differ between healthy and diseased eyes. Better measurement starts with knowing which errors remain.
plos-pone-0353179:
Itismita Mohanty and co-authors present in 2026 a practical method for valuing projects on mental health. The projects serve veterans and emergency workers across countries. Such workers face higher rates of mental illness and suicide, and funders need fair ways to compare very different projects. Standard economic methods handle mixed, real world grant programmes poorly, so the team built a flexible pooling approach.

Applied to one programme, each unit of money invested returned slightly more than its value in health gains, counting both cash and in kind costs. Single projects varied. The method, they argue, gives funders a workable return figure without forcing unlike projects into one rigid mould.
plos-pone-0353379:
Haitian Sun leads a 2026 PLOS ONE engineering study on a soil-dividing device for pineapple planting machines. Pineapple is a major tropical fruit, and strip-tillage furrowers dig its planting trenches. Existing machines let too much loose soil fall back in and leave trenches misshapen.

The team designed a V-shaped divider, modeled its forces in design software, and simulated soil movement grain by grain. Strength checks passed. Field trials varied four settings, including blade speed and forward speed, to minimize soil falling back. The best mix, with a thirty-degree V angle and set spacing and speeds, gave a backfill rate the authors judged satisfactory. The design supports wider mechanization of pineapple growing.
plos-pone-0353479:
Begley and colleagues surveyed health workers across Europe in 2026 about prescribing for brain diseases that worsen over time. The survey covered eight countries and asked when doctors would try a new or unusual drug for patients with early or advanced illness. It also asked what beliefs and pressures shape those choices.

Workers were more willing to move away from their usual drug for patients with advanced illness than for those newly diagnosed. Answers pointed to knowledge, confidence, and support at work as key drivers of the choice. Knowing those drivers can help design training that leads to safer, braver prescribing when standard drugs fall short.
plos-pone-0353679:
Al-Hajj and colleagues, in a 2026 study, price child injuries in Lebanon using five years of closed insurance claims, from 2012 to 2016. The Middle East carries a heavy share of the world's child injury burden, yet cost data from the region are rare. Claims came from the four largest administrators, covering over half the insured market.

About seventy thousand children were treated for about eighty-seven thousand injuries, at a total direct medical cost near nineteen and a half million dollars. Boys made up almost two thirds of the injured. Most children were treated in emergency rooms and released, yet the minority admitted to hospital consumed over half the money. Everyday minor wounds were most common, but broken arms and legs, only a small share of injuries, drove more than a quarter of costs. The authors urge prevention programs and standard treatment paths.
plos-pone-0353879:
Jacek Świdwa, Magdalena Król-Zielińska, and Adam Kantanista ask what makes a handball referee call a game correctly, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Forty-one officials from three league levels took standard temperament and personality inventories, then judged game situations on video against expert answers. Playing level did most of the explanatory work, accounting for about a quarter of the accuracy differences.

One temperament trait helped: sensory sensitivity, a sharpness toward small stimuli, correlated with better decisions and added explanatory power beyond league level. Another trait, activity, mattered differently at different levels. The classic five personality traits showed no link at all. Referee development, the authors suggest, should train perception, not screen personalities.
plos-pone-0354079:
Gokhan Tut and co-authors followed older care home residents through a fifth COVID-19 vaccine dose in the United Kingdom. Earlier waves of the pandemic hit such homes hard, so protection there matters greatly. Their 2026 study measured antibody and cell responses to a bivalent booster and tracked infections for six months.

The booster raised spike-specific immunity to a plateau that stayed broadly steady for over three months. Even so, about three in ten residents caught the virus again during follow-up, and others were infected for the first time. Strong blood immunity, the authors conclude, does not reliably stop reinfection in frail older people. They urge extra protective steps for care homes beyond repeat vaccination.
plos-pone-0354179:
Taisei Mogi, Mari Saito, and Yoshihiro Nakata ask whether a robot that swells and shrinks feels more alive, in this 2026 study. Their robot, MOFU, is a fluffy mobile unit whose whole body expands and contracts through a clever folding geometry driven by a single motor. It grows and settles between two heights as it rolls on two wheels. Living things constantly change volume, through breathing and posture, yet robots almost never do.

In an online survey, viewers watched videos of MOFU in different motion combinations and rated its lifelikeness on a standard questionnaire. Both the swelling motion and simple rotation independently raised animacy ratings, and combining motions with travel helped further. Showing two robots together, contrary to the team's guess, added nothing. The authors suggest that adding volume change is a cheap, powerful design lever for therapy and companion robots.
plos-pone-0354379:
Aisha Mumtaz, Sundus Ali, and Muhammad Aslam model in 2026 how users link to next generation mobile networks helped by smart reflective panels that can run on harvested radio energy alone. Millimetre wave signals carry huge data but are easily blocked in dense cities, and panels can bounce them around obstacles, at an energy cost. Their maths framework counts only panels that both see the user and can sustain themselves.

Denser panel placement raised the chance of a sustainable clear link and cut outages in blocked areas. In very dense settings a trade off appeared between energy use and coverage. A learning based comparison checked that the model fits dense urban use.
plos-pone-0354479:
Pradip Thapa and four colleagues published this 2026 study of common bean landraces collected across twenty-one districts of Nepal. Grown in trials during 2023 and 2024, fifty-eight local varieties were scored on dozens of visible and measured traits, and a smaller set of DNA markers probed their genetic variety.

The beans split into five broad groups, and several named varieties stood out for early flowering, maturity, and yield. DNA results showed modest but real diversity across the collection. Thapa recommends testing the best performers in more places and widening the gene scan to guide bean breeding.
plos-pone-0354679:
Sirikorn Vongseenin and colleagues study in 2026 how low serotonin, a key brain chemical, may make rats prone to migraine. They recorded electrical behaviour in nerve cells from a cluster that carries pain signals from the head. Both small to medium and large cells were tested with fine electrode methods after serotonin was depleted.

Depleted cells became easier to excite, and size based differences between cell groups grew, which may sharpen pain signalling. The authors suggest low serotonin could also upset the balance among its own receptor types, though that step was not tested directly. Understanding the shift may point to treatments that calm the overactive pathway.
plos-pone-0354879:
Liselot Ribbert and colleagues set out in 2026 a Dutch national trial on how long a catheter should stay in men who suddenly cannot pass urine, often due to an enlarged prostate. Practice varies widely because firm evidence on timing is thin. The trial compares trying without the catheter after a few days against waiting about two weeks.

Success means passing enough urine with little left behind. Later checks cover return of the blockage, catheter problems, symptoms, quality of life, and costs over many months. Interviews with staff will explore why practice varies. Results should help write clearer guidance and make care more even across hospitals.
plos-pone-0355179:
Daniel Patryk Karcz and three colleagues benchmark quantum-safe cryptography on a small, cheap microcontroller, in this 2026 study. Future quantum computers threaten today's encryption, and new standardized algorithms must eventually run even on tiny embedded chips in sensors and controllers. The team ran all standardized parameter sets of three algorithms, two based on lattices and one on hashing, on an ESP32-C6 chip, measuring speed, key sizes, and memory use.

Everything ran successfully without external memory. The key-exchange algorithm behaved predictably, with time growing in step with the security level. The lattice signature scheme was costly to generate keys and sign with, though verification stayed quick. The hash-based signature scheme was by far the slowest, reflecting its design. The authors conclude quantum-safe security is deployable on modern microcontrollers, provided designers budget honestly for the latency trade-offs.
plos-pone-0355279:
Juanjuan Li and co-authors designed a cloud encryption scheme that lets owners share files and cut off users instantly. Proxy re-encryption lets a middleman convert a file's lock from one user to another without seeing its contents. Older designs rely on maths that quantum computers may break and handle revocation clumsily. Their 2026 scheme builds on lattice problems instead.

Owners can revoke a user directly, with no central office reissuing keys each time. A subtree method keeps revocation efficient as groups grow. Separate keys for converting and for reading guard against the proxy colluding with revoked users. Li and colleagues argue the design suits modern sharing, where access changes daily and long-term quantum safety matters.
plos-pone-0355379:
Grzegorz Adamczyk and co-authors survey Polish believers on how the COVID pandemic shaped their religious attitudes, using a theory of how mind and religion interact. The core idea is that crisis pushes people to make sense of suffering, a stance known as theodicy, and that this meaning-making reshapes religious life. A large, representative sample of adults who called themselves believers answered four attitude scales.

Pandemic experience emerged as the dominant factor behind religious behavior in the models, outweighing background traits such as age or place, which faded under crisis conditions. Adamczyk and colleagues read this as evidence that the emergency rewired how believers communicated faith itself. Their study offers a rare large-sample test of systems theory on religion under stress.
plos-pone-0355479:
Francesca Chelazzi and Dan Lawrence test when cities began obeying the mathematical regularities seen in modern urban systems, using house sizes from ancient Southwest Asia, in this 2026 study. Their dataset covers more than eighteen hundred buildings at eighty sites, spanning from the Late Epipalaeolithic to the Iron Age. House size stands in for household productivity, letting them track how output scaled with settlement size over some twelve thousand years.

Scaling was absent in the Neolithic and murky in the Chalcolithic; it emerged clearly only in the Bronze Age, exactly when urban complexity took hold, and persisted afterward. Average house size more than doubled across the span regardless. Inequality, meanwhile, tracked settlement size only in politically complex systems and mainly at major centers, suggesting institutions, not crowding, decided who shared in urban gains.
plos-pone-0355679:
Juliana Toboyee and co-authors asked what persuades Ghana's smallholder farmers, in the dry semi-arid north, to adopt climate-smart practices. Such practices aim to raise harvests, cope with a changing climate, and cut emissions at once. Their 2026 survey covered several hundred farmers across eleven communities in the Upper West Region.

Belief that the practices raise yields was the strongest single driver of adoption. Lower input costs also helped. Access to extension advice and to training each raised the odds greatly. Formal schooling raised adoption too, while farmers in the younger middle-age band adopted less. Toboyee and colleagues advise pairing training and extension support with clear proof of yield gains.
plos-pone-0356079:
David Nickle introduces a new statistical measure for comparing genetic diversity between groups in this 2026 paper. Existing summaries either use only allele frequencies or only the shape of the evolutionary tree, ignoring the distances along it. His statistic, a likelihood ratio, weighs both. It asks how probable the observed sequences are under a model where two groups share one diversity level, versus models where they differ. It uses full tree structure and branch lengths.

Nickle demonstrates the approach on two real problems. Applied to coronavirus sequences from different periods, it suggested viral diversity may be waning over time. Applied to leukemia samples ordered through treatment, it found no significant drop in the cancer's genetic diversity. He notes uses from vaccine responses to tumor evolution, anywhere the question is not how diverse a sample is, but whether diversity truly changed.
plos-pone-0356179:
Nuala Ryan, Elaine Berkery, and Patryk Makowski study the working lives of nurses who trained abroad and moved to Ireland, in this 2026 paper. Rich countries increasingly fill nursing shortages with internationally educated nurses, but keeping them is another matter. The authors spoke with just over twenty such nurses in focus groups and viewed their experience through the layers of a whole national ecosystem.

At the national level, housing pressure, childcare access, and visa rules made settling hard. During recruitment, many met a reality gap: roles differed from what was promised, and systems and language caused early uncertainty. Within workplaces, leadership quality shaped daily life for better or worse. The authors argue that governments and hospitals must act together across all these layers, because a nurse's decision to stay is rarely about the job alone.
plos-pone-0356279:
Amy Van Elswyk and three colleagues examine a shortened version of a classic coping questionnaire in this 2026 psychometric study. The full inventory sorts people's responses to stress into three styles, tackling the problem, reacting emotionally, or avoiding it, but it is long. The short form packs twenty-one items into the same three scales. A large community sample of adults completed it three times, about a year apart, letting the team test both structure and stability.

The three-factor structure fitted the data acceptably and held up across gender and age groups. Internal consistency was acceptable, and scores a year or two later correlated moderately, as expected for a fairly stable personal trait. Links with personality and with depression and anxiety symptoms matched earlier research on the full instrument. The authors conclude the short form is a valid, reliable brief measure for research and practice.
plos-pone-0356479:
Obed Chanda evaluates Zambia's long-running farm block program through the ears of the community hosting one block in Kawambwa district. Since the early two thousands the program has leased large rural tracts for commercial farming, promising food security and growth, while host villages' own views stayed undocumented. Local submissions were read qualitatively, and a large household dataset from several thousand respondents was modeled for what shapes income.

Residents voiced quiet unease: fear of displacement, scarce jobs, environmental damage, and cultural loss. Nearly every household earned below the official minimum wage. Schooling, household size, cultivated area, and secure land tenure lifted income, as did nearby health facilities and water access. Chanda urges the program to put community needs at the center and to back them with schools, clinics, machines, and secure tenure.
plos-pone-0356579:
Readers should know first that the entry here is a formal retraction notice from the editors of PLOS One, issued in 2026. It withdraws an earlier study that had claimed a plant compound called quercetin could boost antibiotics against hard-to-treat Pseudomonas bacteria. The original findings should no longer be trusted or cited as valid results.

Editors explain that several figure panels looked alike or partly overlapped even though they were said to show different test conditions. When the authors shared their raw image files, reviewers found still more problems, and the stated statistics did not explain how many comparisons were handled. One author agreed with the withdrawal, while others did not reply or could not be reached.
plos-pone-0356679:
Celeste Dea, Paula Arias, Sol Moroni, Nicolás Rolandelli, and Arlinet Kierbel published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies macrophages, immune cells that swallow threats in a process called phagocytosis. The authors watch these cells handle two targets at once: pathogenic bacteria and apoptotic material, the remains of dying cells.

The key finding idea sits in the title: the cells discriminate and sort, treating dangerous bacteria differently from harmless debris during dual-target feeding. How a macrophage juggles both jobs affects infection control and tissue cleanup. Immunologists studying inflammation and healing are the readers for this look at cellular decision making.
plos-pone-0356779:
Marie Ithurbide and colleagues challenge dairy goats with a bacterial trigger of inflammation. The goats were bred for long or short productive lives. The question is whether the longevity lines answer immune alarms differently. The two lines were created by generations of selection on functional lifespan. First-time mothers from both lines received a dose of the bacterial fragment in a vein. Blood was sampled many times across the following week. A panel of immune signals was tracked, plus a lab test of whole blood response.

Starting levels matched between lines. After the challenge, short-lived-line goats mounted a stronger early inflammatory surge in two key signals, while long-lived-line goats showed more of a later, resolving signal. The lab blood test echoed the in-body result only moderately. Ithurbide and colleagues suggest calmer early responses may be part of what long life is made of.
plos-pone-0356879:
Ugo Okoli and a wide team describe a quality program in Nigeria that tried to catch dangerous blood pressure problems in pregnancy sooner. High blood pressure in pregnancy is a leading cause of death for mothers and babies in Nigeria. From the late twenty tens into the early twenty twenties, the program worked in dozens of public and private facilities across two Nigerian states.

Checks at program sites exposed weak skills and uneven habits among care staff at the start. Training and support then pushed routine checks for blood pressure, anemia, and diabetes sharply upward during pregnancy visits, with gains also after birth and at family planning visits. Okoli and colleagues present the model as one other high-burden settings could copy.
plos-pone-0357179:
Hyobeen Kim and seven colleagues asked a deceptively simple question about glaucoma care: does the way you label worsening vision change how well a computer model can spot it? Their 2026 multicenter study drew visual field tests from five large hospitals in South Korea and trained four machine learning models under two labeling rules, one loose and one strict.

Under the loose rule, where any of five standard tests flagging decline counted as progression, the models separated worsening from stable fields almost perfectly. Under the strict rule, accuracy and sensitivity dropped noticeably. No single test drove the loose rule's success; each added something. The lesson for clinics building alert systems is that the definition of progression matters as much as the algorithm chosen.
plos-pone-0357279:
Mengting Qian, Chunshun Yan, and Xinyi Wang study job satisfaction among lower secondary teachers in Shanghai in a 2026 survey paper. They use a large international teaching survey and ask how warm relations between teachers and students across a whole school relate to how teachers feel about their jobs. Their lens is a theory that treats daily emotional events at work as drivers of attitude.

Teachers who saw stronger school-wide relations reported higher satisfaction, and joy in teaching carried part of that link. A principal's warm leadership style did not change the direct link, though it seemed to strengthen the joy pathway in a result the authors call exploratory. Qian and colleagues limit their claims to Shanghai and suggest longer studies to test cause and effect.
plos-pone-0357779:
Wei Jiang and coauthors published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE on traffic signals that can clear an ambulance through a junction without blocking everyone else. Standard controllers lean on hand-built traffic features and stumble on new emergency patterns. Their framework teaches intersection agents with meta-reinforcement learning, so policies adapt from few examples, and compresses traffic into compact states using contrastive predictive coding. Agents share information weighted by distance and delay, with a priority layer scaling responses to severity.

In simulation, the system cut emergency response time sharply while keeping regular vehicles' waits contained, and high-priority runs succeeded at very high rates. Removing the predictive coding module hurt performance most, marking it as the load-bearing piece. Analysis credited the full design with a large share of the response-time gain. It is presented as a controller that learns fast enough for emergencies it has never seen.
plos-pone-0357979:
Amin Danial Asham published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It offers a new approach to path tracking for a differential drive robot, the common two-wheeled design that steers by spinning its wheels at different speeds. The robot must follow an arbitrary set of waypoints, and the control method is sliding mode control.

Sliding mode control is known for staying accurate even when conditions are rough or the model is imperfect. Extending it to any waypoint set makes one controller serve many routes. Robotics engineers building warehouse and inspection robots are the readers for a tracking method meant to be both general and tough.
plos-pone-0358079:
Junhua Zhang and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about water networks in Henan Province, China. Complex pipe networks can fail in chains, where one breakdown triggers others, a pattern called cascading failure. The authors study the source nodes, the points where water enters the network, and how risk travels in both directions.

Their aim is better management of those source points so a local fault is less likely to spread through the whole system. Mapping how failures and risks move between connected nodes helps planners decide where protection matters most. Water utilities facing aging pipes and rising demand are the audience for this kind of network analysis.
plos-pone-0358179:
Mohammad Al-magableh led a team of eight authors asking Jordanian students how they treat colds, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When students catch a cold or flu, some reach for herbal remedies and others for pharmacy drugs. The team surveyed students at Jordanian universities about the choices they make.

Al-magableh's patterns reveal where herbal remedies still rule campus life and where pharmacy drugs have won. Pharmacists and campus clinics can use that map to advise safely, especially where herbs and drugs might interact. Student habits also hint at wider public behavior, since students carry them into family life. The study respects both paths while insisting that real data on choices, not guesses, should guide health teaching.
plos-pone-0358479:
Jie Zhang leads a team of six pooling the evidence on re-warming up after halftime, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Team sport players cool down during breaks, and coaches increasingly send them through a short second warm up before play resumes. Evidence on whether it works was scattered across small studies. The reviewers searched six databases and fitted multilevel models to twenty qualifying trials.

The pooled verdict favors moving. Countermovement jump, sprinting, and agility all improved over resting. Squat jump, repeated sprint ability, and maximal strength did not. Athletes also reported notably higher exertion, the price of the benefit. Details mattered: how players left the ground and which leg dominated shaped the jump effect, and the break's format shaped sprinting. The authors give practitioners a menu rather than a mandate: re-warm for explosive actions, expect effort, tune the format.
plos-pone-0358579: Elsadig and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in applied mathematics on sound in a channel. They computed how sound waves scatter over time inside a rectangular guide that mixes a membrane with a porous wall. Such guides appear in noise control and building design. Working out the sound field over time helps engineers shape ducts that hush noise without blocking flow.
plos-pone-0358779:
Razan Zatarah and four colleagues review ten years of blood infections in children treated for acute leukemia, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Chemotherapy and the disease itself strip away immune defenses, so germs reaching the bloodstream are a constant danger. The team wanted to know which bacteria cause these infections and which antibiotics still work, and whether the picture changes from infancy through the teenage years.

They gathered just over three hundred infection episodes from one hundred sixty patients treated between 2015 and 2024, nearly all with the lymphoblastic form of the disease. Each episode was sorted by age group, treatment phase, and the germ's drug sensitivity results. A decade scale map like this helps oncologists choose first antibiotics wisely while cultures are pending, and shows where resistance is eroding the usual choices.
plos-pone-0358879:
Jiahui Ding and three colleagues link two blood measures to thyroid nodules in a Chinese health check population, in PLOS ONE in 2026. From over twelve thousand screened adults, fifty-two hundred with data were analyzed. The predictors were a combined insulin resistance score and uric acid, the gout chemical. The outcome was thyroid nodules, graded by a Chinese ultrasound risk system. Blood pressure was tested as a middleman.

Both measures climbed with nodule odds in a gradient. Adults in the highest quarter of either measure had roughly four times the odds of nodules in the lowest quarter, after full adjustment. The relationships bent rather than running straight, and differed across nodule risk grades. Blood pressure carried part of the association, in patterns that depended on the outcome. The study adds thyroid checks to the list of reasons to treat metabolic dysfunction early. Its design is a one time snapshot.
plos-pone-0358979:
Julia Gresky and Lee Clare report the first intact burials found at Göbeklitepe, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The early Neolithic site in southeastern Türkiye is famous for its monumental stone buildings. It also holds a puzzle: fragments of human bone scattered through the buildings' fill. They come from men, women, and children. Two undisturbed burials from the later pre pottery phase, roughly 8,700 to 8,000 BCE, now offer a clue.

The burials' condition suggests how the fragments arrived. Soil sliding down the mound appears to have carried remains from originally intact graves on higher ground into the lower buildings, breaking them up on the way. That process explains much of the scatter without excluding other mortuary rites. The authors stress the variety of burial practice in Neolithic Anatolia, and the two graves give researchers a rare undisturbed reference point at the site.
plos-pone-0359779: Zorrilla González and Travisano published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a yeast used in labs and food work. Some yeast cells share food with the group, while others cheat and take without giving. The study's title states its finding: crowding limits how long sharers and cheaters can live side by side, through touch-based effects that depend on how common each type is. The work speaks to basic questions about how cooperation survives.
plos-pone-0360379:
Felix Laukhardt and colleagues ran a randomized crossover trial in 2026 on warm-ups designed to protect team sport athletes from injury. The warm-ups combine physical movement with mental tasks, a motor-cognitive approach meant to prepare players for the split second decisions of real play. The trial measured their immediate effect on jump landing performance when the jump was unplanned.

Each athlete tried the different warm-up conditions, so the researchers could compare landings within the same bodies. How an athlete lands after an unplanned jump is closely tied to knee injury risk, especially for the anterior cruciate ligament. If a warm-up sharpens landing control at once, coaches gain a practical tool that fits inside training they already run.
pmc-13142779:
Jacob A Lewis is first author on a 2026 chemistry study of peptide amphiphiles, molecules that self-assemble into filaments in water and can act on cells. Such assemblies usually need charged parts to dissolve, but charge can cause cell toxicity and makes structures sensitive to acidity and salt. The team made a nonionic, or uncharged, version.

The uncharged molecules formed long filaments that stayed stable across acidity and salt conditions. Mixing them with charged partners tuned surface charge density, and the mixes were more internally ordered than either kind alone. In a bone-forming cell model, mixes and uncharged assemblies acted more strongly than fully charged ones. Charge tuning may help design safer bioactive nanomaterials.
pmc-13198479:
Matti Viluksela and colleagues tracked metals in osprey eggs across Finland over three decades in a 2026 study. Ospreys are fish-eating hawks at the top of the food chain, so their eggs mirror water pollution. Ringers gathered unhatched eggs from 1972 to 2005 in sea and lake regions.

Lead fell fastest, at about seven percent a year. Chromium and two mercury forms also fell steadily. Levels did not differ much by region, pointing to long-range air drift as the main source. Only a small share of eggs topped harm thresholds for mercury or lead. Osprey numbers in Finland recovered over the same span. Stored egg collections prove valuable for long pollution records.
pmc-13199179:
Mohammad Al-Wardat and colleagues surveyed rehab specialists on remote therapy in Jordan in a 2026 study. Telerehabilitation delivers therapy by phone or video, which could widen access in lower-income settings. Success hinges on what frontline specialists know and accept, so the team asked three hundred of them.

The group held equal shares of physical, occupational, and speech therapists. Most knew of remote therapy, and over half said their workplace used it. Yet only about one in seven used it regularly. Three quarters saw time and cost savings. Top barriers were low public awareness, poor internet, provider reluctance, thin staff training, and privacy worries. Few judged it equal to in-person care.
pmc-13199579:
Yasmin Hefni Abdel Aziz and colleagues tested bending strength of eco-concrete slabs in a 2026 lab study. Geopolymer concrete swaps standard cement for alkali-treated ash waste, cutting carbon output. Hollow-core versions save weight and material, but their bending behavior was little studied, so the team loaded slabs to failure.

Seven slabs were tested: two solid and five hollow with varied void sizes and span layouts. The solid eco slab slightly beat the standard cement slab in bending, with good bonding. Bigger voids cut cracking load, peak strength, and stiffness. Shorter shear spans raised capacity and stiffness, while longer spans bent more. Classic bending theory matched the tests well, backing wider low-carbon use.
pmc-13199779:
Shaun Khanna and colleagues pooled studies on belly fat and heart artery calcium in a 2026 review. Coronary calcium marks hidden artery clogging. Body mass index, a height-weight ratio, may miss central fat, so the team tested whether waist measures track calcium better in people without known heart disease.

Forty-nine studies across ten countries qualified. For calcium presence, waist-to-hip ratio showed the strongest link, then waist size; body mass index showed no clear link. For calcium growth over about five years, waist size again beat body mass index. High blood pressure weakened the links somewhat. The authors back waist measures over body mass index alone for heart risk checks.
pmc-13200279:
Fuad Rzayev and colleagues tested iron oxide nanoparticles against a goose gut worm in a 2026 lab study. Worm infections cut poultry meat quality, and new dewormers are in demand. Iron oxide particles are stable and seen as fairly safe, so the team exposed the nematode Heterakis dispar in dishes.

Particles measured about eight to eighteen nanometers across. They entered the worm through its skin and gut and spread to all body wall layers, gut walls, and reproductive organs. Higher doses destroyed the worms faster than controls. Fine structure checks showed grave damage to the outer coat, muscle layer, nerve parts, and gut. The authors conclude the particles hold deworming promise, pending live-bird tests.
pmc-13201279:
Genetic clues to a dangerous birth defect of the gut are the focus of a 2026 study headed by Karin Salehi Karlslätt and colleagues. The research article examines children whose intestines failed to rotate normally before birth, leaving them at risk of a life-threatening twist called midgut volvulus.

The team sequenced the genomes of ten young children who had malrotation without other malformations and searched a panel of 442 relevant genes. One boy carried two inherited variants in TTC7A, and two other boys carried variants in ROCK2 and LIMK2. Because these genes share one signaling pathway, the findings point to new targets for genetic testing.
pmc-13201379:
Mental health concerns in pregnancy often go unasked about, and a 2026 study by Shreya Agarwal builds a screening form for Indian antenatal care. The research article describes the development and expert validation of a short proforma that obstetric teams can use during routine checkups.

The authors combined a literature review with in-depth interviews of nine pregnant women at a private Indian hospital. Interviews highlighted informed choice, the experience of pregnancy, and social support as central themes for the form. Six perinatal experts then validated the items, and after two wording revisions the final tool held eight domains with twenty questions.
pmc-13202679:
Vitamin D may tune the molecular signals muscles release during training, and a 2026 narrative review by Do-Houn Kim proposes a framework for that idea. Writing alone, Kim synthesizes evidence on exercise-responsive signaling molecules called exerkines and how vitamin D status might modify them in athletes.

Across animal and human studies, vitamin D signaling connects most consistently to signals such as IL-6, irisin, myostatin, and the anti-inflammatory IL-10. Exercise itself may raise vitamin D receptor levels in muscle, making the relationship run in both directions. Kim labels the model the vitamin D-exerkine axis, while cautioning that firm causal evidence in athletes is still limited.
pmc-13202979:
When depression will not lift, should care aim at quality of life instead of cure, and a 2026 qualitative study led by Astrid Gieselmann asks patients themselves. The research article asks how people with chronic, treatment-resistant depression understand and judge the concept of palliative psychiatry.

Semi-structured talks with nineteen adults from special Berlin wards, many treated before, were sorted by theme. Those interviewed welcomed relief from pressure to achieve remission and from repeated treatment failure. They also feared stigma from the word palliative, being dropped too soon, and loss of hope, and they asked for ongoing support in less formal settings.
pmc-13203979:
A whisper of precious metal on copper cubes can reroute a carbon dioxide reaction, and a 2026 study headed by Hirokazu Kobayashi demonstrates that control. The research article coats copper nanocubes with atomically mixed platinum-group metal shells and tests them as electrocatalysts for converting carbon dioxide.

Alloying the surface with iridium switched the main product from ethylene to formic acid in the reported experiments. The iridium version also outperformed a tin catalyst known for formic acid production, in both activity and durability during testing. Just as important, the alloy shell preserved the cubic shape while pure copper crumbled into grains, linking surface design to catalyst lifetime.
pmc-13204579:
When blood cancer returns after a donor transplant, its chromosomes may have changed, and a 2026 study led by Emin Abdullayev examines that evolution. The research article investigates new cytogenetic abnormalities at relapse in patients with myeloid hematological neoplasms treated with allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

Nearly half the patients developed cytogenetic changes by the time of relapse in the studied cohort. Those changes appeared more often in patients whose diagnostic samples already showed complex abnormalities, pointing to an unstable genome as the driver. Earlier chemotherapy, conditioning, and donor type showed no such link, and although early treatment response was lower, long-term survival was not significantly affected.
pmc-13206279:
A bacterial preparation painted on the cervix may clear stubborn HPV infections, and a 2026 retrospective study headed by Hongyan Liu builds a tool to predict who benefits. The article reviews 180 patients treated with topical Nocardia rubra cell wall skeleton for persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection at one center.

By twelve months, the authors report roughly four in five patients had cleared the virus on DNA testing. Age, the HPV subtype involved, and how faithfully patients followed treatment each independently predicted success in their analysis. They combined those factors into a nomogram with good discrimination and calibration, while noting that larger multicenter studies must confirm it.
pmc-13226579:
Jiang and colleagues trace how gut microbes pass from mother to baby in the first months of life. The team used structural variations, large changes in microbe genomes, as fine markers of exact strains. Data came from a long study of 98 mother and baby pairs, plus a second group of 25 pairs sampled at several body sites.

They profiled which marked strains appeared in both mother and child, and how delivery mode, feeding, and the mother's body sites shaped that sharing. Strain-level proof matters because species names alone cannot show true transfer. The work sharpens the picture of how a baby's gut is seeded, and by whom.
pmc-13238779:
Doueiri, Ratnapreya, and Frankenberger present a gentler way to fix front teeth marked by weak enamel. Molar incisor hypomineralization leaves enamel soft and discoloured, and it can strike the visible front teeth as well as molars. Their patient, a girl of fourteen, had cloudy patches on her upper central incisors, exactly where a smile shows them.

Standard fixes range from resin sealing to sanding the surface or building it up with composite. The team's approach removes the damaged enamel selectively, keeping sound tissue. For teenagers, appearance is not vanity but confidence. A case showing strong cosmetic results with less drilling gives dentists a kinder option to offer.
pmc-13240979:
Xie's team at Peking spoke with China's data managers about taking up the CDISC submission standards. Thirty-eight leaders from 38 groups spoke between April and August 2022. China's regulator has pushed the global standard since 2020. Talks probed knowledge, views, daily practice, and obstacles.

Nearly all experts called the CDISC requirement key, and most had filed compliant submissions. Cost, scarce trained staff, weak local fit, and sheer complexity topped the barrier list. Proposed fixes include cheaper tooling, more training, and folding Chinese medicine terms into the standard. Clearer guidance was another common request.
pmc-13241479:
Tsuchiya and colleagues at Chiba University hunted for missing links in how cells dispose of stray proteins outside their borders. Clusterin was the only known carrier ferrying misfolded proteins to lysosomes. Screening plasma factors that bind an amyloid-forming blood protein surfaced a second candidate. The enzyme GPLD1 emerged from the search.

GPLD1 binds the amyloid protein directly and escorts it to lysosomal destruction. Its famous cutting activity against membrane anchors proved unnecessary for the job. Cell-surface heparan sulfate serves as the docking receptor instead. Tsuchiya presents GPLD1 as a scavenger carrier with tastes distinct from clusterin's.
pmc-13242979:
Laura Benestan and co-authors asked whether male and female European spiny lobsters wander differently, using genetics across six Mediterranean marine reserves. Their study appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. Dispersal shapes how a vulnerable, heavily fished species should be protected, yet it had never been tested between the sexes in a marine invertebrate like this. The team genotyped 180 lobsters at thousands of markers and compared population structure by sex.

Both sexes mixed freely across the study area, with no strong genetic structure overall. Females showed a slight tendency toward more structure, but the difference was not significant. The hunt produced a bonus: seventy-two markers cleanly separated the sexes, letting the team sex sixty-one lobsters of unknown sex. Those markers give the first evidence that this species uses a ZZ/ZW sex determination system. They also hand managers a tool for fisheries where rules differ by sex.
pmc-13243179:
Utshob Sutradhar and co-authors built a phone app that prescreens skin disease from photos in real time. Their feasibility study appeared in Health Science Reports in 2026. Skin disease is common where dermatologists are scarce, so a light on-device model could flag who needs care first. Their Android app, SkinLearn, runs a trimmed YOLO11 network directly on the phone with no internet needed, trained on a public seven-class set of skin images.

On its home dataset the model named the right disease almost every time. On a second, different skin cancer dataset its accuracy fell sharply, though it still beat the older model used for comparison. That drop exposes how much image sets differ in lighting, skin tones, and class mix. The authors claim technical feasibility for real-time, offline prescreening on cheap hardware. They insist on more validation before any clinical use.
pmc-13243779:
Janine Murr and colleagues found a drug target in the most stubborn form of pancreatic cancer by blocking a master regulatory enzyme. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. The mesenchymal subtype of pancreatic cancer shrugs off chemotherapy, so the team hunted its specific weaknesses with genetic screens. The screens fingered PPP2CA, the catalytic heart of protein phosphatase 2A, and the inhibitor LB100 indeed hit those cells selectively.

Treating those cells rewired their metabolism and triggered stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, tipping them toward death. Genome-wide screens mapped which genes tune sensitivity to the drug, pointing at gene reading, RNA processing, and protein building. A surprise mechanism surfaced: the drug speeds up gene transcription, especially of short genes, through the kinase CDK9. Phosphatase and kinase appear to hold each other in check. The authors propose exploiting this activation paradox, and PP2A-based drug combinations, against this subtype.
pmc-13244079:
Zuzana Kubincová and colleagues turned routine moth counts from Czech reserves into a test of what shapes moth communities. Their study appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. They gathered lists from 292 reserves covering 941 moth species, accepting that methods and effort varied by site. The question was whether consistent ecological patterns would still show through the uneven data.

They did. Reserves spanning more elevations, and those holding steppe and moist grassland, carried the most species. Height reshaped the whole mix: lowland reserves favored larger moths with several broods a year that feed on herbs, while mountain reserves favored shrub and tree feeders with fewer broods. Regional history mattered too, with Carpathian-Pannonian reserves hosting big-winged specialists. The authors argue that messy real-world data, read carefully, can guide conservation as well as polished surveys.
pmc-13245079:
Nina Karia and colleagues tested how well standard ultrasound measures spot the mildest form of pulmonary hypertension under its new definition. Their study appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. Since 2022 the threshold sits lower, at artery pressures just above twenty, catching a mild group earlier rules missed. Using a British database of nearly two thousand patients, the team graded three echo metrics.

The metrics (jet velocity, estimated artery pressure, and their ratio against heart contraction) separated clear disease well, scoring around eight-tenths accuracy for pressures above the old and new cut-offs. For the mild band specifically, accuracy sagged noticeably. Yet mild disease was far from harmless: within it, a fast jet or a weak contraction-to-pressure ratio flagged patients who died sooner. Echo finds clear disease but under-reads the mild zone, exactly where early risk now hides. Mild, in their data, is worth catching properly.
pmc-13245279:
El-Shalakany, Samir, and Mubarak built a hybrid membrane that cleans several pollutants from water at once, in this 2026 RSC Advances study. Their material layers coconut-shell activated carbon and chitosan, a natural polymer, with graphene oxide nanosheets, forming a sheet riddled with pores at several size scales. Such hierarchy helps dissolved contaminants reach binding sites quickly.

Spectroscopy and microscopy confirmed the three ingredients bonded into a semi-crystalline, porous network with very fine surface pores. The membrane was designed to adsorb both ciprofloxacin, a widely used antibiotic that pollutes waterways, and hazardous heavy metals simultaneously, a harder task than single-pollutant filters. The authors present the hybrid as a multifunctional platform for treating complex polluted water, where medicines and metals arrive mixed together.
pmc-13246779:
Li, Liu, Wan, and co-authors present an artificial intelligence framework for designing crystals in this 2026 Nature Communications paper. Predicting which crystal structures a material can adopt, and how those forms behave, usually takes separate tools. Their system, PolymorphGen-MLPKD, organizes the search around landscapes combining entropy and symmetry to generate candidate structures and model their properties together.

The framework reproduced phase behavior across crystal families, generated partly disordered structures, and traced the pathway between graphite and diamond. Its distilled simulation potentials ran about a million times faster than the calculations they learned from, while staying accurate enough to compare how metals deform by twinning or dislocations, and to resolve stress-driven phase changes in brittle iridium. The authors also report scaling laws for training such models efficiently.
pmc-13247679:
Constantin and co-authors report an urgent inpatient case in this 2026 Case Reports in Psychiatry article. A man in his twenties with bipolar disorder, ADHD, anxiety, and an intellectual developmental disorder was hospitalized with severe intrusive sexual thoughts causing distress and safety concerns. His presentation straddled two diagnoses: obsessive-compulsive style sexual obsessions he found alien, and gratification-driven urges resembling an early compulsive sexual behavior syndrome that formal criteria, requiring six months of symptoms, could not yet confirm.

Standard medication adjustments failed to contain the risk. After doctors started naltrexone, a drug that blunts reward and is used against addictions, his improvement was marked within five days and the intrusive thoughts had resolved by hospital day sixteen. Because other medicines changed too, the authors cannot credit naltrexone alone, but they argue the speed justifies studying reward-targeted treatment for such ambiguous emergencies.
pmc-13248779: The Journal of Healthcare Engineering retracted this 2022 meta-analysis in 2026, and this notice is the formal record of that withdrawal. The paper had pooled studies on two anesthesia depth monitors, Narcotrend and the bispectral index, asking which better predicted thinking problems after tumor surgery in elderly patients. The retraction was agreed between the journal's editor, David Hewson, and the publisher, John Wiley and Sons. Readers should not rely on the paper's pooled conclusions, and the notice links to the original article so its record stays traceable.
pmc-13248979:
Skonieczna and a Polish team repackaged a classic chemotherapy drug, in a 2026 nanomedicine study. They tucked 5-fluorouracil inside cholesterol-modified cyclodextrin, a ring-shaped carrier, at three drug ratios. The goal was stronger killing of colorectal cancer cells with less harm elsewhere, a standing problem for this old but harsh drug.

The richest mixture, three drug parts per carrier part, proved most potent. It cut cancer cell metabolism and survival by more than sixty percent and switched on both major cell-suicide pathways. Healthy fibroblasts and heart muscle cells suffered only moderate effects. The authors nominate that ratio for further development toward colorectal cancer therapy.
pmc-13249179:
Rezende reviewed two immune messengers as outlook markers in liver cancer, in a 2026 narrative review. Hepatocellular carcinoma usually grows in a scarred, cirrhotic liver, where chronic inflammation feeds the tumor. Searching literature from 2010 to 2025, the author weighed studies of interleukin-6, which drives inflammation, and interleukin-10, which calms it, in patients' blood.

Raised interleukin-6 consistently accompanied bigger tumor burden and poorer survival after both drug and local therapies. Interleukin-10 also ran high in many patients, but its meaning shifted with disease stage and tumor surroundings. The author calls for standard test methods and shared cut-off values before either marker guides everyday decisions.
pmc-13249679:
Dey systematically reviewed a DNA repair enzyme's role in autoimmune rheumatic disease, in a 2026 paper. The enzyme, PARP1, also helps regulate transcription and immune responses, and hints linked it to lupus and related conditions. Searching two databases, the author sifted more than thirty-five hundred records and kept forty-one studies covering patients and animal models.

Blocking or removing PARP1 often calmed inflammation and tissue damage in experiments. Yet in lupus and systemic sclerosis, patients showed reduced PARP1 activity and weaker DNA repair, a more complicated picture. Genetic findings were mixed, while antibody and activity measures showed diagnostic promise, especially in lupus. The author calls PARP1 a plausible future target needing sharper human evidence.
pmc-13249879:
Elrashedy and colleagues designed a universal foot-and-mouth vaccine on the computer, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. The livestock virus mutates fast and comes in many types, while current vaccines are whole killed virus with weak cross-protection and safety baggage. Focusing on the types common in Egypt, the team stitched conserved pieces of five viral proteins into artificial chimeric proteins.

Modeling rated their second construct as stable and strongly visible to the immune system, rich in sites that killer T cells, helper T cells, and antibodies can recognize. Simulated docking showed the vaccine designs gripping cattle immune sensors firmly over long virtual runs. The authors call for laboratory expression and animal trials to test the blueprint.
pmc-13250179:
Wang and colleagues report a gentle endoscopic treatment for children with repeated belly pain and hardened deposits in the appendix. Their 2026 World Journal of Pediatric Surgery paper reviews cases treated between 2021 and 2023. Each child had ultrasound evidence of appendiceal fecaliths, small stone-like masses, plus swollen gut lymph nodes nearby.

Doctors washed out the appendix through an endoscope guided by ultrasound, a method called retrograde appendiceal irrigation. The procedure succeeded in all seventy-three children, and pain stopped almost at once in nearly every child followed afterward. Minor bleeding or discomfort affected a small share of patients, with no perforations or major harm. Pain returned in about one fifth over the following months, while lymph node swelling dropped sharply.
pmc-13250879:
Wang and Zhang argue that henipaviruses sit on a threshold, dangerous yet not quite able to sustain spread. Their 2026 Emerging Microbes and Infections commentary covers a virus family known for repeated spillovers from animals, severe disease, and limited person-to-person transmission. Nipah and Hendra are its best-known members.

Growing viral diversity and widening contact between wildlife, livestock, and people keep producing episodic outbreaks. The authors say outbreak counting alone misleads preparedness for such irregular, high-consequence pathogens. They urge combined human, animal, and environment surveillance under a One Health approach. They also want adaptive trial designs and ready-to-test countermeasures, so vaccines and drugs can be judged quickly when the next spillover comes.
pmc-13253779:
L Mansilla Alvarez and co-authors present a 2026 method for tailoring blood flow models to one patient. One-dimensional models can predict flow and pressure in arteries, but patient data are often scarce while model settings are many. The team used a simplified map of the body's artery network and a search method called CMA-ES.

First, a global check ranked which settings shape the model's output most. Then the search method tuned those settings to match a small set of flow and pressure measures. Results showed accurate patient-specific models are feasible even with little data, and the authors map how each setting affects wave shapes and health markers.
pmc-13253979:
Abdolrasoul Safaeeian, Roghayyeh Armand, and Hossein Matlabi survey older adults in Miandoab, Iran, in a 2026 study. They asked 450 older people about their use of traditional medicine and why they choose it. Data came from a structured questionnaire, with participants picked by cluster sampling.

A large majority, 81.6 percent, reported using traditional remedies. Mint, cinnamon, and ginger were the most used herbs, and many would see a bonesetter for fractures. Word of mouth from older generations was the top influence, at 51.4 percent, followed by low cost and fewer felt side effects. Women and less-schooled adults leaned most to these treatments.
pmc-13262279:
Julian Heidecke and co-authors grade a climate model of West Nile virus against thirteen years of European case records. Laboratory-derived thermal curves promise to predict when mosquitoes spread the virus best. Their 2026 study checks that promise against monthly reports of severe human disease from twenty ten onward.

The model's reproduction number nailed the seasonal rhythm and the temperatures where risk peaks. It ranked risky places and months slightly better than temperature alone. But year-to-year outbreak swings and the virus's patchy map escaped it. Finer temperature data helped only at the hot end. Biology alone, they conclude, cannot carry forecasting.
pmc-13262779:
Georgios Petridis and colleagues test whether home device data can flag mental health risk in older cancer survivors in a 2026 journal article. Survivors face higher rates of depression and anxiety, but clinic checks are infrequent and rely on memory. The team used tracker, scale, and smart plug data collected over 12 weeks in daily life.

The study followed 41 survivors with a mean age of 72.3 years, and used a four-question survey to define risk. Machine learning models sorted risk best when smart plug and smart scale data were combined, with strong standard scores. TV use patterns from the smart plug alone also performed fairly, beating tracker-only models. The authors call passive home monitoring a low-burden option needing larger checks.
pmc-13262979:
Jean Zeuikena and co-authors isolate new plant compounds from a traditional medicine tree in a 2026 journal article. The tree, Zanha golungensis, is used as herbal medicine for various ailments. The team extracted flavonoids, a family of plant chemicals, and worked out their structures with mass and magnetic resonance methods. Two of the compounds were new to science.

Alongside three known compounds, the new ones blocked two inflammation enzymes, COX-1 and COX-2, strongly in lab tests at a set dose. The most active compound beat the standard comparison compound on both enzymes. Computer calculations of electron patterns and docking into the COX-2 site supported stable binding. The authors suggest the compounds as leads for anti-inflammatory drug design.
pmc-13264279:
Marutpong Panya and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on sugars from two farmed mushrooms, Lentinus polychrous and Lentinus squarrosulus. Mushroom sugars can act as prebiotics, foods that feed gut germs. The team tested whether crude extracts change the mix of bacteria from human stool in a lab model.

After fake digestion in the lab, much of both extracts stayed intact, which suggests they could reach the colon. In the test jars, the extracts raised helpful groups such as Bacteroides and Parabacteroides. They also lowered pH and two ratios used to sum up gut balance. One group, Fusobacterium, rose too, and the authors say its role needs more study before claims are made.
pmc-13264579:
Damla Atay and Ozlem Ozmen wrote a 2026 study of budgerigars, small pet parrots, struck by a fungal gut disease. The fungus mainly attacks the proventriculus, a part of the bird stomach. Little was known about local immune signals in birds that catch the disease in the wild, so the team examined stored tissues.

They studied gut tissues from 25 infected birds and 5 healthy controls. Damage centered on the proventriculus, with surface erosion, ulcers, worn cells, and clusters of immune cells near many fungal growths. A signal protein called TNF-alpha showed up in surface and immune cells in the damaged areas. Healthy tissues showed little or none. The authors say this gives a baseline for later work on immune pathways in this disease.
pmc-13264879:
Jennifer M Gurney wrote a 2026 review on using whole blood to revive trauma patients who are bleeding heavily. Bleeding is the top cause of death from injuries that could be survived, in both war and civilian care. Modern blood banks split blood into parts for storage ease, yet whole blood matches the body's needs more closely, she argues.

The review sums up military and civilian proof for whole blood, including fresh blood gathered from walking donors at the scene and stored low-titer group O blood used in civilian centers. It traces how practice swung from whole blood to parts and back. Gurney backs a layered approach and more prehospital use. She notes no direct trials yet compare fresh and stored whole blood, and that fresher blood strains blood bank logistics.
pmc-13264979:
Yue Ma and colleagues published a 2026 study sorting Chinese children with ADHD into subgroups to guide tailored nursing care. ADHD varies widely between children, so one-size care fits poorly. The team grouped 403 newly diagnosed, untreated children by behavior, emotion, and social function, then checked the groups with an objective attention test.

Three types emerged. A functionally balanced type made up 25.8 percent, an impulsivity-led type 55.6 percent, and an emotion and cognition dysregulation type 18.6 percent. On the attention test, the impulsivity-led group made the most errors of acting too soon. The dysregulation group showed the most variable response times. The authors say pairing parent-rated grouping with test proof gives a base for precision nursing paths.
pmc-13267979: Juan Antonio Álvaro de la Parra and colleagues' study of Holter reading software in three Spanish hospitals is the subject of a 2026 correction. The 2025 paper reported wide benefits from the software. The correction changes no results. It restores two university affiliations that were left out: one doctoral school affiliation for the first author, and one doctoral program affiliation for Cristina Caramés, both at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid. The affiliations are now added and the rest renumbered.
pmc-13268079:
H A Z Boktor and colleagues present a 2026 letter describing drug-resistant TB in a refugee family with an inherited immune weakness. The family lived in a Syrian refugee camp in Jordan. The letter's first case is a girl born in 2015 who developed a swollen lymph node in her armpit months after the BCG vaccine, a TB shot given to newborns.
