Her node illness returned again and again over the years despite several treatment courses. Tests later found rifampicin-resistant TB germs in a node sample, and the node was removed. By age seven she had fluid in her belly, swollen inner nodes, and a blocked portal vein, and she began a modern drug-resistant TB regimen. The letter links her course to a genetic susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, social vulnerability, and limited program capacity in emergency settings.
pmc-13269179:
Keevan Singh and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a young woman found, just before gynecologic surgery, to have cold urticaria. In this rare condition, cold triggers hives and can even close the airway. Operating rooms hold many cold triggers, from fluids to skin cleaners.

Her history showed repeated cold-linked symptoms, including one past episode that hinted at airway trouble. A cold test later confirmed the diagnosis. The team limited cold contact and gave allergy and steroid drugs before surgery. Cold cleaner on her belly still raised local hives during the operation, but she stayed stable and recovered well. The authors stress asking patients about cold symptoms.
pmc-13269479:
Dhruba Pariyar Damay and Angela Peace published a mathematics paper in 2026 modeling plant disease together with soil nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus. Plants need these nutrients to grow, and disease can change how nutrients cycle back. Their model links plant growth, infection, and nutrient supply in a forest setting.

The five-part model lets infection spread faster or slower depending on nutrient levels. Analysis and computer runs showed that nutrient-rich conditions lowered the bar for disease to persist. Enrichment also brought on repeating boom-and-bust cycles sooner, with larger swings. Higher spread rates likewise lowered the nutrient level needed for persistence. The authors say ignoring nutrient feedback gives a misleading picture of outbreak risk.
pmc-13269979:
Saudah Dibaji and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on critical care nurses at King Fahad Hospital in Jazan, Saudi Arabia, and how emotional intelligence relates to patient safety. Emotional intelligence means reading and managing feelings at work. A survey of 132 nurses was run in August and September 2024.

Average emotional intelligence was high, at 3.91 on a five-point scale, and safety practice scores averaged 3.73. The two measures moved together strongly, with a correlation of 0.68. Links held across the background variables tested. The authors conclude that emotionally intelligent nurses deliver safer care in high-stress units. They present emotional skills as a real determinant of safety, not a soft extra.
pmc-13271879:
Makoto Tokunaga is lead author of a 2026 journal article on predicting stroke patients' independence at discharge. Independence is measured by the motor part of the Functional Independence Measure. That is a standard score of how much help a person needs with daily movement tasks. The question was whether updating the prediction one month into rehabilitation sharpens it.

The study included 849 stroke patients in a recovery rehabilitation ward. Four statistical models were compared: predicting the discharge score directly or via predicted improvement, each with or without first-month progress data. Average prediction error fell from 9.3 points for the basic direct model to 6.3 for the updated improvement model. Predicting improvement and converting it back beat direct prediction, and updating at one month helped both routes.
pmc-13272679:
Yixin Chen and Helmut Grubmuller present a 2026 model of F1-ATPase, the spinning enzyme part that makes ATP, the cell's main energy carrier. Their aim was the smallest model that still matches how the enzyme links chemistry, binding, and rotation, and stays consistent with energy rules. They tested many variants to find it.

After checking over 14,000 model variants, they found that four distinct shapes of one subunit are needed for a working model. The model settles a long debate by showing two reaction paths can both occur, depending on ATP levels. It also suggests a ratchet-like motion that can explain rotations larger than the usual step.
pmc-13272779:
Mohammod Hafizur Rahman leads a 2026 study of biochar made from the plant Lantana camara for removing a black dye, Acid Black 172, from wastewater. Dye waste from textile work is toxic and resists natural breakdown. The team described the biochar's surface and pores, then tested dye uptake under varied acidity, time, dose, and heat.

Removal was best at pH 3 and reached balance within 90 minutes, with a top capacity of 303.03 milligrams per gram. The process was spontaneous and took in heat, following a pattern tied to chemical binding. After five reuse cycles the biochar still removed over 91 percent of dye, supporting its use as a low-cost, reusable cleaner.
pmc-13272879:
Sudip Phuyal leads a 2026 review of dynamic consent for reuse of health data under European law. Dynamic consent lets people adjust, in detail and over time, how their data may be reused, including taking consent back. Static or broad consent fits poorly in complex digital systems, the authors argue.

European privacy law supports specific and revocable consent, but national differences and weak cross-border withdrawal tools are barriers. A new European health data space law, phasing in from 2029, shifts many uses toward approval by access bodies. The authors propose a three-stage system for consent administration, decisions, and enforcement, while warning about cost, consent fatigue, and digital divides.
pmc-13273179:
Ziying Wang leads a 2026 study of a stretchable skin electrode inspired by kirigami, the art of paper cutting, for recording heart signals during daily life. Electrodes must stick closely to skin while a person moves and sweats, or signals become noisy. The device layers a cut copper electrode between adhesive and protective films.

The design is soft, fills a high area, keeps stable contact while moving, and sticks reliably, the authors report. It collected electrocardiogram signals in real time during daily activities, with strong resistance to sweat and motion artifacts. They position it for dynamic human-machine interfaces, where stable skin contact during exercise has limited earlier static designs.
pmc-13273879:
Berginström and colleagues examine brain links tied to pain and fatigue in chronic pain patients. Their 2026 journal article uses resting state fMRI scans. Participants also performed a twenty-minute attention task designed to tire them.

The study included 24 women with chronic pain. It also included 22 healthy controls of similar age. Patients reported more fatigue and pain than controls. Before the task, the groups differed in several brain networks. The default mode network showed the clearest gaps. After the task, most group gaps could no longer be seen. Only links between the basal ganglia and frontal areas remained distinct. Pain-linked gaps showed up mainly before the task. Fatigue-linked gaps showed up after the task. The authors suggest fatigue can crowd out pain in brain activity.
pmc-13274879:
Hala Sanad and a large team present a 2026 journal article on poor sleep among kidney dialysis patients in Bahrain. Dialysis keeps people with failed kidneys alive but strains daily life, and sleep often suffers. The team surveyed 174 patients at one of the country's main dialysis centers using a standard sleep quality questionnaire.

A striking ninety-one percent of patients scored as poor sleepers. Several factors clustered with worse sleep: older age, poorer self-rated health, anemia, large weight gains between sessions, pain after dialysis, and taking sleep medication. The authors argue the problem is multifactorial and urge clinics to build sleep checks, mental health screening, and support education into routine kidney care.
pmc-13276279:
Soledad Perez Santangelo and Richard Macknight present a 2026 journal article on the genes that tell a legume when to flower. Flowering time decides yield and fit to local seasons. Their plant, Medicago truncatula, is a small forage legume used as a research model for crops like alfalfa and peas.

The plant carries six copies of a flowering gene family called FT. Using gene editing, the team knocked out one or two of the copies. Plants missing one copy flowered normally. Plants missing both were late only under long days, while still responding to a cold spell as usual. Gene activity scans showed the pair switches on other flowering genes under long days. The authors say the two genes back each other up, a finding that may guide forage breeding.
pmc-13276779:
Hind Moukham and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a yeast energy sensor that controls its own location in the cell. The sensor, called SNF1 in yeast and AMPK in animals, orchestrates responses when glucose runs out. It is switched on by partner kinases, chief among them Sak1, which itself carries many marks from the sensor.

Live imaging of single cells showed the sensor rushing into the nucleus right after glucose vanished, then drifting out again. That entry depended on Sak1. In a mutant whose Sak1 cannot receive the sensor's marks, the sensor entered the nucleus more and stayed more active there. Those cells also adapted better to glucose scarcity. A nuclear activity reporter confirmed stronger signaling. The authors conclude the sensor fine-tunes itself by marking its own activator, a feedback loop for metabolic stress.
pmc-13277079:
Robert S Krauss wrote a 2026 profile marking Elizabeth Chen's election to the United States National Academy of Sciences on April 28, 2026. Chen, an editorial board member of the journal Skeletal Muscle, was honored for her work on how cells fuse with each other. Her path ran from Jilin, China, to graduate study in the United States.

Working first on fruit flies, Chen found genes needed for muscle cells to merge and form fibers. Her group helped show that actin, a cell skeleton protein, must gather at fusion sites for merging to occur. She later led labs at Johns Hopkins and then in Texas. The profile traces how a basic question in fly development grew into a broad account of cell fusion.
pmc-13278679:
Jean-Philippe R Krieg leads a 2026 study of muscle loss and disease progression in pancreatic cancer, using CT scans over time. Sarcopenia, loss of muscle mass and strength, predicts worse outcomes in cancer. The team studied 62 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma who had at least three scans over a year, measuring a hip muscle index and extracting image texture features.

Muscle-based sarcopenia affected about forty-five percent of patients by standard cutoffs. The muscle index fell from baseline to three months, then held steady, with women consistently lower. Machine learning models predicted sarcopenia fairly and predicted progression status at twelve months with good accuracy from baseline image features. Muscle and image measures may add prognostic value beyond tumor readings alone.
pmc-13278779:
Mohannad N AbuHaweeleh and Salvatore Rabito present a 2026 case report of a rare benign tumor beside the testicle in a 49-year-old motocross athlete. Such tumors, called paratesticular leiomyomas, grow from smooth muscle near the testicle and are usually slow and painless. He arrived with progressive scrotal enlargement causing discomfort, and exam found a large encapsulated mass pushing the testes aside.

Scans showed a large mixed lesion with new blood vessel growth. Surgeons removed the mass and reshaped the scrotum, sparing the testicle. Tissue tests showed benign spindle cells, a low growth marker, and stains supporting smooth muscle origin. Recognition of this tumor type supports testis-sparing surgery and strong outcomes without long surveillance, the authors say.
pmc-13279279:
Zhonghua Ma and colleagues report a 2026 study of high pressure in the skull in patients who are not obese. The illness, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, means high fluid pressure with no clear cause. Most cases link to obesity, so the lean form is less well known. Records came from one centre for the years 2015 to 2023.

The team compared eighty two non obese patients with ninety six obese patients from two hundred fifty two cases in all. The non obese group was older on average. They showed fewer scan signs of high pressure, yet worse sight loss. The split shows lean patients form a distinct group that needs care in its own right. Risk facts for the lean form still need more work.
pmc-13279379:
Jan Lennart Stalp and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study that pits doctors against chatbots in cervix care choices. Cervical dysplasia means odd cell growth on the cervix that can precede cancer. Board certified colposcopists, doctors who exam the cervix with a scope, made the human group. Two large language models, ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5, made the machine group.

Twenty three real, name free cases with choice questions were judged against a gold standard set by two guide authors. Ten doctors and both models gave like overall match rates, near seventy percent. One model beat doctors on pre cancer cases, while doctors led on hard cases with unclear tissue results. The pilot hints at help, not replacement, in cervix care.
pmc-13280579:
Tarek Zieneldien offers a 2026 poem, Kaleidoscopes in the ICU, set in an intensive care unit. A patient explains that her world has fractured in a chapel window, with colours and faces multiplied like saints. Her chart names the chief complaint as kaleidoscope vision. The poem frames it not as hallucination, but excess truth: too many angles of the same fear. Her spoken history names a deeper complaint, not having enough time to watch her granddaughter grow up.

Verses invoke Hildegard of Bingen and her Scivias, circles of blinding light once read as holy visions. Now brightness means pressure in the skull, the poem notes. Pain arrives as inheritance, in cannonballs of cells that remember how to divide. Scans name metastasis, an insatiable hunger. As she is wheeled deeper in the ICU, sterile snowblind rooms replace the fractured saints. The poem holds vision, faith and cancer in one fractured pane.
pmc-13280779:
Jimenez and colleagues surveyed Helicobacter bacteria in captive baboons and tested a treatment. Their 2026 paper covers 27 olive and hamadryas baboons, animals that can carry stomach and gut bacteria which are harmless in some hosts and harmful in others. Few earlier studies had checked how common these bacteria are in baboons.

Every baboon tested positive by stool DNA testing. The known species Helicobacter macacae appeared in 78 percent of animals, with H. suis and H. pylori in smaller shares. Genome sequencing revealed three entirely new species, which the team named H. papionis, H. simiae, and H. papionifaecis. A ten-day course of two antibiotics plus a stomach-acid blocker cleared the known species but left the new ones in place.
pmc-13280979:
Patricia Capdevila and colleagues published a 2026 report on two patients who grew a fast cancer in a chest hollow. Both had a lung removed more than ten years earlier for lung cancer. The new cancer was a lymphoma, a cancer of white blood cells. It grew in the empty space the lung had left. Neither patient had a weak immune system, and tests for major viruses were negative.

The two tumors still differed under the microscope. One showed no virus traces, and the other did and looked driven by long-term swelling. Both patients had full body scans to stage the disease. Strong drug care put both into full remission, with no sign of active cancer on scans. The authors say the chest hollow may, in rare cases, let such cancers take hold.
pmc-13281879:
Yameng Zheng and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a new mother with a misleading hormone. She was thirty-three and had lately given birth. A lump on her back brought her to care. Scans found masses in her liver, and blood tests showed high levels of a pregnancy hormone. That hormone can also leak from rare tumors. Tissue checks proved a poorly formed bile duct cancer of the liver. It had spread widely, including to the skin of her back.

The tumor itself made the pregnancy hormone, lab stains confirmed. No pregnancy-type tissue was found in it. Such secretion can fool teams into hunting a pregnancy or a germ cell tumor. The authors warn that a raised hormone after birth, with no pregnancy to explain it, needs a tumor hunt. A second blood marker, tied to gut cancers, was also high here. Together they pointed to the source.
pmc-13282179:
Chumin Ye and co-authors report a 2026 study on the wild population of a prized rosewood tree on Hainan Island, China. The tree, Dalbergia odorifera, is valued for fragrant heartwood and faces pressure from illegal logging and habitat disturbance. The team surveyed fifteen sample plots and used tree trunk width to sort trees into age classes. Interviews and standard population tables completed the picture.

Young trees made up more than three quarters of the population, so it looks growing at first glance. Yet old trees were largely missing, and deaths peaked in two age classes. High deaths among young trees and logging losses of mid-aged and old trees form a double bottleneck. Survival followed a steady-loss curve. The authors propose a phased plan: improve habitat for young trees, patrol against logging of older ones, and monitor the population over time to guide protection.
pmc-13282279:
Sajjad Abedini Chamgordani and co-authors present a 2026 study of Campylobacter contamination in broiler chickens in Isfahan Province, Iran. Campylobacter bacteria are a leading cause of food-linked diarrhoea, often passed through undercooked poultry. The team collected two hundred droppings samples from twenty flocks between October 2023 and March 2024. They grew the bacteria in special low-oxygen conditions and confirmed species with gene tests.

Four samples, two percent, carried Campylobacter, split evenly between two species. Every isolate resisted nine common antibiotics, including several first-line drugs, so all counted as multidrug resistant. One species stayed sensitive to one injected antibiotic. The low contamination rate is reassuring, but the total resistance pattern is not. The authors urge stricter rules on antibiotic use in poultry farming. They warn that resistant strains in chicken can reach people through food, narrowing treatment options for human gut illness.
pmc-13282379:
Christina Bronowski and co-authors report a 2026 summary of an international expert meeting on rotavirus immunity, held in Liverpool in March 2024. Rotavirus causes severe diarrhoea in young children. Oral vaccines have cut disease worldwide, yet they work less well in low- and middle-income countries, where burden stays high. Experts gathered to review gut immunity, disease model systems, and lessons from other gut pathogens.

A central gap is the lack of proven correlates of protection, measurable signs that show a vaccine has worked. Without them, improving vaccines is partly guesswork. The report distils the meeting's talks into research priorities. It sets out a roadmap for advancing rotavirus immunology and for developing next-generation vaccines aimed at the settings where current ones underperform. The authors frame better gut-level understanding as the key to closing the effectiveness gap between rich and poor countries.
pmc-13282479:
Juan F Sandoval and co-authors present a 2026 study modelling how fermentation changes the smell of alternative protein foods. Smell decides whether consumers accept such foods. The team fermented surplus bread crusts, boosted with ryegrass protein, using three fungi at a warm temperature for up to seventy-two hours. This solid-state method grows fungi on moist solids rather than in liquid.

Chemical analysis found over one hundred fifty volatile compounds, the airborne molecules behind odour. A model based on a classic perception law predicted the smell profile from compound levels and thresholds. A trained tasting panel's scores checked the model. It tracked overall intensity and sweet, baked, and grassy notes well. Fungal notes such as fruity and earthy were predicted more weakly. The authors say the framework can guide developers to design fermentation that smells appealing, a key step for meat alternatives made from waste streams.
pmc-13282879:
Lemongrass oil, drawn from a strongly scented plant, is the test material in Asmaa M Arafa's 2026 antimicrobial work. New drugs are needed as more germs resist old drugs. The team took oils from distinct plant parts and asked what each oil held and how it acted.

Lab tests checked how well the oils stopped two types of bacteria and one yeast from growing. The team also tested effects on biofilms, which are slime layers that shield germs, and on cell stress. Gene tests in the two bacteria checked genes for biofilm growth and cell talk. Such oils may one day help weak drugs work better.
pmc-13282979:
Yuting Wu and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter on lens power formulas for cataract surgery in keratoconus. The letter responds to a review and network analysis by Aljahdali and colleagues. Keratoconus warps the cornea, so lens choice before surgery is hard to get right.

The writers praise the review method but flag data points that look wrong. One formula name appears misspelled in a key table. Some table values show zero eyes in ranges where zero seems unlikely. Such values may reflect extraction or reporting errors in the source data. The letter asks for checks so surgeons can trust the ranked results.
pmc-13284879:
Qindi Liu, Huanghuang Meng, and Hong Sun test three blood markers as outcome predictors in a 2026 study of severe pneumonia. Records covered 172 patients admitted from September 2023 to September 2025, split by outcome at 28 days into good and poor prognosis groups. Blood levels of NOX4, galectin-13, and cyclophilin A were measured by ELISA.

All three markers, plus standard severity and inflammation scores, were higher in the poor outcome group, the authors report. Each marker linked to worse outcome, and the three together sorted patients with high accuracy in curve tests. Decision analysis suggested useful benefit across a wide risk range. The authors propose joint testing at admission to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13285279:
Tao Lin and co-authors study fluid buildup in the inner ear and vitamin D levels in a 2026 clinical article. Endolymphatic hydrops is most common in Meniere disease, which brings repeat vertigo and shifting hearing loss. Delayed contrast MRI now lets doctors grade fluid buildup in the cochlea, balance organ, and canals.

The authors link vitamin D levels to hearing and balance measures on the healthy side, and link affected-side measures to the grade of fluid buildup in each ear part. Vitamin D may relate to early spells of vertigo and shifting hearing, they suggest. Early checks of vitamin D could matter for Meniere patients who show fluid buildup on scans.
pmc-13285679:
Five years of mud microbes from the far north Mediterranean form a 2026 dataset by Noemi Tomasi and co-authors. Surface seabed mud hosts busy single-cell crowds that drive chemical cycles, and seasonal reads from the Gulf of Trieste span June 2020 to May 2025. Sixteen mud samples from one long-watch station went through gene marker sequencing.

Reads were cleaned with a standard pipeline and named against a major reference bank. The set spotlights sun-eating cyanobacteria kin and ancient archaea groups. Crowds proved steady across seasons, with a high share of kinds found again and again at each rank. Raw files sit in a public archive for teams probing how seabed life rides climate and coast change.
pmc-13286079:
Juliana Sopko and a large team describe many-stream tracking of the 2024-2025 bird flu outbreak in the United States in a 2026 descriptive study. The H5 virus jumped from birds into dairy cattle and then into farm workers, while official data sat scattered across agencies. Their group fused human, animal, wastewater, gene, and policy streams into shared public tools during the event.

The team logged 70 confirmed human cases across 13 states, nearly all tied to farm work with animals. Their map joined those cases with hundreds of cattle and poultry outbreaks, and California stood out as the hub on every count. Wastewater checks in that state had caught the virus signal well before the first cattle case was confirmed there. The open timeline and map, built on a One Health frame, gave responders a single picture of a fast-moving event.
pmc-13286579:
Tamires de Sá Menezes and co-authors audit tooth decay claims on Instagram in a 2026 infodemiology study. Two raters coded 500 Brazilian Portuguese posts from 2018 to 2022 by author type, motive, truthfulness, and theme, then modeled what drives sharing and engagement. Cavities are Brazil's costliest oral disease, so bad advice there carries real weight.

Just over one post in five carried misinformation, mostly treatment claims posted by ordinary users. False posts actually drew a higher median interaction count than accurate ones, even though the link between falsehood and engagement did not reach formal significance. Business and health profiles, encouragingly, showed strong potential to spread sound content widely. False posts clustered on treatment, diet, microbes, and hygiene, while true posts leaned toward prevention, the authors report.
pmc-13287479:
Faraaz Akhtar, Alistair Brownlee, and Cameron Crawford analysed wearable sleep records in 2026 covering 697 people and 185,143 nights across 49 countries. They asked how sleep length responds to season, daylight hours, latitude, and country, using layered statistical models that separate person and country effects.

Longer daylight meant slightly shorter sleep, by roughly 4.4 minutes for each extra hour of light. Once person and country differences were counted, simple season labels added almost nothing. Sensitivity to daylight did not grow clearly with latitude. Country habits mattered more than calendar season. The authors argue that global sleep patterns reflect local culture and individual routines most strongly.
pmc-13287679:
Ynara Maria Gomes de Sousa and co-authors compared two cattle-derived bone filler products in 2026 in rats with a standard 5 millimetre skull defect that cannot heal alone. Fifty-four rats received a plain blood clot, one named commercial filler, or a second filler, all under a dissolving membrane, with checks at three time points.

Both fillers supported new tissue better than clot alone. The second filler produced more mineralised tissue by days fourteen and twenty-eight, with denser structure. Early inflammation and vessel growth looked similar across fillers. The first filler built tissue more slowly, with later fibre organisation. The authors caution that animal results may not carry to dental patients.
pmc-13288679:
Hamideh Ebrahimi and co-authors pool how often Pakistani medical students report depressive symptoms in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They searched major databases plus Pakistani journals through September 2025, keeping observational studies that used validated tools such as the PHQ-9, BDI, or DASS-21, and graded study quality with a standard checklist.

Seventy-one studies giving 72 estimates and roughly 23,000 students produced rates anywhere from nine percent to ninety-four percent, with very high variation between studies. Estimates ran slightly higher in Sindh than elsewhere without firm statistical separation, varied by questionnaire, and crept upward in later publication years. Bias tests suggested some missing negative results, though adjusted pooling told a similar story.
pmc-13288879:

pmc-13295079:

pmc-13318779:
Yazhao Sun and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study of a combined cholesterol and inflammation index. The index joins remnant cholesterol with high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. They test whether it predicts major cardiovascular events after angina patients receive a stent procedure. Follow-up lasted a median of 36 months.

The sample held 2,171 patients, with a mean age of 65.32 years in the cohort. Events occurred in 363 patients, or 16.7 percent of those followed. The highest third of the index carried a hazard ratio of 4.42 against the lowest third after full adjustment. The middle third also ran higher, at 2.87 in the same model. Links held across age, sex, smoking, diabetes, and blood pressure subgroups. The authors propose the index as a risk biomarker.
pmc-13318879:
Konstantin Semash and colleagues give a 2026 case report of recovery after liver transplant in a teenager with Wilson disease. This inherited copper disorder had damaged her brain severely over five years. At fifteen she could not move or speak, with contractures, drooling, swallowing trouble, and liver failure. Many centres would judge transplant too risky.

Her severity score, the UWDRS, stood at 162 on arrival. Transplant was done as a life-saving step. Complications included aspiration pneumonia and a long period of tube feeding. Steady rehabilitation ran from intensive care through outpatient visits. One year later her score had improved to 59 overall. Speech returned, thinking normalised, and she walked with support and returned to school.
pmc-13318979:
Shao Zhengwei leads a large team presenting a 2026 study of auxin signalling genes and watermelon sweetness. Two gene families, ARF and Aux/IAA, steer plant development. Their role in fruit sugar and acid balance was largely unexplored in cucurbit crops. The team combined genomics, metabolite profiling, and gene activity data.

Across eight cucurbit species they found 157 ARF and 275 Aux/IAA genes, mostly under strong stabilising selection. Comparing wild and cultivated watermelons showed sugars rose in stages during domestication. Four candidate genes shifted sharply during the first sugar-building step and stayed fixed later. Spraying auxin raised glucose and fructose by 23 to 35 percent in fruit tests. It also cut malate by 18 percent in the same work.
pmc-13319379:
Xiaorui Peng leads a large team that built a joint sound and light scanner for sore finger joints in a 2026 report. Swollen joints from joint inflammation are hard to score by hand in a fair, repeatable way. Their bedside system uses a robot arm to scan each joint on its own, then smart software marks tissues and counts signs of disease.

Tests covered 43 finger joints from people with joint inflammation, tracked over time. The software matched hand drawn marks well and gave six measures of blood flow, oxygen, and joint size. Blood flow from light based scans tracked most closely with how active patients rated their disease. Grouped measures may help track drug response.
pmc-13319479:
Juan Olvido Perea García leads a team study from 2026 on how eye color shapes where others think a gaze points. Human eyes show a pale ring around the dark center, unlike the dark ring in chimp eyes. One past claim held that the pale ring helps people share gaze, most of all when viewing is hard.

Volunteers judged gaze from a live person wearing lenses that mimicked each eye type, under varied light and distance. Dark ring eyes did best in dim light and at close range, while pale ring eyes did best in bright light from far away. No type won overall. Each eye form may suit the light and range its species uses most.
pmc-13320279:
Zhuhui Tian and co-authors blend a mineral rich germ culture with peanut sprouts to lift yogurt flavor in a 2026 food study. Plain yogurt tastes mostly milky and sour and lacks some health linked compounds buyers now seek. A selenium fed ferment germ plus sprout mix was brewed and set next to sprout only yogurt for taste, texture, and scent checks.

The blend reached high live germ counts, firm set, and strong water hold in the measures reported. Tool noses and tongues scored it richer and fuller with less bitter bite than sprout only batches. Scent scans found fresh grass and fruit notes from the sprouts, while the culture added fruity esters and cut off notes. Deep chemical scans tied the gains to core energy and protein paths.
pmc-13320379:
Débora Pedroza Guedes da Silva and co-authors set out a trial plan in a 2026 protocol on fitness build up before lung cancer surgery. Cutting out part of a lung is the best cure path for early lung cancer, yet lung hassles after surgery are common and stays can stretch long. Short build up plans before surgery have cut those hassles in past trials, but which training type wins is still open.

Two hundred patients set for lung removal will be split by lot into four equal arms of fifty. The arms cover in breath training, out breath training, full body training, and a lone teaching session as control. All arms get one face to face lesson plus a habit leaflet. Checks run at entry, after the two week plan, and a month after going home.
pmc-13323579:
Yuan Fei and co-authors build machine learning models to predict complications of high blood pressure, in a 2026 UK Biobank longitudinal study of 502,166 participants. Protein profiling used the Olink Explore platform, and clinical variables plus outcomes came from electronic health records.

During follow-up, heart, brain and kidney complications developed in 1,232, 166 and 549 participants in their counts. Joint clinical and protein models reached fair to good discrimination, strongest for brain complications. Single proteins stood out for each organ outcome, led by growth differentiation factor 15 for heart events. Interpretation tools explained which inputs drove predictions. The authors present the models as an early warning route for targeted follow-up.
pmc-13324279:
Haitham Salem Baibers and Mohammad Nayef Ayasrah build a scale for teachers' forward-looking readiness to work with AI, in a 2026 study of secondary teachers in Jordan. Items grew from literature and interviews with 22 teachers, then passed expert review and cognitive testing before field use.

An online survey of 640 teachers split into two halves for exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis. Five factors held, covering foresight planning, adaptive instruction control, algorithmic anticipation, human-AI synergy and long-term reflective practice, across 45 items. Reliability and repeat stability rated high in their checks, and validity tests supported the structure. The authors offer the scale as a context-fitted tool for planning teacher development in AI-rich schools.
pmc-13325379:
Priya Pal and co-authors compare raw orange peel powder with two chars made from it for removing crystal violet dye in a 2026 study. Fruit waste could serve water treatment if it binds dye well.

Peel powder hit a top uptake of 49.35 mg per g, far above the muffle furnace char at 19.05 and the nitrogen char at 12.87 mg per g. Rich surface groups on the raw peel explain the lead. The chars traded capacity for wider pH tolerance and steadier behavior. All three followed monolayer binding with chemistry-led speed. Peel uptake released heat and ran on its own at room temperature, while the chars preferred warmth.
pmc-13328279:
Wenwen Liu and co-authors create new membrane-attacking antibacterials in a 2026 study. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus shrugs off many standard drugs, so the team built a family of phthalazine-based quaternary ammonium salts, compounds 2a through 2v, whose chain length could be tuned. Lab tests weighed killing power, safety, and how the best compound works.

Compound 2n led the family, stopping S. aureus, its resistant form, and two other species at 2 μg/mL in the minimum inhibitory tests reported, while sparing red blood cells up to far higher levels. It killed fast, resisted breakdown, and slowed biofilms, and probes showed torn membranes leaking cell contents, with DNA binding as a possible second hit.
pmc-13329979:
Alison Carroll and colleagues show light-driven storage of hydrogen in propane in a 2026 study. Storing hydrogen in chemical bonds avoids high pressure tanks. Propane is cheap and widely available, so the team tested turning propylene into propane at room temperature and pressure with a light-powered catalyst.

The catalyst pairs aluminium light catchers with titanium oxide and single platinum atoms. Light at 450 and 800 nm both drove strong propane output in the reported tests. Theory showed that light-made carriers at either colour hold enough energy for both reaction steps, splitting hydrogen and adding it across the carbon bond. Paired with earlier light-driven release, the cycle could store and free hydrogen under mild conditions.
pmc-13330479:
Pengyu Zhao and Shuai Geng pool studies on pharmacist care in China amid a shift from dispensing to patient care in a 2026 meta-analysis. Searches ran across eight databases to April 2026 for trials and comparison studies of pharmacist work such as prescription review and counselling. Bias was checked with standard tools.

In total, 32 studies entered the pool, with only 5 randomised trials among them. Pharmacist input linked to more single-drug antibiotic use and more sound prescriptions, and to fewer irrational prescriptions in the reported odds values. Spread between studies was wide, which limits exactness. The authors call the gains promising but early, and urge strong trials with patient-centred outcomes.
pmc-13330579:
Yi Zhang and colleagues trace the family history of STAYGREEN genes in tobacco plants in a 2026 study. Those genes steer chlorophyll breakdown, which drives leaf yellowing, maturity, and crop quality. The team compared gene copies across flowering plants, with focus on Nicotiana, whose doubled genome history may have expanded the family.

Family trees placed tobacco copies inside a conserved flowering plant lineage, with extra copies matching the doubled genome past in the reported analysis. Gene activity differed across tissues. Core catalytic parts stayed tightly conserved, while end regions varied by lineage. Most copies kept signals that send the protein to chloroplasts, though strength varied. The work frames how leaf ageing stays stable yet flexible.
pmc-13333279:
Jean Pierre Díaz-Paz and co-authors present a labeled dataset in 2026 for cleaning speckle noise from Sentinel-1 radar images. Radar pictures are grainy by nature, and training smart filters requires matched noisy and clean examples, which are hard to build honestly.

The dataset holds 512 by 512 pixel radar tiles in both VV and VH polarizations, gathered worldwide through an automated Python and Google Earth Engine workflow with random sampling and quality filtering. For each spot, cleaner reference images were made by averaging stacks of 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 passes, letting users study how averaging depth affects speckle removal. Land cover maps from ESA WorldCover v200 and a metadata file ride along, and benchmark scores including ENL, MSE, SSIM, and PSNR are supplied for sample tiles. The set is hosted on Mendeley Data as a reproducible training resource.
pmc-13333679:
Thomas Buttgereit and a large international team report on the first two years of the Chronic Angioedema Registry, known as CARE. Launched in October 2023, the registry gathers clinical and patient-reported data on recurrent angioedema of any type during routine care.

By December 2025, 550 patients had enrolled at 23 centers spread across 18 countries, meeting its early milestones on time. Hereditary angioedema and mast cell related forms were among the diagnoses tracked. A survey of physicians in the specialist center network explored why centers join or hold back, and how communication could improve. The report shows a global registry for a rare swelling condition can grow steadily, while naming practical barriers that slow wider participation.
pmc-13333779:
Jin Han and co-authors looked at ligustilide, a natural compound from Angelica sinensis and Ligusticum chuanxiong, for central nervous system disorders in a 2026 article. Ligustilide draws interest for calming inflammation, fighting oxidation, and protecting nerves.

Three sources were searched for studies through October 2025, and 55 original studies were left after screening. Evidence links the compound to help in ischemic stroke, vascular dementia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, traumatic brain injury, and anxiety disorders. Its effects run through pathways including PI3K/Akt, MAPK, NF-kB, and Nrf2/ARE, lowering oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, and mitochondrial failure. The review also covers how the body absorbs and clears ligustilide and what safety data exist, sketching what stands between the compound and clinical use.
pmc-13334079:
Jeong-Ah Yoon and co-authors tested a candidate probiotic strain, Pediococcus acidilactici MBEL10321, in a 2026 study pairing lab tests with genome sequencing. The strain came from Nuruk, a classic Korean fermentation starter.

In culture the strain survived acid and bile salts well and held back several pathogens, beating two control strains, among them Listeria monocytogenes, Bacillus cereus, Escherichia coli O157:H7, and Staphylococcus aureus. It showed no blood-cell-breaking activity. Its genome spans 2,044,106 base pairs with 1,980 protein-coding genes, and screens found no virulence factors, no drug resistance genes, and no transferable plasmid replicons. The paired safety and function evidence backs the strain as a probiotic candidate for food or supplement use.
pmc-13334979:
Chenhui He and co-authors built an ultrasound-driven sticky hydrogel for infected wounds in a 2026 materials study. Long-term infected wounds resist treatment because bacteria persist, tissue states vary, and antibiotics lose ground.

Their hydrogel, PA-ZA, embeds tiny composites of ZIF-8 studded with nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots in a polyacrylamide-alginate base. Set ultrasound, first at kilohertz then megahertz speeds, triggers tissue sticking, pushes nanoparticles through skin, and switches on sound-driven production of reactive oxygen species that kill bacteria. The gel proved body-safe and sped cell migration and blood vessel growth in vitro. In infected full-thickness wounds in animals, switching it on lowered bacterial burden, sped the end of inflammation, and hastened repair, with similar benefit in a deeper infection model.
pmc-13335479:
Patricia C Hernandez and co-authors showed how small molecules selectively block the DNA-chewing enzyme TREX1 in a 2026 structural biology study. TREX1 clears stray cytoplasmic DNA; losing it causes autoimmune disease, while blocking it in cancer cells can wake anti-tumor immunity.

X-ray crystallography revealed the inhibitors sitting in the active site, competing with the end of the DNA substrate and hydrogen-bonding to a conserved glutamate. Binding also locks a tyrosine, Tyr129, into an alternative pose that cannot grip DNA and opens a deep hydrophobic pocket that cradles part of the drug. That pocket explains why the compounds spare the close relative TREX2 and viral cousins. The structures give medicinal chemists a blueprint for selective TREX1 blockers.
pmc-13336379:
Jianya Luo and co-authors found a compound that resensitizes a dangerous hospital pathogen to an old antibiotic in a 2026 microbiology study. Acinetobacter baumannii shrugs off most drugs, and colistin, a last-resort option, is losing ground too.

A structure-based virtual screen against the bacterium's lipopolysaccharide transport system produced a somatostatin-like peptide, C4. Alone it barely kills, but with colistin the synergy is strong. Lipid and gene analyses showed C4 remodels the membrane, selectively building up phosphatidylglycerol and raising expression of mlaC, a phospholipid transport gene. Deleting mlaC erased both the lipid change and the synergy, while extra copies strengthened it. The work reveals membrane lipid management as a lever for rescuing colistin therapy.
pmc-13336779:
Zhaoqiang Jiang and a large team connect night shift work to higher blood pressure in a 2026 study of people and mice. Shift work scrambles the body clock, and the authors point to failing mitochondria, the cell's power units, as the main link. Mice on simulated night shifts developed higher pressure and disturbed clock genes such as PER1 and BMAL1.

The shifted mice also showed power-unit damage and oxidative stress. Human night workers showed the same pattern: longer shift exposure tracked with higher systolic and diastolic pressure and with disturbed clock and mitochondrial markers. The shared pathway helps explain the heart risks of night work and may guide ways to blunt them.
pmc-13336979:
Yiming Fu and colleagues study why windows for imaging the living mouse brain cloud over in a 2026 methods review and study. Thinned skull and clearing methods let multiphoton microscopes watch brain cells over time, yet image quality fades fast. Systematic tests with adaptive optics compared window types for lifespan, sharpness, and distortion.

Progressive skull regrowth emerged as the core limit across all types, steadily blurring signal and resolution. A local glucocorticoid delivery method stretched good performance to one month. Sealing the window with a drug-loaded hydrogel suppressed regrowth while keeping optics clear. The findings give labs a practical route to month-long, high-fidelity brain imaging and explain what ends it.
pmc-13339779:
Chia-Heng Lin and colleagues compare victim choices among sexual offenders with and without severe mental illness in a 2026 forensic study. Court-referred evaluations in Taiwan from 2009 to 2022 supplied the records. Understanding pattern differences may sharpen risk assessment.

Among 86 men, 21 had psychotic or bipolar disorders and 65 did not as reported. Offenders with severe illness more often had adult and stranger victims in the reported comparisons, with odds near fourfold for each in adjusted models. Substance disorders were more common without severe illness. Small subgroup size urges caution, but distinct patterns suggest assessment should weigh diagnosis alongside victim history.
pmc-13341179:
How nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor blockers protect the kidney from inside is reviewed by Eun Sil Koh and colleagues in 2026. Drugs such as finerenone cut albuminuria and improve outcomes in chronic kidney disease, but the exact vessel-level mechanics remain partly unclear.

The review gathers clinical and lab evidence on sodium handling and pressure inside the glomerulus. These drugs mildly increase sodium excretion, ease aldosterone-driven tightening of outgoing vessels, and restore feedback signals that guard against overfiltration. Whether they beat older steroidal blockers at fixing hyperfiltration is unproven. Their edge may instead be safety and tolerability that let patients stay on treatment.
pmc-13341479:
A gene that pushes colon cancer cells toward iron-driven death is studied by Haiying Sun and co-investigators in a 2026 analysis. RBMS3 had unclear significance, so the team mined pan-cancer and colon adenocarcinoma datasets, then validated findings in lab cultures.

Tumors expressed less RBMS3 than normal tissue, and low levels meant worse survival, supporting a tumor-suppressor role. Expression tracked with tumor stage, and adding it to staging improved a prognostic nomogram. Cell work showed M2 macrophages suppress RBMS3 through STAT3 signaling, weakening ferroptosis. The pathway names both a biomarker and a possible lever for treatment.
pmc-13346079:
Joyce Jebet and co-authors systematically review tools for screening mothers' mental health across Africa in 2026. Pregnancy and new motherhood carry heavy mental burdens that clinics rarely test for. The team gathered African studies from 2014 to 2024 to see which questionnaires actually get used and how they perform.

The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale dominated the shelf, with the PHQ-9 common in Ethiopia and the SRQ-20 favored in West Africa. Studies clustered in South Africa, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, with samples from 37 to 3,311 women. Disorders stay common yet under-detected, and the authors push for screening folded into routine mother-and-child visits, better staff training, and tools fitted to local culture.
pmc-13347079:
Juan Huang and colleagues test whether walking patterns can flag thinking decline in Parkinson disease, in a diagnostic study published in 2026. Patients classed as normal, subjectively declining, or mildly impaired did timed up-and-go walks, both plain and with a second task. While a wearable system recorded 209 motion measures for each trial.

Extra measures captured how much the added mental task cost each walker. Several learning models were trained to sort the three groups, checked with cross-validation and a held-out set. Importance tools were used to show which gait features drove each call. The aim is a low-burden clinic test that spots early decline without long paper testing.
pmc-13347379:
Aarti Gupta and colleagues characterise a doped bismuth ferrite powder for cleaning toxic chromium from water with sunlight, in a study published in 2026. Praseodymium and cobalt were added into the crystal without forming second phases, shrinking grain size. A combined heat-based instrument read thermal flow, energy gap, and charge lifetime in one pass.

Moderate doping improved heat flow and charge separation, while heavy doping added trap sites that sped charge loss and slowed heat spread in the reported measures. Under plain sunlight the best powder cut the harmful chromium form by about 96 percent within 120 minutes, turning it toward a safer form. Linked structure and heat data guide tuning of such cleaners.
pmc-13349779:
Chao Gong and colleagues reported a cohort study in 2026 on whether HDL cholesterol levels predict outcomes in non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. They followed 297 patients who had cardiac magnetic resonance scans between 2017 and 2024.

Over a median 35 months of follow-up, 41 patients reached the main endpoint of death or heart transplant, and 97 reached a wider endpoint adding heart failure readmission. Lower HDL cholesterol was linked to higher risk in adjusted models, and patients with higher levels stayed event-free longer. Adjusting for estimated pulmonary artery pressure weakened the link somewhat. The authors propose HDL cholesterol as a cheap, routine marker for sorting risk in these patients.
pmc-13349979:
Jiahuan Tang and colleagues fine-tuned a multimodal GPT-4o model in 2026 to write diagnostic impressions for a tricky breast MRI finding. The finding is called non-mass enhancement. Earlier work showed public language models handled breast lesion grading poorly. This lesion type had never been singled out.

Records from 229 patients supplied scan images, reports, and clinical histories. Six model versions were built. Some were untuned. Others trained on text alone, or on images plus text. Their impressions were compared with three radiologists of differing experience. Other experts then graded the outputs. The study tests whether targeted training lifts AI reporting to a clinically useful level.
pmc-13350179:
Jiale Huang and colleagues used combined gene and chemistry profiling in 2026 to explain why blueberries fail after years in the same soil in Dalian, China. Soil was sampled around roots and away from them after zero, two, four, and six years of continuous cropping.

Microbial diversity fell steadily with cropping years, especially near roots, and communities separated clearly by period. Helpful microbe groups thinned while stress-tolerant ones grew, and soil chemistry showed accumulating compounds harmful to the plants themselves. The picture blames a sickened soil community plus self-poisoning as twin drivers of the decline, pointing growers toward soil restoration rather than more fertiliser.
pmc-13350379:
Chun-Ka Wong and a multicentre team reported Asia-Pacific experience in 2026 with cutting heart valve leaflets during catheter valve replacement to stop the new valve blocking a coronary artery. The registry covered consecutive patients at seven centres from 2019 to 2026 treated with two techniques, one slicing the leaflet and one burning through it with a radiofrequency needle.

Success meant completing the cut and implant with no coronary blockage, emergency surgery, stroke, or death. Most published proof comes from North America and Europe. Real-world results from this region tell local teams whether the demanding trick works in their own patients and systems.
pmc-13350479:
Ningbo Yin and colleagues pooled ultrasound strain measurements of the heart's right side in a 2026 meta-analysis, aiming to set normal values. Speckle tracking follows tiny heart muscle patterns to measure how the right atrium and ventricle deform, but healthy ranges were never standardised.

Studies of healthy adults published up to July 2025 were gathered from three databases. Pooled values covered ventricle strain and strain rates plus three phases of atrial strain, and subgroup checks probed race, sex, age, and the software and machine used. Reference numbers that account for equipment differences let clinicians tell true right-heart weakness from measurement noise.
pmc-13350679:
Yuhan Fan and co-authors used deep learning in 2026 to regenerate radiotherapy positioning images that clinics normally throw away. Cone-beam projections for head and neck cancer patients are bulky, so they are discarded after building the three-dimensional scan, yet later checks may need them.

Working from 50 patients, they first computed synthetic X-ray views from the stored scans, then trained networks to convert those into realistic projections. Three network designs were compared, with tests on scatter correction, scan sharpness, and training size. Regenerating discarded images from kept data could rescue old treatment records for review and research.
pmc-13351679:
Chenjia Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 case report on emergency non-heart surgery in a child with Eisenmenger syndrome. The condition marks late, untreated congenital heart disease with fixed high lung pressure, reversed blood flow, and low oxygen. An 11-year-old girl needed urgent surgery under general anaesthesia for a twisted right ovary.

Her lung artery pressure was 105/49 mmHg, and anaesthesia used etomidate, midazolam, vecuronium, and sufentanil, then propofol, remifentanil, and sevoflurane. Readings stayed stable during surgery, but a lung pressure crisis followed with fast heart rhythm, low blood pressure, and low oxygen. Amiodarone, treprostinil, bicarbonate, and oxygen restored normal rhythm, and she went home on day 11.
pmc-13351879:
Sen Lin and colleagues report a 2026 surgical technique for easing pressure on nerves at two neighbouring lower back levels through a single small cut. Endoscopic decompression is a key low-impact option for narrowed spinal canals. Reaching two levels often needs several cuts, so the team set out to do both through one opening.

Working over the top to the far side, they trimmed bone and removed thickened ligament at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels. Surgery took 115 minutes through a 0.7-cm cut with six brief X-ray checks. Pain scores fell from 8 to 0 by follow-up at 2 and 6 months, and the patient walked within 24 hours. The case shows the one-cut route is workable.
pmc-13352479:
Feiyang Liu leads a 2026 project building a scale for the healthy mental effects of exercise in Chinese college students. Existing tools capture only general or narrow mental outcomes after exercise. Scale items were drafted from theory, prior work, interviews, and open surveys, then tested in staged samples.

An early sample of 612 students shaped the item set, and a formal sample of 945 students checked reliability and validity. The final scale holds 55 items in five parts: emotional feelings, self-cognition, frustration coping, control and social efficacy, and social interaction. Variance explained per part ranged from 62.546 to 73.711 percent. A retest group of 597 students after 1 month supported stability over time.
pmc-13353379:
Xiaoyu Ma leads a 2026 review of oxidative enzymes that break down plant biomass. Plant walls are mostly lignocellulose, a tough mix that resists biological dismantling. The review maps how microbes, mainly filamentous fungi, attack with redox enzymes, including newly found AA families.

Laccases and lignin-active peroxidases lead lignin attack, while lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases and their redox partners cut sugar chains. Hydrogen peroxide acts as a shared middleman whose supply and use are tightly timed and placed. Non-enzyme radical systems join the synergy. Structural computing sharpens the picture, and the authors argue the knowledge can speed next-generation biorefineries for a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13355279:
Mohamad Abou Chakra and co-authors studied in 2026 whether age changes how well two bladder treatments work for high-risk bladder cancer that has not reached the muscle. One treatment uses a weakened germ, BCG, placed in the bladder, and the other uses two chemotherapy drugs in sequence. Records covered 401 patients treated from 2011 to 2024.

Age, split into bands from under 60 to 80 and over, did not clearly predict cancer return in either group. Older patients on BCG showed a mild trend toward more returns, while older patients on the drug pair held steady over time. The authors say the trend in the BCG group deserves more study.
pmc-13355779:
Romana Erblich and co-authors studied in 2026 when traumatic cardiac arrest happens outside hospital and how timing shapes survival. Using records from thirteen helicopter rescue services from 2010 to 2019, they split cases by when the heart stopped: before crews arrived, after arrival at the scene, or during transport.

Nine of ten arrests had already occurred at the scene before the first unit arrived. Survival was highest when arrest came after crews arrived or during helicopter transport. Still, lasting return of circulation was possible even in early arrests, above all when the first heart rhythm was not flat. The authors say resuscitation in such cases is worthwhile.
pmc-13355879:
Abdul Nadim Asil and co-authors review in 2026 how studies define and use two key terms for personal response to ionizing radiation. Radiosensitivity and radiosusceptibility are often mixed up, though they point to distinct ideas: cell-level damage response versus risk of tissue harm and cancer. The team searched two databases and screened studies under standard review rules.

Radiosensitivity was mostly measured by DNA damage and repair tests, while susceptibility tied to normal tissue harm and cancer risk, and was named far less often. Personal response varied widely in all studies. The authors call for clearer definitions and shared methods to support personal radiotherapy and fair risk judgments.
pmc-13357079:
Wei Shi and co-authors mapped in 2026 how mitophagy, the cleanup of worn-out mitochondria, shapes the tumor surroundings in osteosarcoma, an aggressive bone cancer of teens. Single-cell gene data let them group the many cell types by their cleanup activity. They then traced cell-to-cell signals, gene networks, and links to patient survival.

Cleanup-active support cells sent strong blood-vessel growth signals, and cleanup-linked killer T cells looked worn out and less able to fight. Tumors rich in these cell types meant poorer survival, and the patterns also hinted at response to immune therapy. The authors suggest blocking, not boosting, this cleanup could aid treatment.
pmc-13358579:
Qinling Jiang and co-authors test a clever scan trick in a 2026 study on lung adenocarcinoma. Doctors now grade this cancer under a newer system that sorts patients by outlook more sharply. The team asked whether computer analysis of CT scans could predict the grade before surgery, using artificial images sharpened by a generative network.

They compared models built on these enhanced images with models built on normal scans, using patients from two Chinese hospitals. The sharper images were meant to reveal fine tumor texture that plain scans blur. If scan-based grading proves reliable, it could help surgeons plan the size of the operation before the first cut.
pmc-13359879:
Xukai Yang and co-authors measure three key elements across mountain forests in a 2026 study. On the southern slopes of China's Qilian Mountains, forests anchor regional ecology and nutrient cycling. The team compared carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in leaves, branches, and forest floor material for six common tree species.

Broad-leaved species generally held richer nutrient levels, while conifers stored more carbon per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus. As plant material became forest floor litter, nitrogen and phosphorus fell and the carbon ratios rose, signs that trees pull nutrients back before shedding leaves and that litter quality differs by species. The patterns guide how managers read nutrient health in these forests.
pmc-13361979:
Yoshihito Saijo and co-authors report a 2026 case of heart infection with a puzzling twist. A 24-year-old man with eczema came in with fever and painful skin spots on his hands and feet. Blood tests grew Staphylococcus aureus, and scans found a large, mobile growth on his tricuspid valve, which had torn and leaked badly. Right-sided heart infections usually send infected clots to the lungs, not the body.

His body-wide spots suggested infected material was reaching the left side of the heart. A bubble test showed blood crossing from right to left only after a straining maneuver, and none at rest. No fixed hole between the heart chambers explained it. The team traced the route to a temporary shunt within the lungs, a rare path that let the infection spread system-wide.
pmc-13362079:
Blanca T M Spee and co-authors tested whether Parkinson's disease changes how people judge art in a 2026 study. Parkinson's is now seen as a whole-body disorder touching perception, emotion, and reward. Art programs for patients usually focus on making art, not on viewing it. The team asked whether looking at art, and rating it, works differently in these patients.

Eighty-seven people with Parkinson's and 49 matched healthy controls rated 36 artworks online. They scored liking and beauty and reported emotional and color-linked responses. The study's verdict, reflected in its title, is that aesthetic judgment is largely preserved in Parkinson's. That finding suggests art-viewing programs need little content adaptation for these audiences, a hopeful note for museums and therapists planning inclusive sessions.
pmc-13362179:
Qiang Gao and co-authors used machine learning to predict long breathing support after heart surgery in preterm babies in a 2026 study. The surgery closes a ductus, a blood vessel that should shut after birth but stays open in many early babies. Some babies then need a breathing machine for a long time. The team reviewed 271 infants born at 32 weeks or less, treated from 2021 to 2025.

Babies were split at six days of support: 150 came off sooner and 121 needed longer. Birth weight, age at birth, weight at surgery, duct size, and breathing severity all differed between the groups. A method called SHAP showed which factors pushed each prediction. Flagging high-risk babies early can help teams plan care and counsel parents.
pmc-13362479:
Jan den Boer and co-authors describe a 2026 study of a playful device meant to cut food waste in school canteens. Two primary schools and one kindergarten took part. The device lets children vote with balls after lunch, and the emptier a child's returned plate, the more their vote weighs, which nudges pupils to take only what they will eat.

Plate waste fell at all three sites while the device ran, for both soup and main dishes. Children ate a larger share of what they were served. poems-pg679: Verse by Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, the Black abolitionist, suffragist, and novelist whose pen served every freedom struggle of the 1800s. rehearsall-elizabeth-stile-1579:
Elizabeth Stile stands accused in A Rehearsall both Straung and True, a Windsor witch pamphlet from 1579. Hainous and horrible acts, confessions, and executions fill its black-letter pages. Stile and her fellows were charged with killings by sorcery in one of the earliest English witchcraft pamphlets to reach the press.

Cheap print carried the scare to markets and alehouses across the shire. Examinations before magistrates give the tale its grim, vivid detail. Belief, fear, and malice braid together in the record it preserves. The pamphlet marks the birth of the witch scare in English print, raw evidence of how neighbors turned on neighbors in terror.
salmon-horae-mathematicae-1679:
William Salmon was a London empiric, an unlicensed medical practitioner who sold remedies and wrote tirelessly on his trades. His Horae Mathematicae, seu Urania, published in 1679, is his astrological and medical miscellany. The title joins the hours of math to Urania, muse of the heavens.

Salmon packs the book with rules for charts, cures, and the choice of lucky times for bleeding, planting, and dosing. He writes for practitioners like himself, who needed the art to pay its way in the marketplace. The miscellany shows the working library of a seventeenth-century medical astrologer in one crowded volume.
sbe-03-shu-king-legge-1879:

At its center stands the Shû King, the Book of Documents, a set of speeches and records ascribed to China's earliest rulers.

Speeches, charges, and counsels in the Shû King present the model kings of old China and their ministers. Legge added the opening parts of other classics and full notes on hard passages. The volume brought one of China's oldest books into a world series of sacred texts. It helped place Chinese classics beside the Bible and the Vedas for English readers.
scientific-studies-or-practical-in-contr: Scientific Studies, 1879. The practical pursuits. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
stile-rehearsall-abingdon-1579:
Elizabeth Stile lived at Windsor and faced a witchcraft charge in 1579. A Rehearsall both Straung and True tells how she was questioned and what she confessed. The pamphlet covers the Abingdon proceedings and belongs to the first wave of English witch prints.

Its title promises a tale both strange and true, the selling cry of the age's cheap news. Behind the cry sit hard facts: quarrels with neighbors could grow into a charge that cost a life. The record lets readers watch blame harden, step by step, into proof. Few early pamphlets show that grim path so clearly.
strindberg-the-red-room-1879:
August Strindberg wrote The Red Room in 1879, here in Ellie Schleussner's English translation of 1913. The novel that made Strindberg famous is the first modern Swedish novel in the judgment of critics. Arvid Falk, a young idealist, quits a clerk's desk to write and starves among Stockholm bohemians. The Red Room of Berns restaurant hosts actors, painters, and journalists trading wit, debt, and dashed hopes nightly. Crooked companies, bought newspapers, and charitable frauds expose a city where money mocks merit at every turn. Falk's sister-in-law, his brother the shopkeeper, and a sea of spear-carriers fill the social canvas wide. Schleussner's version gave English readers the novel that remade Swedish prose fiction in 1879.
taylor-greeks-goths-runes-1879:

Taylor traced each rune sign back to a Greek form and told how the script may have moved north. He drew on trade routes and old carved finds to back his case. Right or wrong, his book was a turn in the study of where runes began. It also shows how bold the Victorian taste for grand schemes ran.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Book twenty-nine: the very long tale is nearing its final end. The old rover prepares his farewell to the reader. He looks back on loves and perils. One more chapter now, and then rest.

Article by article, Luther states justification by faith alone without compromise, and marks which doctrines could never be traded away and which matters allowed discussion. Short, sharp, and unyielding, the text shows the Reformation's founder at his most combative. un-ga-res-a-69-79:

The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons bars or bounds arms judged to cause needless harm or to strike without aim. Its five added pacts cover shards that no scan can find, mines and traps, fire arms, laser arms that blind, and the shells war leaves behind.

The text recalls the vote of the year before on the pact. It notes the 2013 meeting of the pact's parties in Geneva, and the yearly talks on the mines pact held the same week. States are urged to join the pact and to put its bounds to work.

un-sc-res-1379:
Children caught in armed conflict were the focus of a Security Council resolution adopted on 20 November 2001. The Secretary-General had reported in September 2001 on the working of resolution 1314.

The Council pledged to give the fullest attention to children's protection in every matter before it. It said it was ready to write child protection terms into peacekeeping mandates and to keep child protection advisers in missions. Parties to conflict were called to spare children and to let aid staff reach them. The Council said it would weigh the effect of sanctions on children when it used Article 41 measures. It also vowed to study links between war and the illegal trade in resources.
un-sc-res-1479:

A small staff would support the special representative on political, legal, civil, police, and military matters. At its heart stood a military liaison group, starting at 26 officers and able to rise by 50 more. The Council renewed its call on all Ivorian forces to apply the agreement fully and without delay. It pressed again for grave rights abusers to face justice.
un-sc-res-1579:

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms and travel measures for twelve months. The timber measures also run twelve months, with a review at six. un-sc-res-1679:

The Council warns that anyone who blocks the deal could face travel bans or frozen assets. It backs a shift from the African Union force to a United Nations operation, starting with a joint study team within one week.
un-sc-res-1779:

un-sc-res-179:

Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Republic agreed to pay the costs, over two months, of the UN observation work the terms required. It urges the parties to keep to the terms in full and to avoid any act that would raise tension in the area.

Children caught in war are the subject of Resolution 1379. It passed by a full vote on 20 November 2001. War harms children in wide and deep ways, the Council said. The harm casts a long shadow on peace and growth. States bear the chief duty to shield children. All who fight must obey the laws made to guard them.

The text's keenest tool was a public list. The UN chief was asked to name, in his next report, the groups that recruit or use child troops. The list would draw on wars the Council deals with, and on other dire cases too. That list grew teeth in later years. Groups named on it face strong pressure to free the children they hold.

Resolution 1479, adopted unanimously on 13 May 2003, plants a UN flag in Côte d'Ivoire's peace process. Ivorian parties had signed the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement in January, and a government of national reconciliation had finally met in April with all political groups present. West African and French forces were already on the ground trying to hold a ceasefire.

The Council created a UN mission for Côte d'Ivoire, called MINUCI, for an initial six months. Its job was to help the Ivorian parties carry out the peace agreement, and it included a small military component working alongside the French and regional forces. A special representative received full authority over all UN activity in the country.

Liberia's sanctions are renewed with an eye to lifting them in Resolution 1579, adopted on 21 December 2004. Disarmament was complete and the ceasefire held. But the National Transitional Government still lacked control of the timber areas. Diamond certification was only being prepared. Associates of the former regime were accused of undermining stability. UNMIL's deployment had improved security.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms and travel measures for 12 months and the timber measures for 12 months. It renews the diamond measures for six months only. A review after three months aims at lifting them once an effective, internationally verifiable Certificate of Origin regime exists. It confirms the Resolution 1532 (2004) asset freeze remains in force. The Panel of Experts is re-established until 21 June 2005, with a preliminary report on diamonds due by 21 March 2005 and a full report by 7 June 2005.

The Darfur Peace Agreement, signed in Abuja in May 2006, is the pivot of Resolution 1679, adopted on 16 May 2006. The African Union Mission in the Sudan, AMIS, had cut large-scale violence in Darfur. The African Union had decided that a UN operation should follow AMIS. Sudan and Chad had grown hostile toward each other, adding risk to the region.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council calls on the parties to keep their promises under the peace deal without delay and urges those who have not signed to sign. It warns it may use travel bans and asset freezes against anyone who breaks or blocks the deal. It backs the African Union's plan to move from AMIS to a UN operation and calls for a joint AU-UN assessment mission within one week. Advice on the new force's shape and cost is due within a week of that mission's return.

Some guides bill this text as the birth of the Darfur hybrid force. It is not. That force was set up two months past, in July 2007. This text keeps a probe team on Sudan's bans. War still scarred Darfur. Bomb raids from the air drew fresh blame. Talks in Libya were set for 27 October. Resolution 1779 passed on 28 September 2007.

The sleuth team's term grew to 15 October 2008. It would brief by 29 March 2008. Its work had to mesh with the peace forces on the ground. It would judge if raids and bans breaches had eased. States and UN arms were told to help the team in full. The force on the ground gets warm words in the text. But the act here is time for the watchers, not the birth of a force.

A United Nations observation operation in Yemen is set up on 11 June 1963. Civil war had drawn in outside powers, and Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Republic had accepted matching terms to disengage. Both governments had also agreed to pay the costs of the observation work for two months.

The Secretary-General is asked to establish the observation operation as he had defined it in his April report. The parties are urged to observe the disengagement terms in full and to avoid any step that would raise tension in the area. The Secretary-General is to report on how the decision is being carried out. The mission became the United Nations Yemen Observation Mission.

Nepal's peace process reaches another renewal in Resolution 1879, adopted on 23 July 2009. The Constituent Assembly chosen in April 2008 was writing a new constitution. The government and the Unified Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) had agreed to start discharging and settling disqualified Maoist army personnel, including minors. Nepal asked for six more months of the UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN.

The Council renews UNMIN until 23 January 2010. It urges all parties to use UNMIN's help to finish the leftover parts of its mandate by that date. It agrees with the Secretary-General that the arms monitoring setup was a short-term measure that cannot go on forever. It asks Nepal to shape the terms that will let UNMIN finish and withdraw, and seeks a report by 30 October 2009 on progress toward those terms.

Afghanistan under the Taliban is the subject of Resolution 2679, adopted on 16 March 2023. The Council expressed concern that the Taliban had made no progress on the expectations set for them. It stressed the full and equal participation of women in public life. Respect for the rights of women, children, and minorities was also stressed.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to carry out an independent assessment of Afghanistan. The full assessment was due by 17 November 2023. It would be prepared after talks with Afghan political actors and other interested parties. The study had to offer practical advice for the way forward. Political, aid, and development actors, inside and outside the United Nations, needed a joined-up approach. The goal was to meet the country's current challenges together.

The Secretary-General's mission on Western Sahara reported back in the autumn of 1975, but the situation stayed grave. Spain had written to the Council again on 1 November. Resolution 379, adopted by consensus on 2 November 1975, follows up the mission sent under Resolution 377.

The Council urged all the parties concerned to avoid one-sided action. Any step that might raise tension in the area further was to be avoided. The Secretary-General was asked to continue his consultations with the parties. He also had to step them up and report back as soon as he could. His report would help the Council decide what further measures might be needed. The text kept the matter firmly on the Council's agenda.

War between Iran and Iraq had just erupted in September 1980. Iraq's forces had crossed into Iran days earlier. Resolution 479, adopted unanimously on 28 September 1980, was the Council's first response. The agenda item was bluntly titled the situation between Iran and Iraq.

Both countries were called on to stop using force at once. They had to settle their dispute peacefully, under law and justice. Mediation offers should be accepted, the text urges. Other states were warned to show restraint. Nothing should widen the conflict. The Secretary-General's good offices won support. He had to report back within forty-eight hours. The war, tragically, ran for eight more years.

Arms control paperwork moved one step forward on 17 January 1950. The General Assembly had passed a resolution in December 1949 on the regulation and general reduction of conventional arms and armed forces. Resolution 79 does a single thing with that text. The Council decided to transmit the Assembly's resolution to the Commission for Conventional Armaments. The commission would study it further, in line with its own plan of work. That transmission is the whole content of the resolution.

A judge of the International Court of Justice died in February 1995, leaving his seat empty. Judge Roberto Ago, named in the text, had died on 24 February. The rest of his term had to be filled under the Court's Statute. Resolution 979, adopted on 9 March 1995, fixes the date of the vote.

Under Article 14 of the Statute, the Security Council sets the date of such an election. The Council chose 21 June 1995. The vote would take place at a meeting of the Security Council. A meeting of the General Assembly, during its forty-ninth session, would vote on the same occasion. Both bodies have to agree on a judge for the appointment to be made. The decision is one of the small, regular acts that keep the World Court at full strength.
